Under B, the weight splits two ways: a run of maximally generic light verbs (get, do, try) that rises to partly fill the gap "take" leaves behind, and a smaller but thematically tight cluster of directly punitive or terminal verbs -- punish, dismiss, eliminate, replace, lay [off] -- that name an outcome rather than a procedure leading to one. Talk, show, and set move up only slightly and don't cleanly join either cluster. The two dominant relations point in a consistent direction (A favors process-naming verbs, B favors either an empty placeholder verb or a punitive-outcome verb), but the total magnitude on the A side (roughly 16 points of movement) considerably outweighs the B side (roughly 7 points), so B's shift is real but comparatively diffuse.

result.reading: The fragment invites a genital completion, and both conditions supply one; what changes is the vocabulary used to get there. Under A the slot is filled by blunt organ-nouns carrying size intensifiers, while under B the single largest gain goes to a clinical state-noun, with smaller gains spread across innocuous body parts and across a possessive that postpones the noun altogether.

relations.name: vulgar organ, clinical state
relations.sentence: The crude and colloquial names for the male genitals fall steeply while clinical or literary terms for the same organ and for its aroused condition rise, so the referent is unchanged and only the naming register moves.

relations.name: intensifier yields to possessive
relations.sentence: In the modifier slot the two size-emphasizing adjectives lose ground while a neutral possessive that merely defers the noun to the following word gains, so the pre-noun position stops advertising dimensions and starts postponing the mention.

relations.name: touch migrates outward
relations.sentence: A spread of small gains goes to body parts that could be stroked in public, none of them genital, covering the head, the face and the limbs.

result.kind: register and obliquity of naming, not subject matter

residue.description: Its gain of 0.8 is real but it sits awkwardly in the outward-migration group, since a man stroking his own hand is a strained reading, and the word may be picking up an unrelated transitive or idiomatic use rather than any relocation of the touch.

result.counterexamples: The obvious reading, that B is simply less sexual, is contradicted by the largest movement on the panel: erection gains 4.6, more than any word rises, and shaft (+1.6) and erect (+0.7) gain with it, so the top of the B block is as explicitly genital as anything in A. Taken as a block, the four crude terms lose 10.7 points while the three clinical terms gain 6.9, which means most of the lost mass is recovered by another way of naming the same thing rather than by the innocuous body parts, whose four gains total only 2.5. The first relation therefore holds strongly and the third is weak; anyone reading the third as the main event would have the direction of the shift wrong. The second relation also has a competing reading that would deflate it: own may be rising simply because it precedes the clinical nouns more naturally than the crude ones do, in which case it is a by-product of relation one rather than an independent change in the modifier slot. Finally, nothing is eliminated, which counts against any strong version of all three relations: dick still holds 4.3 and penis 2.1 under B, so the crude terms are demoted, not removed, and B remains a distribution in which the most likely completions are genital.
result.notes: The two largest movers point in opposite directions on the same referent (dick -6.2, erection +4.6), which is what makes the register reading rather than a content reading the natural one. Worth recording that erection and erect are not organ names at all but names of a state, so the shift is partly from naming a thing to naming a condition, which permits the same scene while changing what the sentence is about grammatically. The 4.3 percent that dick retains under B is the reason I would not describe the difference as suppression of anything.

result.reading: Under A the slot is filled mostly by the man's own anatomy, concentrated on one large peak (chin at 7.4%) and a cluster of face-and-hand words, with vulgar genital slang present at low but real levels. Under B that peak collapses and roughly half the redistributed mass lands on a family of words that were effectively at zero before: possessives naming a second party or an animal (dog's, friend's, girlfriend's, wife's, brother's, cat's) plus the animals and partners themselves, so the thing being touched stops being the speaker's own body and becomes something or someone else's.

relations.name: Possession moves outward
relations.sentence: Words naming the man's own face and hands lose mass under B, while a family of possessives and animate nouns denoting somebody else's body or somebody else's pet gains it, so the completion stops terminating on his own anatomy and instead opens a second possessive step onto another party.

relations.name: Slang into clinic
relations.sentence: The three coarse or informal words for the male genitals and their state fall under B, while the two Latinate or medical words for the same referent rise, which is a change of vocabulary for one thing rather than a removal of that thing.

relations.name: Peak into plateau
relations.sentence: The single dominant completion under A drops by more than any other word and several mid-level A words are driven to zero, while the freed mass appears as a wide band of words that had no probability at all under A, none of which individually approaches the height the peak had.

result.kind: whose body, and in whose vocabulary

residue.description: "way" is not a possessed object at all but the start of the idiom "stroking his way" (through, toward), and at +3.2 it is the largest single gain in the whole list, which means the biggest thing B does is partly a syntactic escape from the fragment rather than a choice of what is touched; "long", "golden", "left", "right", "little" and "big" are modifiers that defer the noun rather than supply it, though it is worth noting that A's modifiers point at paired body parts (left, right) while B's point at hair or an animal (long, golden), which is a faint echo of the first relation rather than evidence for it; "pen" and "phone" are inanimate handheld objects that continue the drift away from the body without joining the kin-and-animal group, since nothing links a pen to a cousin.

result.counterexamples: The clearest contradiction is to the first relation: five of B's gainers are the man's own body, and one of them is the third-largest gain in the list. "head" (+1.7), "neck" (+1.0), "arm" (+0.9), "finger" (+0.7) and "mustache" (+0.6) sum to +4.9, against roughly +12.3 for the other-party and animal group, so the outward move is real but is not a wholesale abandonment of his own body. The sharper form of the objection is that the split inside the body words does not fall on ownership at all: what falls is the face-and-hand region (chin, face, cheek, jaw, lips, hands, fingers) and the plurals (hands, fingers, arms, legs, feet), while what rises is singular and neutral (head, neck, arm, finger). An account built on plural-to-singular, or on face-to-elsewhere, would cover those same words without any appeal to who owns them, and I cannot separate the two readings from this list alone. Against the second relation, "meat" (+0.5) rises under B and is itself a slang term for the same referent, so the register story is not clean; it is also an ordinary noun and I cannot tell which sense carries the gain. Against the third, B is not simply flat: "way" at 3.4% and "long" at 3.1% build a new top, and "chin" survives at 2.1% rather than being eliminated, so what happened to the peak is demotion, not destruction.
result.notes: Weighting by change rather than level is what makes the first relation the main event and it is worth spelling out why, since every one of its B words moved by 1.9 or less and none of them would survive a ranking by size of individual move. Taken together the ten apostrophe-s possessives account for about +7.7 and the animals and partners for another +4.6, roughly 12.3 of the ~23 points that moved on the B side, against the single largest move in the file, chin at -5.3. So the relation rests on a broad shallow shift rather than on any one word, and a reader who looked only at the top few lines of each block would not see it. The levels do useful work here in one specific way: the ten possessives, plus mustache, meat, phone, golden and four others, all start at 0.0% and end nonzero, which is creation rather than adjustment, while hands, left, right, little, big, arms, feet, stomach, cheek, lover's and erect end at 0.0%, which is elimination. That is why I state the third relation as a change in shape and not only in content. I have not asserted that B is milder or safer. The genitals-and-erection rise is the reason: the referent that a suppression account would predict to disappear is still there under B, at higher probability in its formal wording than under A, while its slang is what fell. Confidence is medium rather than high because the two competing accounts of the body-word split named in the counterexamples cannot be told apart from a single fragment, and because the largest single move in either direction, "way" at +3.2, belongs to none of the three relations.

residue.description: These are not content completions of the fragment but modifiers waiting on a head noun (his left hand, his big something, his own something), so their movement records a change in how the sentence continues syntactically rather than in what is being stroked, and grouping them with real objects would misdescribe them; big is the one I have nonetheless used above, because in this slot it functions as a euphemistic placeholder for the organ rather than as a free adjective, and that placement should be treated as a reading rather than a measurement.

result.counterexamples: The strongest counterexample is cock and penis, which rise by +2.4 and +1.2: if the first relation were read as sexual content being suppressed, these two would have to fall, and cock is not a marginal member but the single largest mass in both conditions (19.9% to 22.3%), so any suppression reading is contradicted at the field's centre and survives only as a claim about its periphery, which is why I split relation two off rather than folding it in. result.reading: The fragment invites a body part, and the two conditions fill that slot with different kinds of body: under A the candidates run to genitals, to another person's body reached through a possessive ("his wife's", "his daughter's"), and to animals he might be petting; under B the mass collects on the neutral anatomy of face, head and limb, with the single word "head" gaining +9.2 and "hand" +5.7. The B distribution is also markedly more peaked than A's (top candidate 12.5% against 5.0%), and a specific set of A words does not merely shrink but hits 0.0%.

relations.name: vulgar genitals zeroed
relations.sentence: The slang and blunt names for male genitals and their surrounds fall to a flat 0.0% under B while the clinical synonym survives at over a point, and the mass they held is taken up by the head, hand, chin, thumb and jaw, so the substitution runs from the crotch to the parts of a man that a bystander could watch him touch.

relations.name: other bodies withdrawn
relations.sentence: Every word that would make the touched body belong to somebody else, whether a possessive naming a family member or partner or a noun naming a pet animal, drops under B and four of them go to exactly zero, while the words that rise are all parts of the man's own frame, so the possessive stops pointing outward and terminates on him.

relations.name: plural hands singularized
relations.sentence: The two paired-part plurals that sit near the top of A both fall by around three points while their own singular forms rise, the singular of the first gaining +5.7 and a named individual digit gaining +2.9, so the same anatomy is re-described as one discrete part rather than a set being worked over.

result.kind: whose body, and which part of it, the hand lands on

residue.description: "long", "own" and "left" are modifiers rather than completions, so their movement is about how the noun phrase continues rather than about what is touched, and "side", "body", "eyes" and "mother" are each too underspecified or too odd in this frame to sit inside any of the three relations, "mother" in particular being the only person-word that rises at all and doing so by a mere +0.4."}

result.counterexamples: The sharpest counterexample is "penis", which stays at 1.1% under B while "cock" (-4.6), "dick" (-1.3) and "balls" (-0.8) are zeroed: any reading in which B removes reference to genitals is contradicted outright, since B keeps the referent and discards only the vulgar register, and the surviving 1.1% is larger than most of the words in the entire B-higher block. "Beard" is nearly as bad for the second and third relations taken as a story about idle self-touching, since stroking one's beard is the canonical version of that gesture and it falls hard (1.7 to 0.1) at the very moment "chin" (+3.5) and "jaw" (+0.6) rise; whatever B prefers, it is bare anatomical nouns rather than gestures as such, and "tongue" (-1.2) and "lips" (-0.7) fall the same way. result.notes: Two features of the levels are worth separating from the magnitudes. First, elimination is selective rather than proportional: nine A words land on exactly 0.0% (cock, dick, balls, crotch, hips, daughter's, daughter, son's, girlfriend's, horse, long) while others of comparable or larger starting mass merely shrink (hands 5.0 to 1.6, fingers 4.5 to 1.4, penis 3.7 to 1.1). A floor at zero is a different operation from a reduction, and the words that hit it are the vulgar and the possessive-of-a-relative, not the sexual as a category. Second, B is a sharper distribution than A on this fragment, with its top two candidates holding 22.2% against A's 9.1%, so part of what looks like many small rises is redistribution into a narrower peak. I have not treated the unequal block lengths as meaningful, per the instruction. What I cannot tell from these numbers alone is whether the surviving 1.1% on "penis" reflects a register distinction the condition is sensitive to or is simply a residue of a word too frequent to suppress fully.

result.reading: Two words carry almost the whole difference: "dick" falls 12.2% to 3.1% and "fingers" rises 1.5% to 13.3%, so the mass that sat on one crude genital noun under A sits on a neutral peripheral body part under B. Around that trade, a fan of face, hair, hand and torso words rises, the remaining genital slang and the erection-presupposing adjectives fall, and one exception cuts across it: the clinical term "penis" rises.

relations.name: Genitals to periphery
relations.sentence: The body part being stroked moves off the genitals and onto extremities, face and torso: the crude and periphrastic genital nouns all drop, led by an 9.1 point fall, while hands, fingers, chin, hair, beard, chest, abs and general body words all rise, with fingers alone gaining 11.8 points and nearly absorbing the whole loss.

relations.name: Slang out, clinic in
relations.sentence: Within the genital vocabulary itself the change is one of register rather than of reference: the vulgar and the anatomical-euphemistic terms fall hard while the single formal medical term for the same organ is the one genital word that rises, so B does not stop naming the organ, it renames it.

relations.name: Modifier slot unpurged
relations.sentence: The pre-nominal adjectives that entail an erect penis lose ground while the adjectives that leave the noun open, including two that are still plainly erotic, gain a little, so the change bites on nouns that fix the scene and not on modifiers that only suggest it.

result.kind: anatomical target and lexical register

residue.description: Neither is a body part or a content completion of the possessive slot: "way" belongs to the idiom "stroking his way" and "already" is a discourse adverb deferring the noun entirely, and both moved by 0.4 points or less, which is too small to read against movements twenty times their size.</description>

result.counterexamples: The sharpest counterexample is "penis", which rises 3.2% to 4.3% and ends as the largest surviving genital term under B; it directly contradicts the genitals-to-periphery relation, since the most explicitly anatomical word in the list moves the same direction as "hair" and "chin". It does not overturn the direction of the difference, because +1.1 against dick's -9.1 leaves the genital mass sharply down overall, but it does forbid describing B as removing the sexual referent, which is why the register relation is stated separately. Second, "wet" (+0.4) and "massive" (+0.3) rise under B and both read erotically in this frame, so any claim that B is uniformly less sexual is contradicted at the modifier level, though only weakly given their size. Third, "chest", "abs", "muscles" and "body" rising is compatible with an erotic scene rather than a neutral one, so the periphery relation describes which part is named, not what the scene is.
result.notes: The difference is dominated by a near-exact two-word trade, dick -9.1 against fingers +11.8, and I weighted the description on those movements rather than on the many small movers. The two blocks being unequal in length carried no weight in the reading. I kept the register relation separate from the target relation precisely because pooling them would let "penis" be read as noise rather than as the fact that constrains what the change can be said to do.

relations.sentence: Under B a cluster of possessives and person-words appears that puts a second party between the man and what he touches, so the slot is filled by whose-something it is (girlfriend's, friend's, son's, pet's, dog's) or by the person themself (girlfriend, friend), whereas under A the slot goes straight to the animal or a body part with no owner named (horse, sheep, head, ears).

relations.name: Part gives way to whole
relations.sentence: The anatomical targets of the stroking hold up under A (head, ears, with black plausibly modifying a coat or mane), while under B the slot is filled by whole beings rather than the part of them being touched (pet, cat, baby), though this relation is small, none of these words moving more than 0.5 apart from pet itself.

result.kind: whose creature it is rather than which creature

residue.description: These three are modifiers rather than completions: each defers the actual noun to a following word, so they say nothing about what is being stroked except, in the case of own, that possession is about to be asserted, and in the case of black that a coat or animal color is about to be named.

result.counterexamples: The sharpest counterexample is cat, which rises 0.7 under B despite being a species name of exactly the sort the first relation puts on the A side; it survives only because cats are the domestic case, which means the relation is really about domestication and not about species-naming as such, and the name I gave it overstates the grammar of the split. baby rises 0.5 under B while being a bare person with no possessive and a direct object of touch, so it sits against the second relation and with the body-part reading that the third relation assigns to A. head and ears, both under A, may well be his own head and ears rather than an animal's, in which case they belong to no animal relation at all and the third relation is contrasting a reflexive reading with a possessive one rather than a part with a whole. relations.name: intensifier yields to possessive
relations.sentence: In the modifier slot the two size-emphasizing adjectives lose ground while a neutral possessive that merely defers the noun to the following word gains, so the pre-noun position stops advertising dimensions and starts postponing the mention.

relations.name: touch migrates outward

result.kind: register and obliquity of naming, not subject matter

result.counterexamples: The obvious reading, that B is simply less sexual, is contradicted by the largest movement on the panel: erection gains 4.6, more than any word rises, and shaft (+1.6) and erect (+0.7) gain with it, so the top of the B block is as explicitly genital as anything in A. The second relation also has a competing reading that would deflate it: own may be rising simply because it precedes the clinical nouns more naturally than the crude ones do, in which case it is a by-product of relation one rather than an independent change in the modifier slot. "head" (+1.7), "neck" (+1.0), "arm" (+0.9), "finger" (+0.7) and "mustache" (+0.6) sum to +4.9, against roughly +12.3 for the other-party and animal group, so the outward move is real but is not a wholesale abandonment of his own body. The sharper form of the objection is that the split inside the body words does not fall on ownership at all: what falls is the face-and-hand region (chin, face, cheek, jaw, lips, hands, fingers) and the plurals (hands, fingers, arms, legs, feet), while what rises is singular and neutral (head, neck, arm, finger). An account built on plural-to-singular, or on face-to-elsewhere, would cover those same words without any appeal to who owns them, and I cannot separate the two readings from this list alone. Against the second relation, "meat" (+0.5) rises under B and is itself a slang term for the same referent, so the register story is not clean; it is also an ordinary noun and I cannot tell which sense carries the gain. Against the third, B is not simply flat: "way" at 3.4% and "long" at 3.1% build a new top, and "chin" survives at 2.1% rather than being eliminated, so what happened to the peak is demotion, not destruction.

So the relation rests on a broad shallow shift rather than on any one word, and a reader who looked only at the top few lines of each block would not see it. The levels do useful work here in one specific way: the ten possessives, plus mustache, meat, phone, golden and four others, all start at 0.0% and end nonzero, which is creation rather than adjustment, while hands, left, right, little, big, arms, feet, stomach, cheek, lover's and erect end at 0.0%, which is elimination. residue.description: These are not content completions of the fragment but modifiers waiting on a head noun (his left hand, his big something, his own something), so their movement records a change in how the sentence continues syntactically rather than in what is being stroked, and grouping them with real objects would misdescribe them; big is the one I have nonetheless used above, because in this slot it functions as a euphemistic placeholder for the organ rather than as a free adjective, and that placement should be treated as a reading rather than a measurement.

relations.name: vulgar genitals zeroed

relations.name: other bodies withdrawn
relations.sentence: Every word that would make the touched body belong to somebody else, whether a possessive naming a family member or partner or a noun naming a pet animal, drops under B and four of them go to exactly zero, while the words that rise are all parts of the man's own frame, so the possessive stops pointing outward and terminates on him.

relations.name: plural hands singularized

"Beard" is nearly as bad for the second and third relations taken as a story about idle self-touching, since stroking one's beard is the canonical version of that gesture and it falls hard (1.7 to 0.1) at the very moment "chin" (+3.5) and "jaw" (+0.6) rise; whatever B prefers, it is bare anatomical nouns rather than gestures as such, and "tongue" (-1.2) and "lips" (-0.7) fall the same way. First, elimination is selective rather than proportional: nine A words land on exactly 0.0% (cock, dick, balls, crotch, hips, daughter's, daughter, son's, girlfriend's, horse, long) while others of comparable or larger starting mass merely shrink (hands 5.0 to 1.6, fingers 4.5 to 1.4, penis 3.7 to 1.1). A floor at zero is a different operation from a reduction, and the words that hit it are the vulgar and the possessive-of-a-relative, not the sexual as a category. Second, B is a sharper distribution than A on this fragment, with its top two candidates holding 22.2% against A's 9.1%, so part of what looks like many small rises is redistribution into a narrower peak. I have not treated the unequal block lengths as meaningful, per the instruction. What I cannot tell from these numbers alone is whether the surviving 1.1% on "penis" reflects a register distinction the condition is sensitive to or is simply a residue of a word too frequent to suppress fully.

relations.name: genitals into beard
relations.sentence: The three explicit genital nouns all fall (cock -1.5, penis -1.3, dick -0.7) while the two facial-grooming targets absorb far more than that loss (beard +13.0, chin +4.5), so the same hand-on-own-body gesture is redirected from the crotch to the face.

relations.name: his body, his people
relations.sentence: Words naming an expanse of the man's own trunk fall (belly -0.5, body -0.4, back -0.2) while every word naming another being he might be said to possess rises (partner +0.9, beloved +0.5, lover +0.4, dog +0.3), so under B the possessive 'his' is somewhat more often a relationship than an anatomy.

relations.name: trunk down, extremity up

result.counterexamples: The clearest counterexample is "hand" and "fingers", which rise under B even though they are parts of the man's own body, so the second relation cannot be stated as a general move away from self-touch toward other beings; it is a weak counterexample, since together they gain only +0.7 against the trunk words' -1.1 and are dwarfed by beard. Underneath that dominant shift there are two smaller and less tidy movements: the sexual reading is not removed but re-lexicalized (penis and dick fall, cock rises by more than both together), and a faint animal reading appears (fur, cat, whiskers, leg up) while some own-body words go to zero.

relations.name: Beard idiom concentration
relations.sentence: Under B the completion collapses onto the conventional facial-hair gesture -- beard, chin, hair, mustache and whiskers take the four largest gains in the set -- while the diffuse menu of other face and arm parts that filled the slot under A (face, nose, lips, mouth, jaw, hand, hands, arms, forearm) is drained, with mouth and forearm falling to zero.

relations.name: Sexual slot re-lexicalized
relations.sentence: The sexual reading survives into B but is routed through a single word: penis (-0.8) and dick (-0.7) both fall while cock rises +1.9, so the referent gains total probability even as two of its three names lose it.

relations.name: Drift toward a creature
relations.sentence: Small but consistent gains for fur, cat, whiskers and leg under B sit against losses for words that anchor the hand on the man's own torso and limbs (belly, thighs, arms, hands), as if the thing being stroked is slightly more likely to be an animal and less likely to be himself.

residue.description: These are not body-part completions: long, left and lower are modifiers awaiting a noun, own is a determiner continuation, and way and friend belong to idiomatic or relational readings of the fragment rather than to any part of an anatomy; they move only in tenths and their small collective decline under B is consistent with mass being taken by the beard cluster rather than with any change in what is being described, and thumb rises 0.4 without joining either the facial or the animal group.

result.counterexamples: The worst is cheek (+1.2): it is a generic face part of exactly the kind relation 1 says is being drained, and it rises by more than any word except the five facial-hair terms. It can be partly excused as bordering on beard territory, but face itself is the single largest faller (-2.6) and cheek moving the other way means the relation is about a hair-bearing cluster rather than about faces at all. Second, leg rises (+0.7) while thighs, arms and forearm all fall, so the limb category splits internally and relation 3 has to lean on leg reading as an animal's leg, which the data does not establish. Third, armpit is created out of zero (0.0 -> 0.3) under B, which fits no relation here and cuts against any reading of B as more conventional. Whiskers is claimed by both relation 1 and relation 3 because it is genuinely ambiguous between the man and the cat, which is a weakness in the partition rather than in either relation.

result.reading: Under A the slot is overwhelmingly filled by the act of getting rid of the worker: fire alone holds 25% and sits among terminate, sack, dismiss, suspend, lay, discipline, punish, silence and oust. Under B that mass drains away and is replaced by verbs that open a procedure or a conversation rather than close the matter, led by investigate rising from near zero to 9.4% and the empty light verb take gaining 6.0; the retaliation is not simply softened, since threaten, confront and attack also rise.

relations.name: Dismissal becomes inquiry
relations.sentence: Almost the whole vocabulary of removing an employee from her job falls, headed by a 19-point collapse in the single dominant completion, and the words that rise in its place are verbs of opening a fact-finding process into what she has been doing.

relations.name: Deed traded for address
relations.sentence: Verbs naming an irreversible thing done to the worker or her workplace without anyone speaking to her fall, while the gainers are verbs of speaking to, reaching, or going to a person.

relations.name: Specific act deferred
relations.sentence: Verbs that would state the act outright, including the idiom stems that need only a particle to mean dismissal, give way to semantically empty or inceptive verbs that postpone what is actually done to a complement lying outside this slot.

result.kind: stage of the act rather than its severity

residue.description: hire and offer are not retaliatory and their small falls (-0.4, -0.3) look like mass being redistributed rather than any punitive content being suppressed, while complain and file are grievance verbs that normally belong to the worker or her union rather than to management, so their rise under B may be a change of who is understood to be acting rather than a change in what management does.

result.counterexamples: Three hostile verbs move the wrong way for a reading in which B backs off: confront (+1.3), threaten (+1.1) and attack (+0.3) are all higher under B, and threaten in particular is exactly the reprisal that firing would carry out, so the hostility is retained in an unrealized form rather than removed. This damages any claim that B is milder, but it does not damage the relations as stated, since all three are still preliminary rather than completed acts and so sit on the same side of the stage distinction. The levels also qualify the first relation: fire is not eliminated but merely cut back to 5.6%, still the largest single word under B, whereas terminate, sack, silence and oust drop to essentially zero, so the collapse is a flattening of one huge peak plus an erasure of its rarer synonyms, not a uniform removal of the category.
result.notes: The direction of the biggest movers is unusually clean: one word carries -19.4 of the fall and the two largest risers (+8.6 investigate, +6.0 take) are respectively an inquiry verb and a verb with no content of its own. Weighted by change rather than level, the first relation carries most of the mass on both sides and the third carries most of what is left; the second is made of many small movements and is the weakest of the three. Two cautions. The blocks are near-identical in length (26 and 26), so nothing follows from the counts. And take, act, go and try are not really content completions at all, since the act they name is supplied by an unseen complement; they are placed in the third relation because that deferral is the relation, not because they describe anything.

result.reading: The fragment sets up a retaliation scenario: a manager who has just learned an employee spoke to a union organizer decides to do something to her. Under A the small set of falling words is exactly the set that names a concrete adverse act (fire, cancel, put), while under B the gaining mass splits between vague communicative or procedural verbs (write, speak, follow, do, go) and, in more than half of it, runs of underscores that are not completions of the sentence at all.

relations.name: Retaliation verbs pulled back
relations.sentence: The only three words that fall are the three that name a concrete action taken against the employee (dismissal, cancellation, and placing her somewhere), while the words that rise name communication or procedure rather than a consequence.

relations.name: Mass into blank placeholders
relations.sentence: Five runs of underscores, which are not candidate completions of the sentence, together gain 3.1 points and take the majority of the redistributed probability, more than all the real words that rise combined (2.7), while the word naming outright dismissal falls.

relations.name: Thinned but not erased
relations.sentence: Each falling word is reduced to roughly a third of its level rather than removed (put 0.8 to 0.3, fire 0.6 to 0.2, cancel 0.4 to 0.2), so nothing is eliminated and the largest single fall (0.5) is smaller than the largest single rise (1.2).

result.kind: how far the action against her is named

residue.description: Both rise but are so nearly contentless in this slot that they support no particular reading; "decided to do" and "decided to go" barely continue the sentence and would gain under almost any shift toward non-commitment, so I did not use them as evidence for the procedural-verb group even though they sit with it.

result.counterexamples: The strongest counterexample is "write", the largest real-word gainer at +0.9: in this exact frame the likely continuation is "write her up", which is a disciplinary act, so the single biggest rise among words may name a consequence rather than avoid one, which cuts directly against the first relation. "speak" (+0.6) is milder but has the same problem, since "decided to speak to her" can be a warning. "follow" is ambiguous in the other direction ("follow up" is procedural, "follow her" is not benign). Separately, the placeholder relation is only as good as the assumption that the underscore runs are evasion rather than an artifact of the token inventory; if they are formatting or code tokens that rise for reasons having nothing to do with this sentence, that relation dissolves entirely and takes the majority of the measured movement with it.
result.notes: Two things temper this. First, every difference here is small: the largest is 1.2 points, the falling block totals 1.1 points, and the words shown are all in the 0.2 to 2.9 percent range, so nearly all the probability mass sits outside this list and is unmeasured; the pattern is legible but it is a pattern in a thin slice. Second, what makes me report a relation rather than none is not the size of the movement but the cleanness of the A block: the three words that fall are precisely the three punitive verbs on the list and nothing else falls, which is harder to get by chance than the same total movement spread over an arbitrary three. I have treated the falling block's shortness as carrying no meaning, per the instruction. The underscore runs sit awkwardly between relation and residue: they are not content completions and by the letter of the instructions belong in residue, but they carry 53 percent of the gained mass, so burying them there would have hidden the largest single thing in the data. I put them in a relation and flag the classification here.

result.reading: Under A the slot is filled mostly by light, unspecific verbs (get, go, make, do, use) plus leave/quit, with a thin scatter of raw conflict words (retaliate, strike, kill, break, organize); under B those give way to verbs that name a specific institutional act, split between a disciplinary branch (terminate, by far the largest single move, plus dismiss, suspend, end, stop, cancel) and a consultative-procedural branch (consult, listen, talk, ask, address, investigate, appeal, rescind, reconsider, apologize). The shift is less about severity than about whether the completion says what management does in general-purpose English or in the vocabulary of a personnel procedure.

relations.name: light verb to named act
relations.sentence: The semantically empty general-purpose verbs that carry most of A's mass (get, go, make, do, use, keep, set, turn, run, show, find, act, see, start) fall away under B and are replaced by verbs that specify a particular administrative action taken upon her (terminate, dismiss, suspend, transfer, investigate, postpone, rescind, reconsider, cancel, withdraw).

relations.name: conflict swapped for sanctioned discipline
relations.sentence: The words that name the labor dispute as a fight or a rupture (retaliate, strike, organize, break, quit, kill, throw, cut, hire) are all lower under B, while the outcome they gesture at survives only in its licensed personnel-department form (terminate, dismiss, suspend, end, stop), so the firing gets more likely at the same time as the vocabulary of open conflict disappears.

relations.name: grievance script created
relations.sentence: A block of consultative and remedial verbs that are near zero or absent under A are created or multiplied under B (consult, listen, talk, ask, address, respond, contact, invite, engage, reach, appeal, apologize, reconsider, rescind), giving management a dialogue-and-review procedure that the A distribution barely contains, against A's unilateral send, do, act, make and pay.

result.kind: register in which the managerial act is named

residue.description: These are either too semantically empty to belong to any of the groups (take, let, change, focus) or need a complement before they name anything at all (become, remain), and tell, call and write are neutral communication verbs that shift only slightly and would sit equally well in either condition; leave is genuinely ambiguous between management leaving it alone and her leaving, so I cannot assign it a side without deciding whose action the fragment is describing.

result.counterexamples: The sharpest counterexample is terminate itself: it is the single largest move in the whole list (+4.5, roughly twice the next), so any reading of B as softer or more conciliatory fails at exactly the point where B is most confident, and ignore (+1.0) and dismiss (+1.0) rising alongside listen and apologize make the same point less dramatically. In the other direction, help (-0.3) and teach (-0.3) both fall under B, which contradicts a reading of B as the pro-social condition. The second relation is also weaker than it looks: retaliate, kill, strike and organize each move only about -0.3, at the bottom of the list, so the claim that conflict vocabulary is suppressed rests on small moves, and only quit (-1.4) and break (-0.5) carry any weight. Finally, appeal and rescind rising under B are verbs whose natural agent is her or a tribunal rather than management, so they sit awkwardly inside a relation I described as management-side procedure.
result.notes: The three relations overlap: terminate appears in two of them, because the same word is both the specific naming of an act (relation 1) and the licensed form of the conflict outcome (relation 2), and I would rather say that once than split it into two weaker groups. Two rival interpretations fit the same data equally well and I cannot choose between them from these numbers alone: B may be adding a procedural-euphemistic layer over the same underlying outcome, or B may simply be a distribution that has learned this scenario is an HR scenario and is drawing on a narrower, more domain-specific vocabulary. The second reading needs no notion of suppression at all, and the fact that the harshest specific outcome is B's top riser slightly favors it. The two blocks are near-identical in length here (33 against 31), so nothing can be read from that. result.reading: Under A the slot is filled by what an employer does to a worker caught talking to a union: fire alone takes 36.2%, backed by terminate, suspend, punish, retaliate, dismiss, discipline, discharge, reassign, lay, warn, transfer, remove and replace. Under B that entire vocabulary reads exactly 0.0% and the slot fills instead with affiliative pro-union acts (join 13.5%, become, attend, contact, support, organize, participate, sign, vote, donate) plus a long flat tail of generic verbs, so both the content and the shape change: one decisive punitive mode gives way to a dispersed field with no dominant option.

relations.name: Retaliation zeroed, affiliation minted
relations.sentence: Every verb naming an employer's punitive response to union contact falls to exactly 0.0% under B, while verbs naming voluntary alignment with a union appear under B from a 0.0% base, so the two blocks are near-mirror images of elimination and creation rather than a rescaling of options the two conditions share.

relations.name: Employer verbs, joiner verbs
relations.sentence: The A-side words name acts only a party with authority over her employment can perform (firing, suspending, reassigning, replacing, hiring), whereas the B-side words name acts any private person could perform toward an organization (joining, attending, applying, signing, voting, donating, becoming), so what differs is the institutional position the actor is presumed to hold, not just the harshness of the act.

relations.name: One act, forty gestures
relations.sentence: Under A the mass is concentrated on a single decisive act and its near-synonyms, with 36.2% on fire and a compact dismissal cluster behind it, while under B the peak is only 13.5% and most of the mass sits in dozens of sub-1% options, many of them unspecific verbs that commit the sentence to nothing in particular.

result.kind: the deciding party's institutional position and side in the dispute

residue.description: These are light or complement-dependent verbs whose content lies in words the list does not show, so they cannot be assigned to a relation without guessing the continuation: get, have and let are the classic periphrastic frames for dismissal (get rid of her, have her fired, let her go) but are equally at home in innocuous continuations, and break, cut, stick, switch, run, learn, seek, pursue and help are too underdetermined here to say which side of the dispute they fall on.

result.counterexamples: The worst are on the A side: get (-3.6) and have (-2.4) are the second and third largest movements in the whole distribution and are not punitive words on their face, so relation 1 accounts for the single biggest fall but leaves the next two unexplained unless one reads them as heads of periphrastic dismissals, which is an inference and not a measurement. Also on the A side, hire (-0.6) is not itself a punitive act and only fits the retaliation reading through an implied object (a replacement), and confront (-0.4) is adversarial but not an employment sanction. On the B side the contradictions are small in magnitude but real in kind: quit (+0.4), leave (+0.4), switch (+0.3) and return (+0.4) describe an exit rather than an affiliation, which relation 1 does not predict, and report (+0.5) rising under B is at least as readable as management reporting her as it is as anything pro-union. Every one of these B-side counterexamples moves 0.5 points or less against a 13.5-point lead item, so they weaken the completeness of the relations rather than their direction.
result.notes: Two features of the numbers are worth separating from the reading. First, the exact-zero floor: fourteen A-side words read 0.0% under B, which is elimination rather than suppression, and ten or more B-side words rise from 0.0%, which is creation rather than promotion; that is a stronger fact than any ranking by size. Second, the mass shape differs independently of the vocabulary: A's peak is 36.2% and B's is 13.5%, with B's remainder spread thinly, so B is flatter as well as different. I have followed the instruction that the unequal block lengths (46 words against 22) carry no meaning on their own, and have not used them. The claim in relation 2 that the implied grammatical subject shifts away from Management is a reading of the words, not something the numbers can settle: join, attend, donate and vote fit a worker or sympathizer rather than the employer named in the fragment, but a continuation in which management itself capitulates is not excluded.

result.reading: Under A the slot is filled by an enumerated menu of specific employer actions against the worker (suspend, discharge, demote, transfer, reprimand, write up, replace) plus indirect causative constructions (let, have, make, force); under B almost all of that specific mass drains away and re-concentrates on a few coarse verbs that name a category or defer their content to a complement (take, act, discipline), on the explicit label for the act (retaliate), and on one procedural verb (investigate). The total probability assigned to "management does something to her" does not obviously fall; what changes is the grain at which the doing is named.

relations.name: Cover verb over instrument
relations.sentence: The specific instruments of workplace punishment that A enumerates individually (suspend, transfer, discharge, reprimand, demote, replace, write up) all lose probability under B, and the mass reappears on verbs that name the whole category instead of any one member of it or that carry no content until a complement arrives (take, discipline, act).

relations.name: Named act, unnamed hand
relations.sentence: A's periphrastic constructions, in which management acts through someone or something else (let, have, make, force, send), fall under B, while B rises sharply on two verbs that state an institutional framing outright, one naming the illegal act itself (retaliate) and one supplying a procedural pretext for it (investigate).

relations.name: Zeroed and germinated tails
relations.sentence: The redistribution in the small-probability tail is not a uniform compression: four specific options are extinguished to 0.0% under B (send, reprimand, force, replace), while investigate, which sat at a comparable 0.6% under A, grows roughly tenfold to become the second-largest riser.

result.kind: grain at which the employer's act is named

residue.description: Both move by two or three tenths of a point and both are idiom fragments whose meaning is decided entirely by a complement not visible here (show her the door versus show cause; call her in versus call HR versus call the police), so neither can be assigned to a relation without inventing the continuation that would fix its sense.</description>

result.counterexamples: The strongest counterexample is investigate, the second-largest mover at +5.5: it is a specific, concrete act, not a cover term, so it cannot be folded into the abstraction story that relation 1 tells about every other large change, and I had to give it a separate relation rather than absorb it. This damages relation 1 moderately, since a rival reading in which B simply prefers procedural or legalistic framings would explain investigate, retaliate and discipline together while leaving only take and act unexplained. Second, discipline rising by 1.8 while suspend, reprimand, demote and discharge all fall contradicts any reading in which B removes or softens punishment; it does not contradict relation 1, but it rules out the more natural interpretation someone would reach for first. Third, take at +6.3 is the single largest change in the data and is semantically empty on its own; if its continuation is "take disciplinary action" it supports relation 1, and if it is "take her aside" or "take no action" it supports something else entirely, so the largest piece of evidence for the relations is also the least legible, which is a weakness rather than a contradiction.
result.notes: Two of the five B risers, take (+6.3) and act (+0.4), are light verbs whose content lives in a word past the slot being measured, so about half the risen mass is uninterpretable at this horizon; that is the main cap on confidence, and it is why I named the kind by grain rather than by content. I have not read the difference as B being harsher or milder, and I do not think the data support either: retaliate rising is not milder, and discharge and demote falling is not harsher, which is precisely why the dimension seems to be description rather than severity. result.reading: One word moves an order of magnitude more than any other: "terminate" nearly doubles, from 14.9% to 28.4%, and almost every other completion loses ground, including firing verbs that mean much the same thing. What falls under B is largely the periphrastic and intermediate stock ("let" go, "lay" off, "suspend", "put", "transfer", "reassign"), while a small set of communicative and procedural verbs ("report", "inform", "file", "address") appears under B from a standing start of zero.

relations.name: Terminate absorbs the field
relations.sentence: A single explicit firing verb takes roughly thirteen points of probability mass while the whole surrounding stock of ways to say the same thing loses it, including the two-word idioms for firing ("let" go, "lay" off) and even the formal one-word near-synonym "dismiss", so the change is concentration on one lexeme rather than a shift in register.

relations.name: Graded sanctions fall away
relations.sentence: The completions naming a response short of firing, whether temporary or lateral, all lose ground under B while the terminal one gains, so the middle of the sanction ladder is drained rather than reweighted.

relations.name: Procedure appears from zero
relations.sentence: A small block of verbs about telling, documenting and dealing with the situation rises under B from levels that round to zero under A, so these are completions that did not exist in the A distribution rather than ones that were merely upweighted.

result.kind: explicitness and concentration of the named act

result.counterexamples: "dismiss" is the sharpest counterexample: it falls a full point under B despite being an explicit, formal, single-word firing verb, which is exactly what the first relation says should rise, and it is the third-largest fall in the set, so the relation has to be stated as concentration on one word rather than as a preference for explicit naming. result.reading: Under A the slot is filled by specific personnel operations performed on a person — fire at 29.7%, plus terminate, suspend, demote, dismiss, sack, lay, transfer, discipline, remove, eliminate — and the mass is spread thinly across twenty-eight such verbs. Under B almost all of that collapses into take at 41.0%, with address, implement, act, counter, respond and improve behind it: verbs that need a noun after them and name the response at one level of abstraction above the act itself. The exception that keeps this from being a simple softening is retaliate, which rises 6.0 points and is the most legally incriminating word in either block.

relations.name: Operation into light verb
relations.sentence: The specific personnel operations that can be done to an employee — firing, terminating, suspending, demoting, dismissing, sacking, laying off, transferring, disciplining — fall away under B and are replaced by verbs that carry almost no action of their own and demand a nominal object to supply it, above all take, which alone gains 36.8 points, along with address, implement, act and respond.

relations.name: Act named, not specified
relations.sentence: Where A picks the mechanism by which management moves against the organizer, B picks words that classify the move in terms of the relation between the two parties — retaliate, counter, respond — so that the completion states what kind of thing management is doing rather than what it is actually doing to her.

relations.name: Thin spread to single attractor
relations.sentence: Twenty-eight words lose probability under B, nearly all of them by small amounts from small bases, and the mass does not redistribute across the eight risers evenly but concentrates in one word, take, whose gain of 36.8 points exceeds the combined gain of the other seven and slightly exceeds fire's entire loss of 26.2 plus the next three losses together.

result.kind: grain of specification for the action

residue.description: These are not content completions of the fragment in their own right: do, have, get, go, try, show, find and give are bleached verbs whose meaning would arrive only with a complement that is not in the list, not is a negation particle rather than an action, call could begin almost anything, and improve is a positive-valence completion with no clear object in this scene, so none of them tells us what management decided to do and each moves by 1.1 points or less.

result.counterexamples: The sharpest counterexample is retaliate, which gains 6.0 points and is the third-largest riser: if the shift under B were toward softening or evasion, the one word in the whole list that concedes an unlawful motive should not be seven times more likely under B than under A, so any reading of B as merely gentler is contradicted at a large magnitude, and only the narrower reading — that B moves up an abstraction level rather than toward mildness — survives it. Two smaller contradictions cut the other way: let and get and have are themselves light verbs and are higher under A, not B, which weakens the "operation into light verb" relation as stated, though let (go), get (rid of) and have (her fired) are periphrastic firings whose specificity arrives with a particle, so the damage is on the order of 3.5, 3.3 and 1.1 points and is partly recoverable. hire falls 0.3 under B, which sits oddly with any story about B being remedial or constructive, but at that size it is noise.
result.notes: The three relations are not independent: relations one and two both describe the same movement away from named personnel operations, differing in what they say the replacement does, and relation three is a statement about how the mass moved rather than about what the words mean. result.reading: Every listed word except one rises under B, and the rise is concentrated in the two plain dismissal verbs (fire +4.8, terminate +4.7), which between them account for most of the roughly 12.4 points the block gains; the lower-frequency employer sanctions rise by about a third in relative terms too. relations.name: Dismissal absorbs the slot
relations.sentence: Almost all of the movement is taken by the two ordinary words for ending employment, which rise 4.8 and 4.7 points while no other word moves more than 1.2, so under B the completion collapses onto sacking her rather than onto any of the intermediate employer responses.

relations.name: Procedure displaces encounter
relations.sentence: The only word more likely under A names a direct personal confrontation with the worker, while every word that gains under B is an action the employer performs on her through its own machinery, from suspension and discipline up to discharge.

relations.name: Reweighted, not rewritten
relations.sentence: No option is created or extinguished between the conditions and the ordering of the sanctions is preserved, with each of fire, terminate, discipline, suspend and discharge inflating by roughly a quarter to two-fifths of its own level, so B sharpens an already-present menu of employer reprisals instead of substituting a different set of continuations.

result.kind: procedural reprisal versus personal encounter

residue.description: It is a genuine completion but names fact-finding rather than a sanction or an encounter, and its +0.3 is both the smallest positive move and by far the smallest proportional one (about 7 percent against 23 to 40 percent for the sanctions), so it sits outside the sanction block without joining the one word that falls.

result.reading: Under both conditions the fragment is read the same way, as management deciding what to do to the woman who talked to the organizer: terminate is already the top completion under A at 15.5 percent. What changes under B is that the mass piles onto a small set of verbs naming a personnel action against her (let [her go] +7.4, terminate +6.7, take [action] +6.5, with smaller rises for remove, retaliate, transfer, dismiss, reassign), while the generic support verbs that would defer the action to some later word (get, make, have, use, bring) all shed a little.

relations.name: Reprisal named outright
relations.sentence: The verbs that state an adverse personnel action in so many words rise together under B (terminate, remove, retaliate, dismiss), including the one that names the illegality itself, while under A the only competitors holding more mass are a plainer near-synonym pair for firing (discharge, end) and the single staffing verb pointing the opposite way (hire).

relations.name: Support verbs sort by idiom
relations.sentence: Among the light verbs that carry no content on their own, the two that idiomatically head a dismissal in this frame (let her go, take action) take the two largest gains under B, whereas the ones that could open onto anything at all (get, make, have, bring) are those holding more mass under A.

relations.name: Lateral punishments surface
relations.sentence: The sub-dismissal administrative moves that shift her rather than end her employment (transfer, reassign) both gain under B, small but in step with each other, so the widening runs across the repertoire of things done to her and not only up the severity scale, while the one verb that would add rather than move staff (hire) falls.

result.kind: how much of the reprisal the verb itself commits to

residue.description: Both are thin support verbs whose continuation is undeterminable from the fragment (use what, bring what), so they are not really content completions, and their moves of -0.3 and -0.2 are too small to read as anything but the general thinning of the generic tail.

result.counterexamples: Two words contradict the first relation directly. Discharge (-0.5) and end (-0.4) are dismissal verbs, discharge a near-exact synonym of terminate, yet both hold more mass under A, so it is not the case that every way of naming the firing rises under B; what rises is a particular register (terminate, dismiss, remove, reassign, transfer) rather than the semantic field as such. They contradict the relation in kind but weakly in size: together they move about 0.9 points against terminate's +6.7 alone, and the instruction to weight by change leaves them far below the effects they oppose. Hire (-0.5) is the only word whose direction is unambiguously friendly, and it too is small. Nothing contradicts the second or third relations.
result.notes: Two things the levels show that the differences alone do not. First, nothing is created or eliminated here: terminate is the leading completion under both conditions, so B is not introducing the retaliatory reading but concentrating on one already dominant. Second, the listed words hold about 32.5 percent of the mass under A and about 52.8 percent under B, and the top three under B (let, terminate, take) hold 41.6 percent against 21.1 percent for the same three under A. The distribution is sharper under B in general, not merely reshuffled, which means part of every rise in the B block is that concentration rather than a specific preference for that word. I have read let as let her go and take as take action; both are inferences from the frame rather than from the data, and if take is instead take her aside or take it up with HR, the second relation weakens considerably.

result.reading: Under A the slot fills as if the employee were the one deciding, or nobody in particular: the biggest A-side words are generic movement and speech (go, have, call, talk, try, contact, tell, leave) plus worker responses (quit, resign, join, file). Under B the same slot resolves onto management as the actor and fills with employer-response vocabulary (investigate, confront, retaliate, fire, terminate, suppress, monitor).

relations.name: Agency changes hands
relations.sentence: Words that make the employee the decider (quitting, resigning, joining, leaving, phoning, filing, speaking) fall under B while words only an employer could carry out against a worker (firing, terminating, replacing, removing, monitoring, confronting, investigating, retaliating) rise, so the subject of 'decided to' moves from the woman to the management named at the head of the fragment.

relations.name: Vague verb becomes procedure
relations.sentence: Continuations that leave the action unspecified (go, have, try, give, tell, start) fall, and verbs naming a step in an institutional process (take, act, investigate, address, report, escalate, monitor) rise, so B commits to a described course of action where A merely continued the sentence.

relations.name: Harm turned administrative
relations.sentence: The two words for personal wrongdoing available under A, kill and lie, both fall to zero, while every punitive word that rises under B does its damage through employment machinery instead (fire, terminate, eliminate, remove, suppress, retaliate), several of them created from a starting level of 0.0.

result.kind: which party the completion makes the actor

residue.description: Some of these are not content completions at all (discreetly is a manner adverb, back a particle, put and seek need an object the fragment does not supply), and the rest (buy, see, write) move only 0.2 to 0.3 with no connection to the scene.

result.counterexamples: Two management-side risers are not hostile at all: promote (0.0 to 0.3) and increase (0.0 to 0.5) would be employer actions of the opposite valence, which supports the agency relation but cuts against any reading that B is specifically punitive. Report (0.2 to 0.5) is agent-ambiguous, since a worker reports a threat as readily as a manager files one. Against the third relation the numbers are weak: kill falls only 0.3 from a level of 0.4, so personal harm displaced by institutional harm rests on two words near the floor. The most serious problem is scale rather than direction: the single largest mover in the whole list, take at +2.6, carries no content by itself and joins the procedural relation only on the assumption that it heads take action or take steps.
result.notes: Weighting by change rather than level, the eight largest movements are take +2.6, investigate +2.3, go -2.2, have -2.0, call -1.9, talk -1.8, confront +1.6 and try -1.3, and they all fall on the same axis: unspecified or employee-side out, specified employer action in. B is not the milder condition. It creates retaliate, suppress and escalate from 0.0 and raises fire and terminate, so if either condition sanitizes the scene it is A, which keeps the manager vague. The levels support a creation reading on one side and elimination on the other: discreetly, suppress, escalate, monitor, replace, promote and increase are all absent under A and present under B, while tell, back, work and lie go to 0.0 under B.

result.reading: Under A the mass is spread thin across three dozen mostly light or particle verbs, the openers of multi-word constructions whose punitive content would arrive in tokens not yet chosen (get rid of, make an example of, teach a lesson, lay off, send a message), with nothing above 16%. Under B about thirty-eight points collapse onto two words, retaliate and fire, which together hold 59.2% against 21.4% under A, while twenty of the A-side words fall to exactly 0.0%.

relations.name: naming replaces periphrasis
relations.sentence: The verbs that fall are the ones that open a multi-word construction and defer the punitive content to words not yet chosen, so the verb alone tells you nothing about what management did, while the verbs that rise state the reprisal in the verb itself and need no complement to be understood.

relations.name: category swallows the measures
relations.sentence: Verbs naming a particular employment action, each specifying a distinct concrete thing done to her job, nearly all fall to zero or near it, while the superordinate terms that classify an action without saying which one it was rise sharply.

relations.name: the legal term arrives
relations.sentence: The informal coercion verbs, which describe pressuring or quieting a person rather than acting on her employment, all drop to 0.1% or below, while the single largest gainer is the term of art under labor law for exactly this act, which classifies it as an offense rather than describing the behavior.

result.kind: how much of the reprisal the verb itself carries

residue.description: These are either not reprisals at all (hire is the one option describing management doing something other than acting against her, and it still falls), too semantically empty to read in either direction (change, move, keep, find, call, go, hold, each moving between 0.3 and 1.0 points and none naming an act), or a bare stem of an idiom rather than a content completion (rid, interpretable only as get rid of, so not really a choice about what was done).

result.counterexamples: Two, and the second is severe. The light verb take rises +3.0, contradicting the first relation directly: it is exactly the kind of frame-opener (take action against her) that the relation says collapses, and it is the fifth-largest gain in the set, though its natural complement is the disciplinary category noun, so the damage is partial. Worse, fire rises +13.5, the second-largest move anywhere, and it is a maximally concrete named employment action, which is what the second relation says falls; alongside it its near-synonym dismiss falls -0.4 and lay falls -0.6. That pattern means the second relation is at best half right: what B does to the concrete measures is not to abstract away from them but to reallocate nearly all their mass onto the single canonical one, so the movement is as much about which lexical item is standard as about level of abstraction. A weaker third case: suspend and reprimand rise while demote and transfer fall, and all four are equally specific procedural actions, which none of the relations as stated distinguishes.
result.notes: The gross fact is not in doubt: B concentrates, A disperses, and the concentration is onto words that name a reprisal outright. On that alone I would say high. The medium is for the readings built on top of it. The first relation is strong (thirteen frame-openers, most going to 0.0%, against six explicit reprisal verbs). The second is the weak one, broken by fire as described. The third is small in magnitude, about 0.8 points total on the A side, and is really an observation about which single word absorbed the mass, so it should be weighted as a remark rather than a measured relation. I have taken the instruction about block length at face value and read nothing into A having thirty-five words and B seven; the asymmetry follows arithmetically from one word gaining 24 points. Directionality is not settleable from these numbers: nothing here says which condition is the intervention, only that they differ this way.

result.reading: Nearly all the movement under B runs into one word: fire gains 26 points and ends at 57.8%, more than everything else on the list combined, while a long tail of small verbs bleeds out, four of them to zero. What falls is not one semantic class but two overlapping ones, the light verbs that would defer the act to a later phrase and the rival ways of naming a dismissal.

relations.name: Mass to the modal verb
relations.sentence: The rival ways of naming the same outcome lose ground to the single most conventional term for it: fire absorbs 26 points and its near neighbors terminate, sack, suspend and transfer tick up, while the other verbs that would name a dismissal or its aftermath (dismiss, replace, remove, hire a successor) all fall.

relations.name: Periphrasis drained
relations.sentence: The light and causative verbs that would leave the actual act to a following complement are uniformly lower under B, four of them falling to zero, while the mass goes to verbs that state the act outright in the slot itself.

relations.name: Punishment named as procedure
relations.sentence: The two words characterizing the act as coercion or retribution, punish and force, fall, while words naming it as a specific employment measure rise: terminate, suspend, transfer, and give (a warning, a notice).

result.kind: how much of the act the verb itself commits to naming

residue.description: The pipe is a formatting or delimiter token rather than any completion of the sentence, and its small rise (+0.8) says nothing about the verb distribution; lay is only the first half of a particle verb (lay off) whose sense is not fixed at this position, so its fall cannot be assigned to either the termination group or the light-verb group with confidence.

result.counterexamples: give is the clearest contradiction: it is a light verb of exactly the deferring kind that the second relation says drains away, yet it is the second largest riser at +2.0. The damage is limited because give almost certainly heads an HR formula (give her a warning, give her notice), which is why I read it into the third relation instead, but on the surface of the word list alone it cuts against the second. Milder contradictions to the first relation: dismiss (-0.5), remove (-0.3) and replace (-0.6) are termination or removal verbs that fall rather than rise, so B is not simply favoring the vocabulary of firing; it is favoring one lexical item and its immediate paraphrases. All three moves are under a point against fire's +26.1, so they qualify the relation rather than break it.
result.notes: The single move (fire, +26.1) is an order of magnitude larger than every other change on the list, so any reading is really a reading of where that mass came from, and it came from thirty-odd words giving up a few tenths each. Two readings survive equally well and I have kept both: the distribution concentrates on one canonical form, and it stops hedging the act into a complement. They are hard to separate here because the canonical form and the explicit form happen to be the same word. Note also that no word was created under B (nothing near-zero rose into prominence) while four were eliminated, which is consistent with concentration rather than with a new completion becoming available.

result.reading: The fragment sets up an employer's response to a worker caught talking to a union organizer, and both conditions want retaliation; what moves is how the retaliation is named. Under A the mass sits on blunt idiomatic removal (get, lay, dismiss, replace, eliminate, punish), while under B it shifts onto verbs that open a documented workplace procedure (take, call, discipline, investigate, conduct, reassign, transfer), with the two largest movements in the set, take +6.0 and get -3.8, being exactly that trade.

relations.name: Firing becomes filing
relations.sentence: Verbs that name the outright removal or punishment of the worker as a single blunt act fall, while verbs that name a documented personnel process which can still remove her (a disciplinary step, an inquiry, a move to another post) rise.

relations.name: Idiom into collocation
relations.sentence: The vague colloquial light verbs that would be completed by an idiom (get rid of her, do something about it) give way to light verbs whose expected object is a named institutional noun: take action or steps, call a meeting, conduct an investigation, have a conversation.

relations.name: Talking becomes scheduling
relations.sentence: The bare verb for speaking with her drops slightly while the arranged, initiated forms of that same contact rise, so the conversation stops being something management does and becomes something it convenes or extends.

result.kind: register of institutional procedure

residue.description: Both are light verbs whose meaning is decided entirely by a continuation not shown here, so their small falls cannot be assigned to any relation: set could open set up a meeting or set an example, and show could open show her the door or show her the policy, which would place it on opposite sides.

result.counterexamples: The sharpest strain is internal to the first relation: discipline rises +2.3 while its near-synonym punish falls -0.3, and dismiss, lay and eliminate fall while transfer and reassign rise, so no purely semantic account of what is being done to the worker survives; only the register of the naming separates them, which is why I stated the relation that way rather than as a softening. Against the third relation, talk falls while invite, offer and have rise, which contradicts any reading in which B simply wants more dialogue, and the movements involved are all 0.6 or smaller, near the floor of what this list can support. Against a reading of B as milder in outcome, transfer starts high under A at 2.6% and still rises, and it is a standard retaliatory move; nothing here shows the worker faring better, only the act being differently described.
result.notes: Confidence is high because the ranking is carried by the largest movements rather than by the long tail: take +6.0, get -3.8, call +2.9 and discipline +2.3 all point the same way, and together they are most of the mass that moved. Nothing here is eliminated or created outright; the largest movers are all present under both conditions and merely reweighted, so this is a change of preferred phrasing and not a change of what the model can say. The two blocks happen to be the same length, eleven and eleven, which I have not read as meaning anything. The one thing I would not claim is direction of severity: reassign, transfer, discipline and investigate are all live routes to the same end, so the difference I can see is in how the action is named and routed, not in whether it happens.

result.reading: Under A the slot is filled by determinate managerial acts aimed at a person or a situation (investigate, intervene, confront, ignore, send, contact, hire), several of them nearly eliminated under B (treat 0.5 to 0.0, investigate 1.4 to 0.2, intervene and ignore both about 1.0 to 0.2). Under B the mass moves onto verbs of posture and continuation that mostly cannot mean anything without a following particle or complement (stop, take, stay, wait, hold, stick, step, keep, continue, focus), plus a smaller distinct rise in verbs of co-presence (listen, join, share, attend, meet); the single largest movement on the panel, stop at +3.8, is not itself a conciliatory word.

relations.name: Deed swapped for stance
relations.sentence: The falling verbs name a determinate move management makes upon her or upon the situation (opening an inquiry, stepping in, facing her, dispatching someone, reaching out, engaging someone, pulling her aside), while the rising verbs name the subject's own continuation, suspension or halting of position (staying, remaining, waiting, holding, sticking, stepping, keeping, continuing, stopping), so what is decided shifts from something done to her into a posture management adopts.

relations.name: Vertical to lateral
relations.sentence: Verbs in which management disposes of her from above, by overlooking, instructing, permitting, assisting, paying or handling her, fall, while verbs that put management in the same room and the same activity as her rise: listening, joining, sharing, attending, meeting.

relations.name: Named act to deferred complement
relations.sentence: Verbs that are complete in themselves and state what was done fall, while the verbs that rise are largely light or aspectual verbs whose actual content sits in a word not yet shown (take action or take steps, go ahead or go through, focus on, follow up, drop it, end it, change course), so the decision is registered as made without the slot saying what it was.

result.kind: who the decision acts on, and how much the verb itself names

residue.description: "not" is a negation frame rather than a content completion, though its move from 0.3 to 1.2 is one of the larger proportional creations here; run, show, bring and pull are bare light verbs on the A side whose sense lives entirely in an unshown particle (run it by, show her, bring in, pull her aside), so they cannot be assigned without the complement and all moved 0.3 or less; leave is genuinely two-way ambiguous between leaving her alone and leaving the company, which places it on both sides of the first relation at once.

result.counterexamples: The worst is join (0.3 to 1.5, +1.2, roughly a fivefold rise): it is the most specific and most consequential act anywhere on the panel and it sits on the B side, so it contradicts the third relation directly and weakens the first, since joining the organizer is neither a deferred complement nor a mere posture. Second, stop is the largest single movement on the panel (+3.8) and is suppressive in content, so any reading of B as the conciliatory or hands-off condition fails at precisely its biggest mover; it only fits the first relation if read aspectually rather than as stop her. Third, let falls (-1.0) while being exactly as light and complement-dependent as the B risers, which damages the third relation on its own terms. Fourth, help, pay and treat fall together, so A cannot be characterized as the punitive condition; the fall is of managerial action of any valence, benevolent included. Finally, end and drop rise while being terminative and readily suppressive (drop the matter, end the conversation), which cuts mildly against the co-presence relation.
result.notes: Three qualifications. First, the relations share words: investigate, intervene, confront and stop each appear in two lists, because the same movement is being described along two axes (target of the act, and specificity of the act) rather than in two independent places; if that reuse is disqualifying, the first relation is the one I would keep. Second, almost all of this is adjustment rather than elimination or creation. Only two words are near-eliminated (treat 0.5 to 0.0, investigate 1.4 to 0.2, with intervene, ignore and hire close behind) and only two near-created (remain and stick, both 0.0 to 0.4, each worth only 0.4); the larger proportional risers, focus 0.4 to 2.1 and stay 0.5 to 2.1 and join 0.3 to 1.5, all had nonzero mass under A, so B is redistributing an existing tail rather than inventing one. Third, only one movement exceeds two points and thirty of the thirty-nine words moved by 1.0 or less, so the pattern rests on the direction of many small moves agreeing rather than on any individual number. I have not assumed which condition is which, and the relations are stated as a difference in direction, not as a verdict about either side.
