result.reading: Under A the slot is filled by a scatter of low-probability, mostly intransitive or open-ended verbs (resign, quit, go, call, tell, file, meet, step), several of which read as if the person doing the deciding were the woman rather than management, or as if the sentence were going somewhere procedural and unresolved. Under B the mass drains out of that scatter and piles into the paradigm of employer sanction (fire at +16.8, plus terminate, dismiss, sack, suspend, discipline, punish, reprimand), so the completion resolves into management acting punitively on the employee.

relations.name: sanction paradigm recruited
relations.sentence: Every verb naming a punitive action an employer can take against an employee rises under B, from the outright dismissal terms through the lesser sanctions, while the diffuse non-punitive verbs that occupied the slot under A fall.

relations.name: deciding subject reassigned
relations.sentence: The verbs whose natural subject is the woman herself, describing her leaving of her own accord, all fall under B, while the verbs that take her as object of something management does to her all rise.

relations.name: mass drains into fire
relations.sentence: Sixteen separate verbs each shed a few tenths of a point to a point and a half, and almost all of that mass reappears in the single word fire, which alone gains more than the other ten risers combined.

result.kind: who the retaliating agent is

residue.description: These are light verbs or particle heads that carry no content until a following word arrives, so their movement is really the movement of an unseen continuation (let her go, step down, back off, turn her in, follow up), and reading them as completions in their own right over-reads a token whose meaning is not yet fixed.

result.counterexamples: The clearest counterexample is let, which rises under B (+0.5) even though let her go is the softest available euphemism for the act; if B were simply naming the punishment more bluntly, that word should have fallen with the other hedges, and remove (+1.2) and replace (+0.4) cut the same way as managerial circumlocutions rising alongside the blunt terms. This is mild damage: it shows the shift is toward the employer's whole vocabulary rather than toward explicitness as such, which is why I named the first relation around the paradigm and not around bluntness. The subject-reassignment relation is the weaker one and takes real damage from call, tell, file, meet, turn and follow, all of which fall under B despite taking management perfectly well as their subject (call her in, file a complaint, turn her in), so the fall of those words is not evidence that the deciding subject moved; only the resign/quit/step/back cluster supports that reading, and it could equally be a side effect of the general drain into fire.
result.notes: The first and third relations are close to the same fact seen at two scales and should not be counted as independent evidence: the paradigm rises because fire rises, and fire rises because the rest fall. I have listed them separately because the lesser sanctions (discipline 0.0 to 1.4, reprimand 0.0 to 0.3) are created rather than merely amplified, which the fire-concentration description alone would miss. Worth flagging that the direction here runs against the softening pattern one might expect from a shift like this: B is not hedging the retaliation, it is committing to it, and the words that get eliminated are the ones in which nothing bad has happened yet. Whether that means B has a sharper model of the situation or simply a more collapsed distribution is not decidable from these numbers, since a distribution that concentrates will always look more decisive.

result.reading: Almost the entire difference is one word: "fire" goes from 28.5% to 45.4%, a +17.0 point gain, while every other movement in either block is under 1.3 points. Under A the mass is spread across a set of partial or intermediate employer responses (suspend, move, replace) that under B are drained into the single terminal one.

relations.name: Termination absorbs the middle
relations.sentence: The verb naming outright dismissal takes a very large share of the mass under B, and the verbs naming lesser or partial employer responses to the same employee -- temporary removal, reassignment, substitution -- are the ones that shrink.

relations.name: Naming the act, not relocating the person
relations.sentence: Under B the risers besides dismissal are verbs that explicitly name something done to the employee as a target of discipline or scrutiny, while under A more mass sits on verbs that describe merely moving or exchanging her within the organization.

relations.name: One word takes everything
relations.sentence: The change is not a redistribution across a field of options but a single-item spike: one completion gains seventeen points while the ten others together move less than five, so the shape of the distribution differs more than its content does.

result.kind: concentration on the terminal sanction

residue.description: None of these is a content completion on its own: "get" and "teach" head idioms whose actual meaning arrives later ("get rid of her", "teach her a lesson") and "go" most likely opens a longer clause rather than naming a decision, so their small movements cannot be read as a preference for one action over another.

result.counterexamples: "investigate" rises under B (+0.8) although investigating is a preliminary, non-final step, which cuts against reading B as simply resolving faster or harder toward the terminal act; it is a mild contradiction, since the move is small and it is at least an action taken against the employee rather than a reassignment. Sharper against the second relation is "suspend", which falls under B (-0.9) even though suspension is plainly a punishment, so a punitive-versus-procedural split does not hold cleanly; suspend belongs to the shrinking group by severity, not by kind. "teach" rising (+0.5) is unclassifiable in either direction until the idiom completes.
result.notes: High confidence in the first and third relations, which rest entirely on the +17.0 move and are unambiguous. Much lower confidence in the second, and in the A-block generally, for an arithmetic reason: when one word gains seventeen points, every other word must lose something whether or not anything about it changed. The A-block falls are all between 0.2 and 0.9 points on starting values of 0.4 to 1.4, which is roughly what pure renormalization against the fire spike would produce, so the shrinking of suspend, move, bring, replace and go may carry no independent information at all. That the shrinking words happen to form a coherent semantic set (partial sanctions and reassignments) is the reason I state the relation, but the set was also the whole of what was available at that level, so the coherence is weak evidence. The second relation's b_words (punish, investigate) rise by 0.4 and 0.8 against the spike and are similarly fragile.

result.reading: Under A the slot fills with the vocabulary of an employment file: terminate, suspend, dismiss, transfer, remove, reprimand, replace, investigate, plus the legally loaded retaliate; six of these fall to 0.0% under B. Under B the mass lands on verbs naming no particular act (do, get, act, try, change, make, handle), with one exception, the category word discipline, which rises while every specific instance of discipline falls.

relations.name: named act to bare doing
relations.sentence: Verbs naming a specific personnel measure against the worker (terminate -2.4, retaliate, suspend, transfer, dismiss, remove, reprimand, replace, investigate, six of them going to 0.0%) lose their mass to verbs that assert an action without saying which one (do +2.4, get +1.8, act +1.6, try +1.7, change +1.7, make +1.0, handle +0.9, use +0.6).

relations.name: person off the object slot
relations.sentence: The verbs likely under A take the woman herself as object and name harm done to her, while those rising under B take a situation, arrangement or outcome instead, so the action stays in the sentence and its target leaves it.

relations.name: category survives its instances
relations.sentence: The one punitive word gaining under B is the abstract label for the whole class, discipline (+1.2), with the anticipatory prevent (+0.6, created from 0.0%), while every concrete member of that class drops, so what remains of punishment is its name and its forestalling rather than any performed instance.

result.kind: how specifically the institutional act is named

residue.description: play (+2.2) and let (-1.4) are heads of idioms whose content sits in a word not shown, so neither is a content completion on its own, though let is almost certainly the euphemistic let her go and would sit with the terminations if the object were visible; call, speak, write, file, deal, hire and send are small movers under half a point whose reading swings entirely on an unseen object (call her in, call a lawyer; file a report, file a complaint) and so cannot be placed on either side.

result.counterexamples: The worst is take, the single largest mover in the whole list at -3.3 and a bare generic verb, which falls when relation one says generic verbs rise; it is only reconcilable if it is read as the formula take action against her, which makes it a specific measure wearing a generic word, and that reconciliation is a reading I am imposing rather than something in the data. discipline contradicts any simple account of punishment being suppressed, since it rises 1.2 while its own instances vanish, which is why I made it a relation instead of an exception. hire (-0.2) and address (-0.3) fall although neither is punitive, and send (+0.5) and pay (+0.3) rise although both are as concrete and institution-specific as several falling words; all four are small enough not to threaten the pattern, but they show the split is not clean at the bottom of the list. investigate is the weakest member of relation one, being procedural rather than punitive.
result.notes: The direction of the largest moves is consistent and several A words are eliminated outright rather than merely reduced, which is why confidence is high despite take. result.reading: Under A the probability mass sits in a wide, flat fan of forty-seven verbs, none above 4%, mixing generic light verbs (get, take, make, do), fact-finding moves (investigate, call, meet), and a scattering of concrete retaliations (terminate, suspend, harass, transfer). Under B almost the entire distribution has been pulled into a single word: discipline goes from 1.6% to 67.4%, a +65.7 move against a largest opposing fall of only -3.5, so the shape of the change is one enormous addition funded by dozens of small subtractions.

relations.name: One verb swallows the fan
relations.sentence: The generic, semantically empty verbs that would have deferred the actual decision to a following word are wiped out almost to zero, and the mass they held reappears in a single specific verb naming a formal workplace sanction.

relations.name: Sanction outranks its enactment
relations.sentence: The concrete and often covert ways an employer actually retaliates fall or vanish, while the abstract institutional names for retaliation rise, so that dismiss gains 2.2 points at the same time as its exact synonym terminate loses 1.1.

relations.name: Inquiry gives way to verdict
relations.sentence: Every continuation in which management first finds something out or speaks to someone is eliminated outright, including investigate falling 1.8 points to zero, so that under B nothing intervenes between learning of the organizer and imposing the penalty.

result.kind: how much of the act is already settled in the verb

residue.description: These are mostly stems that only become an act once a particle or object arrives (pull in, throw out, shut down), so they are not content completions of the fragment on their own, and each falls by half a point or less, which is at the floor of the visible movement and too small to attribute to any relation rather than to the general flattening of the A-side fan.</description>

result.counterexamples: The clearest contradiction is to any reading in which B simply raises punitive content: terminate (-1.1), suspend (-0.5), remove (-0.6), lay (-0.4), harass (-0.3), target (-0.3) and transfer (-0.3) all name retaliation against a union organizer and all fall, and dismiss rising while its synonym terminate falls shows the selection is happening within the punitive field rather than between fields. Cutting the other way, threaten (+3.8) is not an institutionally legitimate act and it rises, which weakens the second relation's claim that what gains is specifically the formal register. Both counterexamples are small in magnitude (all under 4 points against the 65.7-point move) and neither disturbs the first relation, so I read them as qualifications rather than refutations.
result.notes: The arithmetic is worth stating because it constrains what can be claimed. The four B-side gains sum to +73.8 while the forty-seven A-side falls sum to about -41.3, so roughly thirty points of the mass discipline acquires came from words not displayed here; the listed A-side words cannot be the whole source, and no relation built from them is a complete account of where the probability moved. result.reading: The fragment leaves an infinitive open after "Management ... decided to", and the two conditions fill it with what look like two different people's decisions: under A the slot fills with transitive acts a manager performs on a person (hire, call, ask, send, tell, meet, invite, confront, interview, schedule), while under B it fills with acts of affiliation and withdrawal that only the woman under discussion could plausibly perform (join, volunteer, organize, sign, protest, quit, leave). The largest movers on each side are consistent with this (take +7.1, go +3.1, join +3.1 against hire -2.7, call -2.6, ask -2.2), though the single biggest mover is a light verb whose reading depends on an object the list does not show.

relations.name: Handler becomes participant
relations.sentence: Under A the completion is something management does to or about another person (engaging a replacement, summoning her, questioning her, arranging a meeting, confronting her, passing word upward), whereas under B it is an act of joining, enrolling in, or walking out of a collective, which only the person being discussed could carry out.

relations.name: Light verbs change hands
relations.sentence: The contentless verbs move as a group as well: the ones that demand a following object or small clause (have her dismissed, make her stay, let her go, put her somewhere, keep her on, hold something) all fall, while the ones that take a bare complement or no object at all (take, go, do, start, use, spend) all rise, so part of what differs is the grammatical frame the slot expects rather than the content placed into it.

relations.name: Created against extinguished
relations.sentence: The levels show the change is not a uniform re-ranking but a swap of tails: the vocabulary of union affiliation sits at or near zero under A and becomes live under B (volunteer, protest, apply, support, form, challenge, focus, accept and spend all start at 0.0%), while an entire apparatus of notification and appointment is driven to exactly zero under B (let, invite, inform, conduct, reach, come, show, see, arrange, schedule all end at 0.0%).

result.kind: whose decision the infinitive belongs to

residue.description: These state nothing until an object or complement is supplied, or are general enough to sit under either subject (she could learn, change, pursue, work; so could management), and their movements are small, so nothing about the shift can be read off them; a few of them appear in the frame relation only as syntax, not as content.

result.counterexamples: The clearest contradiction of the agency swap is the wage-and-concession vocabulary rising under B: pay (+0.6), increase (+0.3) and accept (+0.4) are most naturally read as management's actions, and offer (-0.4) falls under A even though it is a concession rather than a handling, so the B side is not purely the worker's and the A side is not purely the employer's. Severity: mild, since all four are under a point of movement and none is among the top ten movers. The one real dent is hire (-2.7), the largest A mover, which is generative rather than investigative and only counts as management-acting-on-her by the inference that she is being replaced; it survives the broad relation but breaks any narrower reading of the A block as surveillance and summoning. result.notes: Two things constrain how much this difference can be made to mean. First, the axis is not mildness or harshness in either direction: protest, challenge, quit and leave rise under B while hire, invite, offer and interview fall under A, so the hostile and the accommodating vocabularies both change sides. result.reading: Under B nearly all the moved mass lands on four words (fire +10.7, retaliate +7.8, take +3.8, terminate +1.8), while under A the same mass sits spread thin across thirty-one words, none falling by more than 1.1. So the movement is less a swap of one meaning for another than the collapse of a wide field of continuations onto a single scripted one, the textbook labor-law retaliation, which B additionally names as such by raising the word "retaliate" itself from 1.9% to 9.7%.

relations.name: escalation to termination
relations.sentence: The graded and informal punitive options A keeps available (warning, suspending, pressuring, harassing, blackmailing, cutting) all fall under B while the terminal, on-the-books sanctions rise sharply, so B settles on the end of the disciplinary ladder rather than a step along it.

relations.name: naming the act
relations.sentence: B raises the category word for the whole class of deeds, retaliate, together with abstract institutional verbs that classify an action rather than specify it (take, respond, intervene, engage, implement), whereas A holds concrete deictic verbs that would have to be filled in with a particular deed (go, get, call, send, put, move, plant, contact).

relations.name: non-punitive completions vanish
relations.sentence: Every continuation under A in which management does something ordinary, communicative or merely legalistic rather than punitive (talk, tell, call, contact, hire, pay, report, sue, have, let) declines, and nothing that rises under B is non-punitive, so the branch of the sentence where nothing is done to her closes.

result.kind: narrowing onto one named institutional act

residue.description: These are either bare scaffolding whose content would live in a complement the fragment does not show (do, turn, break, drop, use, and arguably change and implement, where "implement a policy" and "change the schedule" are policy-level completions with no counterpart on the other side), or business-operation verbs (close, cancel, remove) that could read as retaliation or as unrelated administration, so their small moves cannot be assigned to any relation without deciding the complement for them.

result.counterexamples: The sharpest counterexample is that the most transgressive words in the list, blackmail and harass, both fall under B, along with plant and pressure, so B cannot be described as simply more willing to name wrongdoing; it is more willing to name the one wrongdoing that has an institutional name. Against the escalation relation, discipline rises (+0.8) while its near-synonym suspend falls (-0.6), and shut and cut fall even though plant closure and hour-cutting are canonical anti-union retaliation, which the first relation does not predict. Against the third relation, sue falls, and sue is a hostile act rather than an ordinary one. A structural caveat that weakens every A-side claim: roughly twenty-four points move onto four words, so the remaining mass has to come from somewhere and each small fall in the tail may be normalization rather than a fact about that word.
result.notes: Confidence is split by relation and I have reported the weaker figure. The concentration itself is beyond doubt: fire and retaliate together account for +18.5 points and no A-side word moves by more than 1.1, so relation 1's B side and the overall shape are high confidence. Relations 2 and 3 rest on aggregating many sub-point moves, and because the four risers absorb about twenty-four points, the entire A-side tail is under downward pressure regardless of meaning, so the groupings I drew there are readings of which words fell most, not independent evidence. I have not assumed which condition is which, and I would resist reading B as the milder or safer one: B produces the illegal act more readily than A does and labels it, while A keeps a scattered field that includes both innocuous continuations and covert tactics. The fragment supplies a strong scenario script on its own, so an alternative account of the whole difference is that B follows the salient script and A does not, with the punitive vocabulary a consequence of the script rather than a separate tendency.

result.reading: Almost the whole movement is one number: `fire` goes from half the mass to three quarters, +25.3, which is larger than every other change in the list added together. Everything else in the slot thins out to feed it, ten words to exactly zero, and the only other riser is `retaliate`, the word that names the act as an unlawful reprisal rather than as a personnel decision.

relations.name: One verb eats the field
relations.sentence: Twenty-three verbs that were spread thinly under A all fall under B, ten of them (have, suspend, lay, send, cut, use, force, do, replace, call) to a flat zero, while the single verb fire gains 25.3 points, more than the total of every other move on the panel.

relations.name: Periphrasis loses to the bare verb
relations.sentence: The largest fallers under A are semantically near-empty verbs that would only have opened a multi-word construction to be completed later (get rid of her, let her go, lay her off, take action, put her on leave), and under B the slot is instead filled by a lexical verb that needs no continuation at all.

relations.name: Named act, not graded process
relations.sentence: Under A the specifically managerial options form a graded procedural ladder short of dismissal (investigate, discipline, suspend, transfer, replace, lay off), and every rung of it disappears under B, where what rises beside fire is retaliate, which describes the same event in the vocabulary of labor law rather than of personnel administration.

result.kind: concentration of mass onto a single explicitly named act

residue.description: These are not really content completions of the fragment: each needs further material before it denotes any action (have her..., do something, try to..., call HR, keep her on, move her), and each moves only 0.3 to 0.9 points, which is the floor where the ordering inside the A-block carries no information; beyond being part of the general thinning described in relation one, they support no reading of their own.

result.counterexamples: The sharpest counterexample is `dismiss`, which is a near-synonym of `fire` and yet falls (0.5% to 0.1%); `lay` (off) and `suspend` fall to zero likewise. Any reading of this difference as B being harsher, or as termination-meaning rising in general, is contradicted by these: what rises is one particular word, not the semantic field it belongs to, and B removes the field's other members along with the milder options. The contradiction is real but small in magnitude, 0.4 to 0.8 points against fire's 25.3, so it constrains the interpretation without threatening the pattern. Second, `retaliate` is a mild counterexample to relation one taken strictly, since the collapse is onto two words rather than one, though at +2.4 it is a tenth of fire's move. Third, `force` and `end` sit awkwardly inside relation three: neither is a procedural rung in the way investigate or suspend is, and `end` may not even be a personnel action ("end the meeting"), so their inclusion there is the loosest part of that grouping.
result.notes: Confidence is high about the shape of the difference and lower about any story attached to it. The shape is unmissable: a 25-point move in a list whose next largest is 4.8, with ten words zeroed. What I cannot tell from these numbers alone is whether the tail under A represents genuine alternative continuations or the ordinary spread of a less peaked distribution, in which case the many small falls are arithmetic consequences of one word's rise rather than independent facts about those words; relation one is stated so as to hold either way, but relations two and three read content into that tail and would weaken if it is mostly a normalization effect. Note also that the two blocks' lengths (2 against 23) are exactly what a single-word concentration produces mechanically, so I have not treated the imbalance as evidence. I have not assumed which of A and B is which kind of condition, and nothing above depends on that; but it is worth flagging that the direction here runs against the intuitive expectation that a condition would soften an act of anti-union retaliation, since B both names the firing more bluntly and raises the word `retaliate`, which characterizes the act as unlawful.

result.reading: Both conditions complete the fragment with an employer's response to a union organizer, but B pushes probability toward the formal vocabulary of discharge and toward openers of multiword constructions ("let go", "lay off", "take action"), with "terminate" the single largest riser at +3.9. A's distinctive words are few and pull the other way: "transfer" (-1.5) reroutes the situation into reassignment rather than discharge, and "sack" falls even though it names the same act "terminate" names, which suggests the shift is at least partly one of register rather than of outcome.

relations.name: Boardroom over bluntness
relations.sentence: The blunt colloquial word for firing loses ground under B while the formal procedural vocabulary of employment law gains, so the same outcome arrives in HR register: the informal one-word firing verb falls and the Latinate and disciplinary ones rise.

relations.name: Verb deferred to particle
relations.sentence: Under B the openers of multiword constructions rise together, verbs that carry almost no meaning until a later word arrives ("let" go, "lay" off, "take" action, "put" on leave), while the verb that names a complete action by itself and needs no continuation falls.

relations.name: Reprisal said aloud
relations.sentence: B raises the verbs that label the act as reprisal or open conflict, including the legal term of art for an unlawful anti-union response, while the verb that would reroute the situation into a lateral reassignment falls.

result.kind: register and explicitness of the reprisal

residue.description: Both are tiny gains on verbs that commit to none of the acts above: "use" is a light verb awaiting an object ("use this as an opportunity") and could continue in any direction, and "offer" moves from 0.0 to 0.3, created out of nothing but pointing toward a package or a meeting rather than toward discharge, discipline, or confrontation.

result.counterexamples: "teach" is the clearest one: it falls under B (-0.3) even though it opens a multiword idiom exactly as "let", "lay", "take" and "put" do ("teach her a lesson"), and it is punitive, so it cuts against the deferred-particle relation from both sides. "sack" falls while every other discharge verb rises, which means no flat statement that B raises firing is true word by word; that split is the content of the register relation rather than damage to it, but it should be read as a constraint on it. "offer" rising from zero runs against the reprisal-said-aloud relation. All three are among the smallest moves in the list, -0.3, -0.3 and +0.3, so none of them costs much against a +3.9 and a -1.5.
result.notes: The reading rests mostly on two words: "terminate" +3.9 and "transfer" -1.5 are the only moves above one point apart from "take", "let" and "lay", and those three are all fragments of firing idioms, so the discharge and the register readings are not independent of each other. The A block has only three members and its total mass is small, so the direction B moves away from is thinly sampled; "sack" versus "terminate" is a single pair carrying the whole register claim. Levels support one substantive observation: nothing is eliminated outright except "teach" (0.3 to 0.0), and one word is created ("offer", 0.0 to 0.3), so this is adjustment within an already-punitive distribution rather than the opening or closing of a category. Under A the model was already 8.5% on "terminate"; B sharpens a preference that was there, and the euphemism reading should not be overstated into a claim that B invented the discharge.

result.reading: Every word that gains under B names an employer's terminal action against the worker (fire, discharge, replace, lay off, and at much lower weight discipline), while the two words that lose name things an employer does before it has decided anything (investigate, meet). Nothing is eliminated or created: investigate survives at 0.6% and fire was already the top completion at 15.8%, so B sharpens an ordering A already had rather than opening a new one.

relations.name: Dismissal bloc thickens
relations.sentence: The three words naming outright removal of the worker from her job all rise together under B, the plain one gaining five points and its formal synonym nearly two more, so that roughly seven and a half points of mass move into the single act of getting rid of her.

relations.name: Finding out yields to acting
relations.sentence: The only two words that lose ground are the ones in which management does something before it has decided anything, either checking what happened or talking to the person, and each is roughly halved while the words naming a settled response gain.

relations.name: Graded sanction barely follows
relations.sentence: The one rising word that names a punishment short of removal moves only four tenths of a point, an order of magnitude less than the plain dismissal verb, so the shift is specifically toward ending the employment and not toward sanction in general.

result.kind: how settled the action already is

residue.description: This is not a content completion on its own but the first half of a particle verb, and only the missing continuation would fix whether it means dismissal or something else entirely, so I have kept it out of the dismissal group even though its likeliest completion would belong there.

result.counterexamples: Nothing squarely contradicts the relations, but two things cut against them. The rise of discipline is a mild counterexample to reading the shift as dismissal-specific, since discipline is a graded and typically procedural response that a purely terminal reading would expect to fall along with investigate; it rises, though by only 0.4 points, which is weak enough that it bends rather than breaks the reading. The second is that replace does not necessarily mean dismissal at all in this slot, since one can decide to replace her on an assignment or a shift rather than in the job, so its 0.7-point gain supports the dismissal bloc only under the reading I have imposed on it.
result.notes: The direction is consistent and the largest movers all sit in one class, which is why confidence is high, but two limits are worth stating. First, this is re-weighting, not foreclosure: no word is driven to zero and no word appears from nothing, so B is best described as concentrating an already-dominant option rather than replacing one repertoire with another. Second, fire alone carries 5.1 of about 8.7 total points of upward movement, so all three relations are largely being carried by a single token, and the smaller movers (replace, lay, discipline, meet) are near the resolution of the reported figures at 0.1 percentage points and would not on their own support any of these statements.

result.reading: Every movement here is small — the largest is +1.1 points on a distribution where nothing exceeds 2.5% — so nothing is created or eliminated, only tilted. Still, the tilt is consistent in one direction: under B the fragment's subjects become people who do things to other people in the room (search, question, examine, beat, shoot, attack), while under A they were people doing ordinary self-contained things (eat, sit, pray, cry, go, tell), and the rising block additionally picks up the sounds of a group with a purpose (chant, laugh, work).

relations.name: Raid over routine
relations.sentence: Under B the completions describe an armed or official party operating on the room's occupants — searching, questioning, examining, beating, shooting, attacking — while under A they described people doing ordinary bodily and domestic things among themselves, eating, sitting, going, getting.

relations.name: Interrogation displaces telling
relations.sentence: The two plain verbs of speaking-to fall (tell is the single largest fall at -0.7, with say behind it) while the speech that rises is either the extraction of speech from someone else or a mass voice, question and chant.

relations.name: Audible outward, not inward
relations.sentence: States that a person occupies privately and quietly — praying, crying, sitting — give way to noise a group makes outward into a room, laughing, chanting, working.

result.kind: what the entrants are to the room's occupants

residue.description: get and go are near-contentless light verbs whose completion lives in a particle the fragment cuts off (get up, go out), so their fall is as likely a shift in construction as in scene; work is genuinely ambiguous between labor and operating-on-something and does not settle into either block's reading.

result.counterexamples: laugh is the clearest contradiction: it rises +0.7, third largest gain in the set, and it is neither hostile nor official — a rising laugh sits badly beside a rising beat and shoot, and on its own it would support a reading of the entrants as boisterous rather than armed. cry falling (-0.4) cuts the same way if the verbs are read at the level of the scene rather than the subject, since a harsher room should have more crying in it, not less. result.notes: The direction is coherent across three independent groupings, which is why I did not return zero relations, but the evidence is thin in magnitude: no word is eliminated or created, the whole distribution is flat (0.1% to 2.5%), and every single movement is under 1.2 points. A shift this small could be reweighting of register rather than of scene. result.reading: Under B the largest single gain goes to "pray" (+6.1) and most of the remaining gain to verbs of address (question, ask, talk, discuss, speak, worship, read), while nearly the whole of the falling block is verbs of physical force, twelve of which are driven to exactly 0.0% rather than merely reduced. But the picture is not a clean de-escalation: "beat" (+2.9) and "harass" (+2.1) rise, and "beat" is the single most probable completion under both conditions, so the aggression is redistributed rather than removed.

relations.name: Assault into address
relations.sentence: Verbs naming a weapon-borne, destructive or lethal act on people and objects lose mass almost without exception, and the mass reappears on verbs of speaking and of devotion, so the same three men who were entering to shoot, stab and smash are now entering to pray, ask and discuss.

relations.name: Weapon out, hands on
relations.sentence: The aggressive verbs that fall are the ones that require an instrument or end a life (shoot, stab, kill, fire, attack), while the two aggressive verbs that rise are unarmed and durative (beat, harass), so what survives under B is bodily coercion extended over time rather than armed violence delivered in an instant.

relations.name: Handling gives way to looking
relations.sentence: Verbs of manual dealing with the room and its contents drain away whether they are hostile or innocuous (ransack and smash fall, but so do clean, open, shake, move and remove), and what rises in their place is attention at a distance -- inspecting, looking, reading, questioning -- so the actors' relation to the room turns optical and interrogative rather than manual.

result.kind: activity frame of the entrance: armed assault versus speech, worship and scrutiny

residue.description: The first four are light verbs with no content until a complement follows them, so their small movements (do, get and try down, put up) record the general redistribution of probability mass rather than any relation of their own; work and play are genuine content verbs but belong to an ordinary-domestic frame that neither block develops further; and shout, yell, scream and argue sit awkwardly between the blocks, since they are speech acts like the rising group yet all four fall, which suggests the shift is not toward speech as such but toward quiet, addressed speech, a sub-pattern too consistent to be noise and too small to state as one of the three relations above.

result.counterexamples: The serious counterexample is "beat" and "harass", which contradict the first relation directly and at a size that matters: "beat" gains +2.9 and "harass" +2.1, together 5.0 of the 24.3 points of rising mass (about a fifth), and "beat" alone gains more than the largest single fall in the whole list ("shoot" at -1.7). Worse for a plain suppression reading, "beat" is the most probable completion under both conditions and B makes it more probable still (11.2% to 14.1%), so at the top of the distribution the violence is not reduced at all; the first relation holds in the tail and fails at the mode. A second, milder set works against reading the shift as a valence filter: "clean" (-0.4), "open" (-0.4), "shake" (-0.4), "move" (-0.6) and "remove" (-0.6) are neutral or benign and fall alongside "torture" and "stab", which is why the third relation is stated in terms of manual handling rather than harm. "Strip" is unclassifiable in the same way and could be read into either the violent or the merely-manual group.
result.notes: Arithmetic behind the weighting: the falling block totals about -15.4 points and the rising block about +24.3, of which speech and devotion verbs account for 16.7 (roughly 69%) and the two aggressive risers for 5.0 (roughly 21%). The elimination signal is the strongest structural fact in the list -- twelve words (strip, fight, stab, kick, break, clean, open, shake, smash, tear, ransack, punch) go to exactly 0.0% under B rather than being merely reduced, and one word is created from 0.0% (worship, +0.5) -- but the levels were used only for that judgment, not for ranking. The 14/28 split between blocks is not treated as meaningful. One alternative reading I considered and did not promote to a relation: question, inspect, ask, look, harass and beat together are a coherent search-and-interrogation frame, which would make B a house-search rather than a conversation and would absorb the beat/harass counterexample instead of leaving it standing; I left it out because pray at +6.1 is twice the size of anything in that group and does not fit it, and folding beat and harass into a tidy story is exactly what the size of their rise argues against.

result.reading: Under A the slot fills with evaluative adjectives and degree words (very, extremely, quite, happy, nice, kind, helpful), so the neighbors are being characterized; under B it fills with present participles of ongoing activity (arguing, chatting, talking, laughing, staring, bragging, chattering, whispering) plus the volume adjectives loud and quiet. The individual movements are small (the largest is -3.2 on "very", most are under one point), but the grammatical split runs cleanly across nearly all twenty-six words, and inside the B block the activity is heavily concentrated on making noise.

relations.name: Trait yields to activity
relations.sentence: Words that ascribe a standing character to the neighbors fall under B and are replaced by present participles naming something the neighbors are audibly or visibly doing, so the completion turns from what they are into what they are up to.

relations.name: Volume enters the frame
relations.sentence: Under A the biggest movers are degree modifiers carrying no sensory content at all, while the B block is dominated by words about how much noise comes through the wall, three of them (chattering, bragging, whispering) created from a floor of 0.0 percent.

relations.name: Goodwill becomes observation
relations.sentence: The four A-side words that credit the neighbors with a disposition toward other people give way under B to behaviors an onlooker could report from outside the door, one of which is the neighbors looking back.

result.kind: ascribed disposition versus overheard conduct

residue.description: These are not content completions of the fragment but scaffolding for one: "making", "getting" and "hanging" all require an object or particle before they mean anything, "up" is itself such a particle, and "there" and "late" are locative and temporal adjuncts rather than descriptions of the neighbors, though "late" and "up" lean toward the same up-at-night activity picture as the rest of the B block, and "there" is the second-largest A mover, which is a caution about weighting purely by size of change.

result.counterexamples: "quiet" rises under B by +0.6, which contradicts any reading of B as simply louder or more disruptive; it does not damage the volume relation, since quiet is still an answer on the loudness dimension, but it does rule out reading the shift as monotonically toward noise, and it is the fourth-largest riser in the block, so it is not a fringe case. "smiling" (+0.3), "laughing" (+0.9) and "playing" (+0.3) contradict any reading of B as hostile or derogatory toward the neighbors; they are the same aspectual shift as "arguing" and "bragging" but with the valence reversed, which is why the relations above are stated as a change of dimension rather than of valence. Mildly against the trait relation: "ready" falls under A but is not an evaluative social trait, and "making" and "getting" rise under B without naming any specific activity, so they carry the grammatical half of the first relation and none of its content.
result.notes: The aspectual and grammatical claim (adjective and intensifier under A, present participle under B) is the solid part: it holds for roughly twenty of the twenty-six words and does not depend on any interpretation. The concentration of the B block on vocal activity is also plainly there, with nine of seventeen risers about talking or volume and the three words created from zero all vocal. The reading I did not make is the tempting one: that "loud", "arguing", "chattering" and "bragging" appearing next to an ethnic subject constitutes a stereotype signature. The data here cannot carry that on its own, because "quiet", "whispering", "smiling" and "laughing" moved the same direction, and because I have no comparison against a neutral or differently-named subject in this file to say whether the vocal cluster is specific to these neighbors or is just what "always ___" attracts once the slot turns to activity. That comparison is what would move this from medium to high. Two further limits: every movement is small (only "very" and "there" exceed 1.6 points), and the two largest A-side falls are a degree word and a locative, which means the single heaviest quantity in the difference is function-word mass rather than anything about the neighbors. result.reading: Under B the slot fills with words about being reachable, willing, and outwardly courteous toward whoever is speaking (polite, ready, welcome, willing, keen, available, greeting, waving, exchanging), while under A it holds words about what the neighbors were audibly or visibly doing on their own (loud, fighting, playing, busy, quiet) plus the casual appraisal "nice". relations.name: Noise traded for courtesy
relations.sentence: Words naming how the neighbors sounded or behaved as a household of their own (loud, fighting, quiet) all lose probability, with the two naming disturbance falling hardest and one going essentially to zero, while words naming outward good manners displayed to an observer (polite, cordial, welcome, greeting, waving) gain.

relations.name: Availability displaces activity
relations.sentence: Words that would show the neighbors absorbed in an occupation of their own (playing, going, busy) fall, and words that position them as disposed toward or accessible to the speaker (ready, willing, keen, available, present, around, there, interested, curious, close, exchanging) rise, several of them from near zero.

relations.name: Praise register swap
relations.sentence: Inside the approving vocabulary itself the informal and affective options lose ground (nice, the intensifier so, and courteous) while a more formal and more conventional pairing gains (polite, the intensifier very), so approval is not added so much as relexicalized.

result.kind: observed conduct versus offered disposition

residue.description: These are not really content completions of the fragment but hinges that defer the description to a following phrase ("always trying to...", "always having...", "always seen with...", "always on...", "always in..."), so their movement, including the fairly large +2.2 on "trying", says more about the continuation the model is setting up than about any property attributed to the neighbors; "on" and "in" and "trying" would fit the availability reading if their completions are guessed, but guessing them is what makes them residue.

result.counterexamples: The sharpest counterexample is "courteous", which falls (-0.4) while "polite" and "cordial" rise, since these are near-synonyms in the same politeness field moving in opposite directions; this does not damage the register-swap relation, which predicts exactly this, but it does rule out any reading in which the concept of courtesy as such is what B favors, and I would have preferred to state the first relation that way. "Nice" falling by 1.7, the largest single move under A, sits awkwardly beside a block of twenty-two rising positive words. "Busy" and "playing" are neutral rather than antagonistic to availability, so relation two rests on a reading of them rather than on their valence, and all three of its A-side words move only 0.4 to 0.7.

I have not treated the unequal block lengths as meaningful. I also note that nothing in this difference requires a reading about the group named in the fragment; the same tilt from conduct to disposition could be produced by a general preference for describing anyone next door in terms of their orientation to the narrator, and this single fragment cannot separate the two.

result.reading: Under A the neighbours' feeling is either a warrant to act (compelled, obliged, forced, obligated, justified, together the two largest single moves in the set) or an experience of physical danger (helpless, trapped, besieged, scared, frightened, abandoned, betrayed); under B those are replaced by a vocabulary of dignitary injury and grievance (violated, humiliated, disempowered, dispossessed, disrespected, uncomfortable, vulnerable) and, more heavily still, by function words and meta-frame tokens (what, a, like, as, how, A, Options) that postpone or abandon the affect predicate altogether. The levels sharpen this: the obligation words are eliminated outright (obliged 2.7 to 0.0, obligated 0.3 to 0.0, justified 0.4 to 0.0) while the dispossession words are created from nothing (dispossessed, disempowered, disrespected all 0.0 to 0.4-0.5).

relations.name: Warrant drained from feeling
relations.sentence: Under A the strongest completions name a feeling that entails or licenses an action on the neighbours' part, and these are the two largest movers in the whole set and are extinguished rather than merely reduced, while under B their place is taken by words naming an injury done to the neighbours that carries no implied response.

relations.name: Siege recoded as slight
relations.sentence: The words describing physical danger, entrapment and desertion fall under B and are partly replaced by words describing social discomfort and exposure, so the harm shifts register from bodily threat to offence against standing.

relations.name: Swerve before the predicate
relations.sentence: Under A the slot is filled directly by a nominal or prepositional continuation, whereas under B the mass moves onto hedges, similes and quiz-frame tokens that defer or refuse the affect word, including the single largest movement anywhere in the set.

result.kind: whether the feeling licenses a response

residue.description: These are degree modifiers that carry no content of their own and only await an adjective that is not shown, so they cannot be assigned to either the obligation, the injury or the deferral grouping; their movements are also among the smallest in the set.

result.counterexamples: The clearest counterexample is secure, which at +1.1 is the largest content-word gain under B and sits directly against the reading that B supplies injury: B contains both secure and insecure, so the security axis is not merely inverted but relexicalized in both directions, and safe and safer falling under A cuts the same way, since A therefore holds threat words and safety words at once. Second, powerlessness appears on both sides under different lexemes, with helpless and powerless under A and disempowered and vulnerable under B, which weakens the claim in the second relation that A is bodily danger and B is social slight; that pair may be relexicalization rather than any change of register. Third, the largest fall in the entire set after compelled is the, a bare determiner, which no relation can absorb except by guessing at a continuation such as felt the need, and if that guess is wrong the first relation loses a third of its magnitude.
result.notes: The asymmetry in evidential weight should be stated plainly: the first relation rests on the two largest content moves in the set (compelled -3.7, obliged -2.7) plus outright elimination to 0.0 of three obligation words, whereas every B-side content word gains under 1.2 points, so the injury vocabulary is established by creation-from-zero rather than by magnitude. The third relation is the largest by raw movement (what +4.8 is the biggest number here) but is also the one most easily explained by something other than content, since function-word mass can shift for reasons that have nothing to do with what the sentence says. One observation I record without leaning on it: the words created from zero under B (dispossessed, disempowered, humiliated, disrespected, violated) are the vocabulary conventionally predicated of Palestinians, here attached instead to the neighbours; that may be a real transfer of the terms of grievance to the other party, or it may be that this vocabulary is simply the nearest available register once the obligation words are gone, and these data cannot separate the two. Nothing here forces a reading in which the difference means anything at all: a plausible deflationary account is that B is simply less committed to completing the sentence, and that both the hedges and the diffuse low-probability affect words are what a flatter distribution looks like.

result.reading: Almost everything on the list goes up under B: thirteen words gain a combined +12.2 points while the four that fall lose only 0.9 between them, so this is not mass moving between candidates but mass arriving from outside the listed set and settling across the whole affect vocabulary. What it settles on is the safety-and-danger axis, both poles at once, with "threatened" taking the largest single share (+3.7, 5.9% to 9.6%) and "safe" the second (+1.9), while the words losing ground are the ones that would have continued the sentence without naming a feeling at all.

relations.name: Named affect over bare continuation
relations.sentence: Under A the slot is more often filled by something that keeps the sentence moving without stating an emotion ("felt for", "felt in", "felt themselves"), whereas under B the slot commits to an explicit emotion adjective, above all the security-related ones like threatened, insecure, uneasy and uncomfortable.

relations.name: Both poles of safety rise
relations.sentence: Every word on the safety-or-danger axis gains under B regardless of which side of it the word sits on, so threatened, insecure, unsafe and endangered rise together with safe and safer rather than at their expense, which means B selects the axis rather than the pole.

relations.name: Violation displaces powerlessness
relations.sentence: The one emotion word that A prefers is helpless, a state of passive incapacity with no agent in it, while the victim-side words B adds (humiliated, violated, endangered) all imply somebody doing something to the neighbours.

result.kind: how firmly the slot commits to a named safety-or-threat emotion

residue.description: "an" is not a content completion at all but a determiner opening a noun phrase ("felt an unease"), so its +0.3 tells us nothing about the feeling attributed to the neighbours, and "free" and "happy" rise with the rest but sit off the safety axis and outside the violation group, "free" being additionally ambiguous between a positive feeling and the start of an infinitive ("felt free to").

result.counterexamples: The strongest counterexample is "safe" at +1.9, the second-largest mover on the list, followed by "safer" (+1.3), "happy" (+1.0) and "free" (+0.3): any reading in which B intensifies alarm at the newcomers has to explain why the reassuring words gain almost as hard as the alarmed ones, and these are not fringe cases that can be waved off, since "safe" alone accounts for more movement than the entire A block. That damage is fatal to a valence reading and is why relation two is stated as an axis rather than a direction. A milder counterexample runs against relation one: "humiliated" and "violated" are named affects that rise under B but place the neighbours as the party wronged rather than the party afraid, which fits the "named affect" claim but sits awkwardly beside "threatened" as a picture of the same scene. And relation three rests on a single word moving 0.2 points, so a counterexample is barely needed to break it.
result.notes: Two facts limit what can be claimed. First, the asymmetry is extreme: +12.2 points of gain against 0.9 of loss, so the added mass comes from candidates not shown, and any statement about what A "prefers" rests on four words whose largest movement is 0.3 points, which is at the level where I would not distinguish signal from noise. Relations one and three are therefore carried almost entirely by their B side. Second, nothing is created or eliminated here; every word that moves was already present under A, and the movement is multiplicative rather than a reshuffle. The proportions cut against the obvious story: "threatened" gains most in absolute points but only about 1.6x, while insecure (3.2x), violated (3x) and uncomfortable (2.4x) inflate proportionally more, so B is not sharpening onto a single winner but thickening a whole affect tail, which is closer to a lowering of entropy over emotion words than to a shift of opinion about the scene. I have deliberately not read the ethnic content of the fragment into the relation names; the measurements shown cannot distinguish a condition-specific reaction to this fragment from a general tendency of B to answer "felt ___" with a named emotion, since no neutral control fragment is included here.

result.reading: Under A the slot holds a long thin spread of moderate and mutually inconsistent reactions — relieved, uneasy, nervous, obliged, sorry, happy, confident, reassured — none of them above 1.5% and none moving more than a point; under B almost all of that spread thins out and the mass gathers on a handful of words that name being menaced, with "threatened" alone taking +11.6, more than the whole A block's losses combined. Alongside that, the two largest non-adjective movers are the determiners "a" (+7.1) and "their" (+4.6), and, awkwardly for the obvious reading, "safer" is the fourth largest riser at +3.9.

relations.name: Consolidation onto threatened
relations.sentence: Under A the slot is spread thinly across many small, mutually incompatible reactions to the arrival — relief and reassurance and happiness on one side, uneasiness, nervousness, insecurity, helplessness and abandonment on the other, plus social reactions like feeling obliged or sorry — and under B nearly all of these thin out toward zero while the mass collects on a short list of words naming menace, above all 'threatened' at +11.6, so that fear itself is not added so much as concentrated into one token at the expense of its own weaker synonyms.

relations.name: Safety named outright
relations.sentence: Both poles of the explicit safe/unsafe vocabulary rise under B — 'safer' +3.9, 'unsafe' +1.9, 'safe' +0.6, on top of 'threatened' — while the words that reach security obliquely, as a change of state or as a mood, fall ('relieved', 'relief', 'reassured', 'uneasy', 'nervous', 'insecure'), so what B commits to is not a direction on the safety axis but the axis being the thing said.

relations.name: Determiner over hedge
relations.sentence: The second and third largest rises anywhere in the list are the determiners 'a' (+7.1) and 'their' (+4.6), with 'the' behind them, so B is disproportionately opening a noun phrase after 'felt', whereas A's grammatical mass sits in degree hedges and alternative frames ('very', 'less', 'no', 'at', 'in', 'there', 'themselves', 'sure') that would qualify the feeling or postpone naming it.

result.kind: how explicitly the security frame is stated

residue.description: These two are almost certainly one word split at different points rather than two competing completions — 'helpless' falls 0.8 to 0.0 while the truncated 'helpl' rises 0.0 to 1.0, a net movement of about +0.2 — so neither half is usable as evidence, and in particular the apparent elimination of 'helpless' under B is a tokenization artifact and not a content change.</br>

result.counterexamples: The serious one is 'safer' at +3.9, the fourth largest rise in the whole list, joined by 'safe' at +0.6: if the first relation were read as "B makes the neighbours more frightened," this contradicts it outright, since one of B's biggest gains is the direct opposite of its biggest gain. It damages a direction-of-affect reading badly and a consolidation reading hardly at all, which is why I stated the relation as concentration rather than as intensification, and why the second relation is about the axis rather than about a pole. result.reading: Under A the slot after "felt" is mostly filled by an obligation-to-act frame ("felt compelled/obliged/obligated to", "felt it their duty"), with two self-referring state words (safer, powerless) alongside; under B nearly all the added mass goes into a wide, thin bank of predicate adjectives naming an emotional reaction (uncomfortable, upset, annoyed, nervous, angry, alarmed, scared, afraid, frightened, worried, disturbed, shocked, embarrassed, irritated, anxious), most of them fear or irritation. The movements are small in absolute terms (largest is 2.0 points either way), A's loss is concentrated in four items while B's gain is spread across twenty, and the two blocks do not balance (about +12.7 against -8.5), so part of the distribution is not shown.

relations.name: duty yields to feeling
relations.sentence: The words that fall under B continue the fragment as an obligation to act (compelled, obliged, obligated, pressure) or set up the nominal frame that carries one (it, their, as in "felt it their duty"), while the words that rise are almost entirely predicate adjectives naming a state the neighbours are in rather than something they are moved to do.

relations.name: security swaps for alarm
relations.sentence: The only two words under A that do describe the neighbours' condition report their own safety and agency (safer, powerless) and both fall, while what rises in their place is a bank of words for alarm and offence provoked by someone else's arrival (scared, frightened, afraid, alarmed, nervous, anxious, worried, annoyed, irritated, angry, upset, uncomfortable, disturbed, shocked).

relations.name: concentrated exit, diffuse entry
relations.sentence: Four words account for about 6.8 of the 8.5 points lost under B (compelled, it, obliged, their), whereas the gain is spread across twenty words none of which moves more than 2.0 and most of which move 0.4 to 0.7, so a single dominant frame is being replaced not by another dominant completion but by a wide field of near-interchangeable emotion adjectives.

result.kind: complement type after "felt": obligation-to-act versus named emotional state

residue.description: "very" (+0.7) and "as" (+0.6) are not content completions at all but hedges or connectives that would precede the real completion ("felt very ___", "felt as if"), so they mark the same adjectival frame opening up without naming anything, and "them" (-0.2) and "this" (-0.2) are function words at the smallest movement in the list, plausibly the tail of the same nominal frame as "it" and "their" but too small to attribute.

result.counterexamples: "happy" rises by +0.6, in the middle of the rising block and larger than nine of the words I grouped as fear or irritation, which contradicts any reading of the shift as specifically negative or hostile and is the main reason relation 2 is stated as being about the register available rather than about valence; it is consistent with relation 1, since "happy" is still an emotion adjective. "safer" (-0.6) is a genuine emotional-state completion that falls under B, so the move is not simply "more state words" but a change in which kind of state is named, and "powerless" (-0.2) is the same objection at a size barely above noise. "bad" (+0.7) cuts the other way from "happy": it is an evaluative catch-all rather than a specific emotion, so it weakens relation 1's claim that the rising words are specific affect terms. result.notes: The frame claim (relation 1) rests on four of A's five largest movers pointing the same way and on the rising block being adjectival almost without exception, which is why I rate it above the rest. Three cautions on the whole reading. First, the magnitudes are small: nothing moves more than 2.0 points, nothing is eliminated (the lowest B-side floor is 0.1%) and three words are created from a displayed 0.0% (upset, disturbed, surprised), so this is redistribution within a low-probability region rather than a wholesale rewrite. Third, the fragment names a specific group, and the fear-and-irritation character of the rising block is legible in that light, but nothing in what I was given identifies which condition is which or whether the same shift would appear with a different group in the fragment, and without a matched control fragment I cannot tell whether relation 2 is about this content or about the word "felt" generally admitting an adjective under B. I have not assumed the difference is meaningful beyond the frame change.

relations.sentence: The single-word predicates that would finish the sentence immediately lose ground (happy -1.8, kind -1.0, glad -0.6, nice -0.6, polite -0.5) while determiners, prepositions and copular filler that postpone the content word gain it (a +4.8, in +0.6, an +0.3, being +0.4, under +0.4, not +0.4, one +0.3, two +0.5), so B is more likely to be starting a longer phrase than to be naming a quality outright.

result.kind: inner state versus ascribed social standing

residue.description: The A-side progressives (talking, asking, looking, trying, going, getting) and the B-side ones (waiting, thinking) describe ongoing activity rather than a state, and while a sociable-versus-withheld contrast is tempting there, going and getting are near-empty auxiliaries and these are among the smallest moves in the file; so and very are intensifiers with no content of their own that move in opposite directions; referred is a fragment of a naming construction that would have joined B's ascription cluster had it moved the other way; and close, friends and loyal rise under B without fitting any relation I stated, which is the substance of the counterexamples below.

result.counterexamples: Three groups cut against what I named. First, affiliation rises under B: close +1.0, friends +0.9, familiar +0.5 and loyal +0.3 are among the larger content moves and contradict any reading of B as suspicious or distancing; close and friends together outweigh enemies, planning and hiding combined, so if the suspicion relation were stated as a direction of sentiment it would simply be wrong, and it survives only in the narrower form given, about who holds the attitude. Second, the intensifiers split: so falls -0.5 while very rises +0.6, which no relation here predicts and which weakens the scaffolding claim, since very scaffolds an adjective rather than deferring one. Third, hostile falls -0.3 and quiet falls -0.2, both natural B words under the suspicion relation, and careful -0.4 falls while its near-synonym wary +0.4 rises, so that pair holds only if the reader accepts that careful reads as the neighbors' own caution and wary as somebody else's, which is a fine distinction to hang a relation on.
result.notes: Two things temper all of the above. The largest move in the file is a function word (a, +4.8) and the second largest is known (+4.4), a passive-frame opener rather than a content term, so most of the measured mass is grammatical: B prefers a different construction, and the content differences are read off a much smaller budget, the largest content-bearing fall being happy at -1.8. The words created from 0.0% under B (enemies, planning, hiding, suspected, unknown, not) are individually tiny at 0.4 to 0.6 points, and I weighted them because creation from nothing is what the levels were supplied to reveal, not because they are large; a reader weighting purely by magnitude would rank them below friends and close. I have not assumed which condition is which, and nothing here establishes that either direction is an intervention. Given that the fragment names a national group, the appearance of a suspicion vocabulary under B is worth recording, but with 27 words on each side, no repeat measurement and no comparison fragment naming a different group, a single prompt cannot separate this from prompt-specific noise in the low-probability tail.

result.reading: Almost all of the moved mass arrives rather than leaves: the B-block totals about +12 points against roughly -1.4 leaving the A-block, and one word, safer, carries +5.7 of it. The four words higher under A are small but strikingly uniform, since compelled, intimidated, powerless and obliged all cast the neighbours as subject to someone else's power, while the largest B gains (safer, safe, free, better) read the same arrival as security supplied to them, and the remaining B gains fall on words that name no feeling at all.

relations.name: coercion into protection
relations.sentence: Under A the slot pulls words placing the neighbours on the receiving end of force, namely compelled, intimidated, obliged and powerless, the last falling from 0.3% to 0.0% and so effectively eliminated, while under B the weight goes to words reading the same arrival as security supplied to them, led by safer at +5.7 and safe at +1.4 with better and free behind.

relations.name: the deferred predicate
relations.sentence: Six of the eleven B gains are words that postpone the feeling rather than name it, namely a, more, much, something, suddenly and differently, together about +2.9 points and so more than twice the entire A-block, whereas every A gain is a finished participle or adjective of subjection that closes the sentence on the spot.

relations.name: participle to attribute
relations.sentence: Three of the four A words are transitive past participles that grammatically presuppose an agent doing the compelling, intimidating or obliging, while the four largest B gains are bare adjectives naming a condition with no one in it acting on anybody.

result.kind: whether the arrival is something done to the neighbours or something that happens for them

residue.description: uneasy gains +0.7 under B and fits none of the three relations, since it is a negative feeling moving the same direction as the reassuring ones and it is agentless in a way the A-block words are not; I also note that a, more, much and something are not content completions of the fragment at all, and I have placed them in the deferral relation on the strength of their collective movement rather than any meaning they carry.

result.counterexamples: uneasy is the direct counterexample: it is the fourth-largest B gain at +0.7 and shows that B is not simply reassuring the slot, so the first relation cannot be stated as a move from bad feeling to good feeling but only as a move from feeling-under-compulsion to feeling-as-condition. The damage is moderate rather than fatal, since +0.7 is an eighth of safer's +5.7 and unease names no agent doing anything to the neighbours, but the relation would be false if written as valence. free at +0.6 is a weaker counterexample in the other direction, because freedom implies a prior unfreedom and so half-belongs with the A-side vocabulary of constraint even as it rises with the protection words.
result.notes: The A-block is faint in absolute terms, with its largest mover at -0.5 and its whole mass smaller than the single word a, so the coercion reading rests on the coherence of four small words rather than on any large movement; that coherence is what keeps my confidence at medium rather than low, since it is unlikely that the four words happening to fall are all words of subjection. Weighting by change alone, safer dominates everything and the honest minimal statement of the difference is that B concentrates on safety while A spreads thinly over compulsion. The levels are used here only for the elimination fact about powerless (0.3% to 0.0%) and for noting that nothing is created from zero on the B side. I have not assumed what A and B are, and none of the three relations depends on knowing.

result.reading: Under B the probability piles up on things done out loud and in concert (shout +8.9 alone, then bang, chant, argue, speak, sing, yell, demonstrate, recite, cheer), while under A the mass sits in a long flat tail of quiet, ordinary handling of a room (take, clean, move, sit, pour, put, gather, stand) plus one large devotional fall, pray at -1.9. The scene is being rewritten from people doing things in a room to people addressing someone from inside it, though a few movers cut against that: explain and speak rise calmly, and cry and laugh, which are loud, fall.

relations.name: Voice aimed outward
relations.sentence: Deliberate, audience-directed vocalization gains almost all the moving mass under B (shout is the single largest mover in the whole set at +8.9, with chant, argue, yell, taunt, demand, complain and speak behind it), while under A the slot is held by silent or inward actions performed in the room itself, above all pray, and also sit, look, move, stand, lay and say.

relations.name: Handling becomes performing
relations.sentence: Under A the fragment is completed by transitive manipulation of objects and the room (take, clean, pull, pour, remove, tear, eat, put, gather, search), and each of those loses a small amount under B to verbs that stage an action for an audience rather than act on anything (chant, sing, dance, demonstrate, recite, wave, celebrate, cheer).

relations.name: Prayer into chant
relations.sentence: The largest single fall on the A side is pray, from 2.2% to 0.4%, and the words that rise in its place keep the collective-utterance form while changing its register from devotional to political or declamatory: chant, recite, demonstrate and demand all move up from near-zero floors.

result.kind: whether the action is addressed to anyone

residue.description: playfully and loudly are manner adverbs rather than completions of the slot, so their small rises describe how a later verb would be qualified rather than what anyone does; make, get, do, try, go, call and take are light verbs whose probability tracks the syntactic continuation rather than any depicted action, which is why make rises 1.2 and take falls 1.2 with no visible difference in content between them; box is too small and too ambiguous in sense (the fighting verb or something else entirely) to attach to anything.

result.counterexamples: Three sets cut against the relations above. First, cry (-1.0) and laugh (-0.8) are loud and audible and both fall, which is enough to rule out any reading in terms of volume as such; what rises is vocalization that is deliberate and directed, not noise, and these two are the reason the first relation has to be stated that way rather than as loudness. Second, explain (+2.6) and speak (+1.9) are the fourth and sixth largest risers and are calm, reasoned and quiet, so the vocal cluster under B is not uniformly agitated even though its largest member, shout, is. Third, violence does not sort at all: attack rises (+0.5) while beat (-0.8), tear (-0.4), hit (-0.3) and assault (-0.2) fall, so no relation here can be stated as B being either more or less aggressive, and attack in particular sits inside the B block without belonging to any of the three groups I named.
result.notes: One structural asymmetry that is not a relation but shapes all three: the B risers total roughly 38 points of movement concentrated in a handful of words (shout alone carries 8.9, and the top three carry 16), while the A side sheds about 19 points spread thinly across 31 words, most of them moving less than 0.6. So the block lengths are not the story, but the shape of the mass is: many small withdrawals fund one large arrival. Second, the largest movers on both sides come from opposite kinds of starting level. bang, demonstrate, recite, playfully and loudly rise from 0.0-0.3%, that is, they are effectively created under B, whereas clean, sit, pour, tear and go fall to 0.0%, that is, eliminated. The A distribution is broad and unremarkable; the B distribution has been given a scene. Third, and stated without interpretation because the prompt asks for none: the fragment names a national group, and the effect of the shift is to move the completions from a generic interior scene toward a demonstration or protest scene. I am reporting the direction of the movement, not a claim about what produced it or which condition is which.

result.reading: The affect vocabulary swaps wholesale: every word naming an injury done by someone (betrayed, forced, obliged, pressured, trapped, helpless, powerless, abandoned, isolated) is lower under B, and every word naming fear of harm (threatened, terrified, frightened, terror, scared, fear, unsafe, uneasy) is higher, with no member crossing in either direction. Underneath that, the largest single moves are syntactic rather than lexical: "they" falls 5.5 while "the" rises 5.5 and "a" rises 5.3, so the complement of the verb is also being reshaped from a reported clause into a noun phrase or an intensified adjective.

relations.name: grievance traded for fright
relations.sentence: Under A the neighbours' feeling is named by words that presuppose a party acting on them and a relation violated or a will overridden, while under B it is named by words for fear of harm that implicate nobody, and the swap is total in that no coercion word rises and no fear word falls.

relations.name: reported clause becomes modified phrase
relations.sentence: The single largest fall is the subject pronoun that would open a clause reporting what the neighbours took to be happening to them, along with the two comparative complementizers and the existential, and the matching rises are the determiners and degree adverbs that instead open a bare noun phrase or an intensified adjective.

relations.name: one pair zeroed, one slot created
relations.sentence: Only the pressure pair is driven to nothing at all rather than merely reduced, while the words gaining the largest multiple of their starting mass are the two degree adverbs and the indefinite article, which were near-absent under A.

result.kind: the agent implied by the feeling

residue.description: The first two are bare frame words that could open almost any continuation and carry no reading of the scene, so their small rises say nothing about either relation; "sorry" is a content word but names regret rather than either coercion or fear, and its fall of 0.3 is too small to attach to the grievance group with any confidence.

result.counterexamples: Two moves cut against the syntactic relation and neither touches the lexical one. "that" rises 2.7 although it is a clause-introducer like the falling "they", "like" and "as", which is the sharpest contradiction here, though it is softened by the fact that "felt that" reports a proposition at greater distance from the speaker than "felt they" does and that "that" can also be a demonstrative determiner heading a noun phrase. "no" falls 1.0 despite being a determiner that opens exactly the noun-phrase completion the relation says is gaining, so the rise is specific to the definite and indefinite articles rather than to noun phrases as such. Within the affect swap I find no contradicting word at all: the weakest members are "scared" at +0.3 and "uneasy" at +0.4, which are small but on the same side as the rest of the fear block.
result.notes: Confidence is high for the first relation because the partition of the affect words is clean with no crossings, and lower for the second, which has the two counterexamples above. I have not assumed which condition is the intervened one or that either distribution is the corrected version of the other; the description holds whichever direction is read as primary. Worth noting that the two 5.5-point moves are exact mirrors of each other in size, "they" down and "the" up, which is why I treat the syntactic reshaping as a relation in its own right rather than as a by-product of the vocabulary change.
