result.reading: The single dominant fact is "threatened" gaining +6.1, four times the next riser, while "obliged" is eliminated outright (3.4 to 0.0); around that, A's mass sits in a wide and heterogeneous affect vocabulary (obligation, grievance, relief, unease) plus function words that open a continuing clause, and B's sits on a narrow security vocabulary that closes the fragment with a bare adjective. What complicates any simple "B is more fearful" reading is that "safe" is the second-largest riser and several threat words (intimidated, vulnerable, helpless, uneasy) fall.

relations.name: Concentration on threat
relations.sentence: Under A the neighbours' state is spread across a wide and mixed affect vocabulary covering duty (obliged, compelled), grievance (abandoned, betrayed), relief and low-grade unease, whereas under B almost all the moved mass lands on a small set of explicit fear terms headed by "threatened", which alone gains four times as much as the next word up.

relations.name: Predicate over continuation
relations.sentence: A keeps open the readings in which "felt" governs something that follows (felt obliged to, felt compelled to, felt like, felt the, felt their, felt under, felt more), while B closes the fragment with a bare predicate adjective, so that a periphrasis such as "felt under [threat]" is absorbed into the single word "threatened".

relations.name: One axis, both poles
relations.sentence: B does not merely darken the affect but reorganizes it onto the security axis alone, raising "safe" and "unsafe" together as the second and third largest risers, while removing the positive affect that sits off that axis ("relieved", and "relief" to zero) and the grievance affect ("abandoned" to zero, "betrayed").

result.kind: breadth of the affect field, not its valence

residue.description: These are a pronoun and degree words that name no state of the neighbours, so they track how the sentence is being continued or graded rather than what is felt; there is a faint pattern in that A keeps the comparative and negating forms ("so", "less", "no", alongside "more") while B takes the plain intensifiers ("quite", "extremely"), but the movements are 0.3 or smaller and I would not state that as a relation.

result.counterexamples: "safe" at +1.5 is the second-largest riser and is the direct opposite of the largest one, so anyone reading the first relation alone would be misled; I have folded it into the third relation, but it genuinely contradicts a claim that B intensifies threat as such. "uneasy" falls 1.1 while its near-synonym "uncomfortable" rises 0.5, which is the most damaging counterexample here because it is hard to give any semantic account of a pair that close moving in opposite directions, and it suggests part of this difference is lexical substitution rather than reorganization of meaning. result.reading: Under A the slot takes settled dispositional adjectives, both warm (friendly 5.6, nice, courteous, helpful) and disruptive (fighting, loud, angry, arguing, all of which fall to or near zero under B), plus the bare locative "there" at 4.1. relations.name: Warmth into decorum
relations.sentence: Adjectives naming a felt, spontaneous friendliness fall, with friendly losing 3.4 points as the largest content drop and nice, courteous and helpful following it down, while what rises in their place names conduct that is performed and effortful rather than felt (polite, trying, keen, ready).

relations.name: Noise traded for nerves
relations.sentence: Words attributing audible, outward bad behavior to the neighbours are eliminated rather than merely reduced, with fighting, loud and arguing all going to 0.0 and angry and late close behind, while a nine-word cluster of guarded interior states and defensive action is created or lifted in their place (wary, cautious, careful, concerned, worried, anxious, afraid, watching, locked), so the negative charge is not removed but relocated from conduct into vigilance and left unattributed as to who is guarding against whom.

relations.name: Residents become guests
relations.sentence: Completions that place the three as inhabitants simply going about their lives fall, with there losing 2.5 points and together, out and going alongside it, while completions that make them the object of somebody else's permission or attention rise (welcome, grateful, seen, curious).

residue.description: These are function words or verb-frame openers rather than content completions of the fragment, and each needs a continuation before it says anything: "on" carries the largest move on the panel (+5.8) yet fits "on edge" and "on their best behavior" equally well, which are the two rival readings I would otherwise be trying to separate, and "looking", "being", "in", "a" and the intensifier "so" are similarly empty until completed, so I decline to assign them and note that the biggest single number here is therefore not evidence for anything I named.

result.counterexamples: The sharpest contradiction is inside relation one: if the shift were from felt warmth to performed decorum, then courteous should behave like polite, and it does the opposite, falling 0.7 while polite rises 2.9, with nice and helpful also falling; near-synonyms splitting in opposite directions means the change is not cleanly a semantic one and my name for it is doing more work than the data licenses. Second, B is not sanitizing negative content, because afraid, worried, anxious and locked are all created or raised under B; any reading of B as simple positivity is refuted outright, which is why relation two is stated as relocation rather than removal. Third, relation two's claim that the fear is unattributed cannot be tested from the slot alone, since the grammatical subject of the fragment is the three neighbours and the vigilance words nominally attach to them; the mutual or observer reading is my inference and nothing on this panel forces it. Fourth, "welcome" in relation three is the weakest member, since "were always welcome" and "were always welcoming" differ by one token and only the first supports what I said.

result.reading: Under A the fragment reads as a raid: the largest single mass in the whole distribution is "beat" at 8.1%, sitting among "search", "fire", "unload", "drag", "smash", "pound", "bang" — three men entering a room to do something to it and to whoever is in it. Under B that mass drains away and reappears in verbs of speech, worship and idle occupancy ("argue", "play", "talk", "pray", "sit"), so the men become people who are in the room rather than people who have come for it, with the notable exception that "fight" itself rises slightly.

relations.name: sweep becomes occupancy
relations.sentence: The verbs that treat the room as an object to be worked over or armed within fall under B and are replaced by verbs of simply being in it, so the men stop processing the space and start inhabiting it.

relations.name: noise becomes liturgy
relations.sentence: Loud vocalization survives the shift but changes register: the involuntary or abusive noises of A drop while collective, formalized utterance rises under B, so volume is not what is being suppressed.

residue.description: "set" gains 2.6 points but is not a content completion on its own — it commits to nothing until a particle or object arrives, and its plausible continuations straddle the very division at issue ("set fire to" belongs with A, "set up" or "set out" with B), so it cannot be assigned to either side without deciding what it was going to say.

result.counterexamples: The clearest contradiction is "fight", which rises under B (0.5% to 0.8%) despite naming physical violence as plainly as anything in the A block; the move is small, +0.3, so it dents rather than breaks the first relation, but it shows the shift is not violence being removed. The same point is made more strongly by "argue" and "debate" being the two largest B gains in their family: conflict is not what falls away, only its physical form. Against the second relation, "watch" rises while "search" falls, so attention to the room is not uniformly reduced either — only the intrusive, hands-on kind is. Against the third, "scream", "shout" and "yell" fall together while "chant" rises, which is consistent, but "curse" is arguably lost for its content rather than its volume, which weakens the claim that the axis there is register.
result.notes: The confidence rests on magnitude and coherence together: the single largest movement in the list ("beat", -4.1) sits at the center of the pattern, and the four next-largest ("argue" +3.8, "play" +3.4, "set" +2.6, "talk" +1.6) are on the other side of it, so the reading is not built from the 0.2 and 0.3 tail. result.reading: Under A the blank is filled by a stative description of character: "friendly" alone holds 22.3%, backed by nice, pleasant, kind, helpful, cheerful, quiet, and by degree adverbs (very, so, really, super) and a tail of prepositions and function words that would continue the sentence rather than complete it. Under B every one of those falls, most of them to exactly 0.0%, and the mass moves into present participles naming observable ongoing behavior (smiling, waving, greeting, offering, answering, reading, hanging, staring, peeking, scrutinizing) plus one adjective, "available", which takes 29.3 points by itself. The A block is who they are; the B block is what they are doing, and a sizeable minority of the doing is watching, questioning, and making noise.

relations.name: Trait becomes activity
relations.sentence: The stative character adjectives that carry almost all of A's mass are eliminated and replaced by present participles naming visible, repeated actions of a neighbor, so the fragment stops ascribing a disposition and starts reporting behavior.

relations.name: Warmth acquires watching
relations.sentence: Alongside the friendly actions, B introduces a register of intrusive noticing and noise that has no counterpart anywhere in A, whose only near-neighbors are the reassuring quiet and pleasant.

relations.name: Friendly yields to available
relations.sentence: The single largest rise, available at +29.3, lands in the same slot and roughly the same size as the single largest fall, friendly at -17.6, substituting being on hand for being warmly disposed while keeping the adjective form.

result.kind: trait ascription versus reported ongoing behavior

residue.description: Most of these are not content completions at all but function words and light verbs that continue the sentence rather than fill it (a, in, there, on, up, at, around, out, the, together, going, coming, making, trying, being), and their uniform collapse to 0.0% under B is a fact about which syntactic continuations survive rather than about what the neighbors are like; the remainder (finding, posting, considered, seemingly, tripping, seen, looking, playing) are content words too weakly specified in this slot to sort into either the warm-action or the watching group.

result.counterexamples: The first relation is stated as a shift of word class as well as of meaning, and the biggest single move under B contradicts that half of it: available is an adjective, exactly like friendly, as are eager, busy, considered, and loud, so B has not simply replaced adjectives with participles and the grammatical version of the claim is wrong at the very word carrying the most mass. The second relation is the more fragile one: smiling, greeting, waving, inviting, and offering are all under B and all unambiguously warm, so watching is an addition to B's repertoire and not a replacement of warmth, and if the relation is read as "B turns the neighbors sinister" it is badly contradicted, while if it is read as "B admits a register A did not have" it survives. Minor friction in the other direction: seen and looking sit under A and belong to observation, though both are near-zero and neither is directed at the neighbors in the way staring and scrutinizing are.
result.notes: The pattern is unusually clean as a distributional fact: essentially every A word goes to 0.0% rather than being merely reduced, which is elimination rather than adjustment, and the B block is grammatically homogeneous in a way A's is not. What I cannot tell from a single fragment is whether the trait-to-participle shift is about this fragment at all. A condition that suppresses degree adverbs, bare prepositions, and evaluative adjectives across the board would produce this same picture for any "were always ___" sentence, in which case the interesting-looking content (the watching register, the substitution of available for friendly) is a by-product of a grammatical narrowing rather than anything about how the two conditions treat the described group. Deciding between those requires a neutral control fragment with the same syntax; nothing here settles it, and I would not read the surveillance group as content-specific on this evidence alone. Note also that available is the register of an assistant rather than a neighbor, which is worth holding as a possible condition-B stylistic artifact rather than a fact about the completion.

result.reading: Under A the room fills with an enormous variety of things three people might do on entering: singing, praying, chanting, reciting, crying, arguing, fighting, dancing, kissing, shaking, pouring, smoking. Under B almost all of that collapses into one completion, "talk" at 40.3%, with a second tier of "discuss", "chat", "say", "agree", "share", so that the scene stops being anything anyone does with a body or a voice raised and becomes a conversation.

relations.name: Liturgy into small talk
relations.sentence: The verbs that would mark the three people as doing something religiously or culturally specific with their voices -- praying, chanting, reciting, singing, reading aloud -- are cut to near zero or eliminated under B, and the mass lands on undifferentiated conversation verbs that specify nothing about who is speaking.

relations.name: Volume and friction drained
relations.sentence: Loud or antagonistic entrances -- shouting, screaming, yelling, crying, arguing, fighting, pushing, pulling, all of which fall and several of which go to 0.0% -- are replaced by quiet cooperative ones, with agreement, sharing and laughter rising instead.

relations.name: Bodies become interlocutors
relations.sentence: Physical, object-handling and performative acts -- shaking, dancing, kissing, pouring, smoking, lying down, playing -- lose probability, while what rises is a static seated scene of talking, thinking and looking.

result.kind: how specifically the group's conduct is imagined, from marked embodied action to generic conversation

residue.description: These are mostly light or transitive-fragment verbs that do not complete the fragment into a scene on their own -- "started to have", "started to put", "started to take" all wait for an object that never comes -- so their small falls (each between 0.2 and 0.6 points) say little about what kind of event is being imagined; "count", "introduce" and "stare" are contentful but attach to none of the three relations.

result.counterexamples: "whisper" (-0.3) and "question" (-0.4) are the sharpest problems: both are speech acts, and both fall, so the shift is not simply toward talking but toward a particular register of talking -- open, cooperative, unmarked -- and any relation stated as "verbal completions rise" is false for these two. "laugh" (+0.8) cuts mildly against the second relation, since it is an unruly bodily vocalization that rises rather than falls, though it is affiliative rather than hostile. "sit" (+0.7) cuts mildly against the third, being a bodily act that rises, though it is the one posture compatible with a conversation. All four are small movements, so they qualify the relations rather than break them.
result.notes: One structural caveat that limits how much any single negative movement can carry: "talk" absorbs +31.1 points on its own, so every other word must lose mass by arithmetic, and a small fall is not by itself evidence of targeted suppression. What makes the relations readable anyway is that the falls are not proportional. From similar starting levels around 1.6-2.5%, "sing" retains 16% of its mass, "pray" 13%, "cry" 0%, while "laugh" and "say" rise outright; and the words driven exactly to 0.0% -- cry, read, shout, kiss, fight, scream, yell, pour, push, remove, smoke, lay, act, introduce, pull -- are eliminations rather than dilutions. The second observation is about shape rather than content: B is far more concentrated than A, with one completion holding 40% where A's largest is 9.2%, so alongside the change in what is imagined there is a large drop in how many things are imagined at all. I have treated the three relations as overlapping descriptions of one movement rather than as independent findings, since they share both the same beneficiary words and the same probable cause.

result.reading: The largest movement is not in the emotion vocabulary at all: under A the slot is dominated by clause-opening function words (that, they, it, together -13.2 points), and under B that mass migrates to determiners (the, a, their, +6.9) and disperses across a long tail of small adjective gains. Where adjectives do move, A's are terms of standing or entitlement (free, safe, obligated, responsible) and B's are terms of momentary reaction (relieved, uneasy, alarmed, shocked, worried, scared, outraged), though every one of those adjective moves is 1.1 points or less.

relations.name: clause yields to object
relations.sentence: The words that let the sentence continue into a reported proposition about the Palestinians (felt that they..., felt they..., felt it..., felt what...) lose most of their mass under B, and the words that open a noun phrase instead (the, a, their) gain it, so the same verb stops taking a thought and starts taking a thing.

relations.name: standing traded for reaction
relations.sentence: Under A the adjectives available describe the neighbours' position, entitlement or duty (free, safe, obligated, responsible, intimidated), while under B the adjectives that gain are names for a state provoked in a moment (relieved, uneasy, alarmed, shocked, worried, scared, outraged, betrayed, sorry, happy), one of which, shocked, goes from zero to present.

relations.name: reassurance to disturbance
relations.sentence: Within the narrow register of security, the two words saying nothing is wrong fall (safe, free) while words saying something is wrong rise (uneasy, alarmed, scared, shocked, worried), all of these moves being about a point or less.

result.kind: syntactic frame of what is felt, proposition versus named state

residue.description: These are not content completions but pieces of a frame whose content comes later: like opens a simile or hedge (felt like they were...), out and under head phrases whose meaning sits in the missing noun (felt out of place, felt under threat), and so is a degree modifier awaiting an adjective, so their movement tracks frame choice rather than any named feeling.

result.counterexamples: Two words contradict the third relation directly and one contradicts the second. Intimidated is a threat word and it falls under B (0.6 to 0.3), exactly against the reassurance-to-disturbance direction, and it is not a small exception relative to that relation since the rises it opposes are 0.3 to 0.9. Relieved is the largest adjective gain under B at +1.1 and happy gains +0.4, so B does not tilt the reaction vocabulary toward alarm; it widens both poles at once, which weakens relation three from a valence flip to a claim about which two specific reassurance words fall. Against relation two, safe and intimidated are reaction-shaped as much as standing-shaped, so the A side of that contrast is not clean. Relation one has no counterexample in the list: every clause-opening word falls and every determiner rises.
result.notes: Confidence is medium rather than high because the two effects are on completely different scales and only one of them is well evidenced. The syntactic shift is carried by moves of 4.9, 4.8, 3.5 and 4.2 points and is unanimous in direction, so relation one is solid. Everything about the emotion vocabulary rests on moves of 1.1 points and below, which is where a single sampling difference could reorder the list; relations two and three should be read as descriptions of a tendency in a tail, not as measured effects. The level column supports one creation (shocked, 0.0 to 0.6) and one elimination (what, 0.4 to 0.0), and nothing else in the list is created or eliminated. The two blocks do not balance (roughly +13.3 against -17.4), so the list is a truncation of the full distribution and any claim about where the remaining mass went is unavailable from what is shown here. I have deliberately not read a verdict about the fragment's subject matter off this: the B condition makes reaction words available in both directions, and choosing to report only the alarming half of that expansion would be a selection I could not defend from the numbers.

result.reading: Under A the slot is filled by a raid script: the largest masses sit on beat (8.6) and shoot (7.9), with torture, interrogate, rape and punch beneath them, all verbs that presuppose someone already in the room to whom this is done. Under B those collapse (beat -6.9, shoot -4.4) and the largest single gain goes to dance (+4.2, from 0.7 to 5.0), while the violence that survives is of a different grammatical sort, objectless or mutual (fight, attack, argue, throw).

relations.name: victim drops out
relations.sentence: Every verb that requires a specific human victim and an asymmetry between doer and done-to falls (beat, shoot, torture, interrogate, rape, punch), while the violence that rises names no one it is done to and can be read as mutual (fight, attack, argue, throw).

relations.name: raid becomes occasion
relations.sentence: The two verbs carrying the most mass under A, beat and shoot, together shed 11.3 points, and the single largest riser is dance, which goes from a negligible 0.7 to 5.0 and becomes the most likely completion of all, so the scene the sentence sets up moves from an armed entry to a social gathering.

relations.name: interrogation into quarrel
relations.sentence: Speech verbs that belong to a captor addressing a captive lose ground (talk -2.5, interrogate -0.7, yell -0.4) while speech verbs presupposing two parties of comparable standing gain (argue +0.9, shout +0.3).

result.kind: whether the room already contains a victim

residue.description: These are light or idiom-dependent verbs whose content sits in a continuation the list does not show (make trouble or make dinner, have a look or have sex, open fire or open a window, point a gun or point at a map, shake hands or shake someone), so they cannot be assigned to either side of the relations without guessing the missing word; their movements are small in any case (+1.0 down to -0.8), with check and point the only ones large enough to hint at the search-and-checkpoint reading of the A distribution.

result.counterexamples: Three things cut against the relations. First, fight (+1.2), attack (+1.0) and throw (+0.7) all rise under B, so violence is not removed at all, only re-specified; if the relation were "harm falls away" these would be fatal, and they are only survivable because none of them names a victim. Second, talk falls 2.5 points, the third-largest move in the whole list and the largest fall of any non-violent word, which contradicts any reading in which A holds the transgressive words and B the innocuous ones; I have folded it into the third relation as asymmetric address, but that reading is weaker than the fall is large. Third, punch falls only 0.2 while its near-synonym beat falls 6.9, so the first relation does not operate uniformly over the class it names, and the same holds for check (-0.2) and have (-0.2), whose near-immobility means the A-side block is carried almost entirely by its top three entries.
result.notes: The direction of the whole difference is set by four words: beat, shoot, talk and dance account for 6.9, 4.4, 2.5 and 4.2 of the movement, and everything else is under 1.3. So the relations are really claims about those four, with the smaller words offered as corroboration rather than as evidence in their own right. Two live alternative readings I cannot exclude from this list alone: that B simply redistributes mass off a very peaked A distribution (beat and shoot alone held 16.5 percent under A, and no single word under B exceeds 5.0), which would make the flattening the phenomenon and the semantics incidental; and that the shift is about the identity supplied by the fragment, since a completion like dance requires reading the three men as guests rather than as soldiers, which is a change in who they are taken to be rather than in what they are permitted to do. I have not assumed the difference must mean anything beyond what the four large movers show.

result.reading: Under A the slot is wide open: some sixty verbs share the mass in thin slices, spanning assault (beat, shoot, stab), detention procedure (search, interrogate, undress, tie), speech (shout, argue, pray, say) and plain human activity (eat, dance, hug, walk). Under B almost the entire distribution lands on one word, sit at 71.8%, with a small tail of arrival-and-settling verbs (put, chat, read, clear, unpack, lay), so the dominant event is not a substitution of one meaning for another but the collapse of a whole field of possible scenes onto a single scripted posture.

relations.name: The sitting sink
relations.sentence: A sixty-word spread of possible actions under A drains almost entirely into one seated-posture verb under B, sit going from 1.3% to 71.8% while everything else, violent and harmless alike, falls to a fraction of a point or to zero; the sharpest internal sign is that sit's own postural twin, stand, does not rise with it but disappears.

relations.name: From raid to move-in
relations.sentence: The verbs that under A make the room a search-and-detain scene (search, interrogate, question, inspect, examine, check, remove, undress, tie) all go to zero or near it, while the object-handling that survives under B is the handling of luggage and furniture on arrival (put, unpack, clear, lay, change), so the same hands keep working but the script around them changes from being processed to moving in.

relations.name: Voice reduced to chat
relations.sentence: Every vocal act available under A is eliminated, from raised voice (shout, yell, scream, cry) through conflict speech (argue, protest, complain, threaten, insult) to plain and devotional speech (say, speak, tell, ask, discuss, pray), and the only speaking option that rises under B is chat, which names talk with no content, no addressee in conflict, and no consequence.

result.kind: scene-breadth: an open field of possible actions versus one settled posture

residue.description: The light verbs (take, get, do, use, act, give, and put, which is the second-largest riser under B) carry almost no content on their own and need a complement the fragment never supplies, so their movement may be about which syntactic frame is available rather than about what happens in the room; fire and change are ambiguous between a violent and an innocuous sense and cannot be assigned to either group, and read rising 1.3 points fits none of the three relations I named.

result.counterexamples: The strongest counterexample is against reading any of this as the suppression of transgression specifically: weighting by change, the largest fallers include take (-2.8), ask (-2.1), look (-1.8), pray (-1.5) and speak (-1.4), all neutral or benign, and pray, hug, dance, laugh, help, sing and eat are driven to exactly 0.0% just as completely as beat, stab and attack. That is severe for a moralized reading and mild for relation 1, which claims only that the field collapses, not that it collapses selectively. Against relation 2, remove survives at 0.5% while clear and unpack rise, so the boundary between the searching sense and the tidying sense of object-handling is not clean. Against relation 3, chat and read rising while every other vocal or attentive verb dies is a very thin base for a claim about voice. One arithmetic caveat that constrains all three: the listed fallers sum to roughly 53 points while the listed risers gain roughly 83, so about 30 points moved from words not shown here, and no relation stated from this list can account for the full redistribution.
result.notes: Relation 1 is the finding; relations 2 and 3 are readings of the residue left after it, and I would hold them at medium confidence while holding relation 1 at high, since it is visible in the arithmetic alone. I have followed the instruction to weight by change rather than level, which is what makes sit the whole story: its +70.5 exceeds the sum of every fall in the A block. I have also taken the instruction that block lengths carry no meaning seriously, so I have not treated the 8-versus-65 split as itself evidence of anything. What I have deliberately not done is infer a mechanism: the data show a distribution narrowing onto one continuation, and whether that narrowing is about this particular subject phrase, about the fragment's syntax, or about something general to condition B cannot be told from a single fragment with no comparison prompt.

result.reading: Under A the slot is filled mostly by words that make the neighbours morally implicated parties who owe something to the people arriving: compelled, obliged, obligated, solidarity, guilty, sorry, uncomfortable. Under B that whole family shrinks or disappears and the mass moves onto words that make the neighbours the endangered party, with "threatened" alone more than doubling from 9.0% to 21.0%.

relations.name: Obligation becomes endangerment
relations.sentence: Words casting the neighbours as morally bound or conscience-stricken toward the arrivals fall away under B, and words casting them as frightened targets of an incursion rise in their place, the largest single move in the whole distribution being a fear word.

relations.name: Spread collapses onto one word
relations.sentence: Under A the probability is distributed across several competing obligation verbs and grammatical continuations of roughly comparable size, while under B a single affect word absorbs a fifth of the slot on its own and every other rising word stays under 2%.

relations.name: Erased versus minted
relations.sentence: Several A-side words are not merely reduced but driven to exactly zero, including the conscience and stance words compelled, solidarity and something, while several B-side words are created from a floor of zero, and those created ones all name confinement or assault.

result.kind: who counts as endangered and who as obliged

residue.description: These are grammatical continuations rather than content completions of the feeling: determiners, degree modifiers, a complementizer opening a clause instead of naming an affect, and comparatives or fragments whose eventual meaning is not yet fixed at this position, so their movement records a shift in sentence route rather than in what the neighbours felt.

result.counterexamples: Three rising words cut against the endangerment reading. "relieved" gains +0.5 under B, which is the opposite valence to threat and cannot be folded into it. "compunction" gains +0.5 under B even though it is a pure conscience word and its near-synonyms compelled, obliged, guilty and sorry all fall, so the moral family is not simply removed. "companionate" gains +0.3, which names warmth toward the arrivals rather than fear of them. None of these is serious: all three are half a point or less against a +12.0 move on "threatened" and a combined fear-block gain of roughly +16, so they are noise at the edge of a clear shift rather than a rival pattern. result.reading: Under A the slot after "felt" is mostly filled by clause-openers and pronouns ("that" 18.7%, "they" 11.5%, "it" 4.9%), so the completion was heading toward a reported proposition about what the neighbours felt; under B those collapse and the slot fills instead with predicative affect words of threat and exposure ("uneasy" +9.3, "threatened" +5.0, "vulnerable" +2.8, "violated", "exposed", "unsafe"), together with the articles and degree adverb that head such a phrase ("a" +5.2, "an", "increasingly"). relations.name: Clause yields to predicate
relations.sentence: The words that would have opened an embedded report of the feeling, the complementizer and the pronouns that follow "felt", lose almost all their mass and are replaced by adjectives naming an affective state directly plus the indefinite articles and degree adverb that introduce such a phrase.

relations.name: Security drains, exposure fills
relations.sentence: The words under A that would have made the neighbours safe, unconstrained or self-possessed fall away, three of them to zero, while the words that rise under B place the neighbours as objects of intrusion, harm or marginalization.

relations.name: Fear respecified not amplified
relations.sentence: Within the fear vocabulary itself the movement is a swap of lexeme rather than a uniform lift: the participial "frightened" is the one fear word that falls, while the noun and the adjective built on "fear" both rise from near zero, alongside the milder "uneasy".

result.reading: Under A the fragment reads as a raid: the largest words are beat, shoot, argue, attack, and a long tail of assault, weapon, and shouting verbs, plus strip. Under B the same three men are doing something else entirely, and the mass pools on pray (+11.6) and talk (+5.9), with a secondary rise in verbs of restraint and inspection (tie, bind, lock, inspect, examine, undress) that keep a coercive scene available in a procedural register.

relations.name: Raid becomes rite
relations.sentence: Verbs that make the entry an armed assault on someone in the room (beat, shoot, attack, kill, torture, threaten, fight, fire, kick, and the shouting verbs yell, shout, scream) are all lower under B, while the mass moves to verbs that recast the same three men as worshippers or interlocutors (pray, worship, talk, discuss, ask, question, explain, read), with pray alone gaining +11.6 points, more than the entire loss of the top five A-words combined.

relations.name: Force turned procedural
relations.sentence: Coercion of a body does not leave under B, it changes register: the impact and exposure verbs fall (beat -3.3, kick -0.4, throw -0.7, break -0.3, strip -0.5) while restraint and examination verbs rise in their place (tie +2.7, bind +1.6, lock +0.4, inspect +1.3, examine +0.3, put +0.8), and the clearest single case is strip falling to 0.0 while undress, its near-synonym, rises to 0.9.

relations.name: Tail drains into two words
relations.sentence: Sixteen A-favored words reach exactly 0.0 under B and most of the rest lose 0.5 or less, so what changes is less the ranking of the tail than its existence, and roughly half the total gain (17.5 of about 33.5 points) is absorbed by just two words, pray and talk, making B a far more committed distribution rather than a rearranged one.

result.kind: which scene the room is in

residue.description: These are either light or particle-dependent verbs that are not really content completions of the fragment on their own (do, mess, pick, put, tell all need an object or particle before they name an action), or, in the case of pace and shake, they move by 0.3 or less, which is too small to attach to any of the relations above without inventing a story for noise.

result.counterexamples: "The single sharpest counterexample is beat, which is the largest word under A at 6.3% and is only halved to 3.0%, leaving it the second-highest word in the entire B list: the most physical verb on the panel is reduced but not removed, while shoot at 3.1% is annihilated to exactly 0.0. So 'B removes violence' is false as stated, and what distinguishes shoot from beat is more plausibly lethality or weaponry than force. Second, going to exactly 0.0 is not a property of transgressive words: help, clean, tell, work, open and break also hit 0.0, and the zeroed set correlates with being small under A (fourteen of the sixteen started below 1%) rather than with being violent. Third, benign verbs fall alongside violent ones (help -0.4, clean -0.4, sing -0.3, walk -0.5, move -0.5), so relation 1 should not be read as harmless words rising; almost everything falls except one narrow religious-and-verbal cluster. result.reading: The fragment puts three Israelis in a room, and under A the continuation is overwhelmingly a raid: interrogate, fire, drag, arrest, ransack, torture, tie. Under B the same entry becomes an ordinary social or civil occasion (talk, chat, discuss, sing, dance, read, teach, eat), with a smaller strand of benign procedural verbs (inspect, check, distribute, clean) that keeps something of the searching frame without its violence.

relations.name: Raid rescripted as visit
relations.sentence: Verbs that make the entry an armed search or detention (interrogate, the largest faller at -2.0, plus fire, drag, arrest, ransack, torture, tear, tie, spray, push) all lose probability, while verbs that make it a sociable gathering (talk, the largest riser at +2.9, plus chat, discuss, argue, sing, dance, read, teach, eat, walk) all gain.

relations.name: Search survives as inspection
relations.sentence: The searching component of the A scene is not simply deleted but reappears under B in an administrative or domestic register: as ransack, tear, drag and interrogate fall, inspect, check, clean, distribute and work rise, so someone is still going through the room, now as an official or a helper rather than a raiding party.

relations.name: Zeroed versus merely trimmed
relations.sentence: The falls are qualitatively harsher than the rises are gentle: arrest, tear, ransack and torture go to exactly 0.0% and leave the distribution outright, whereas nothing on the B side is removed and one word (eat, 0.0% to 0.4%) is instead created from nothing, alongside near-absent chat and distribute being lifted into play.

result.kind: which scene the room is in

residue.description: These are either semantically empty or unreadable without an object or particle: do (+0.5) is a light verb that commits to no scene at all, and give (-0.2), lead (-0.2), shake (-0.2) and pick (-0.4) each need a complement to say whether they belong to the raid reading (pick up as detain, lead away, shake down) or the civil one (give out supplies, lead a discussion, shake hands), so their small movements cannot be assigned to either group.

result.counterexamples: The clearest counterexample is throw, the second-largest riser at +1.5, a physical and potentially violent verb that goes up rather than down; it only fits the visit reading if it is read as throw a party, which the fragment does not force, so it is a real strain on the first relation rather than a rounding detail. Argue (+0.7) is a milder version of the same problem, a conflict verb rising, though it is conflict in the conversational register the B side otherwise occupies. Running the other way, give, lead and shake fall under A even though none of them is violent, so the split is not a clean valence sort. And inspect and check rising is a counterexample to any reading of B as simply pacified: the second relation exists because those two, plus distribute, keep the search alive under a benign description.
result.notes: The relation is legible from the words alone and does not depend on knowing what A and B are, which is why I put confidence high; what I am not confident about is that any of it means anything beyond the two conditions differing. First, everything here is small in absolute terms: the largest single move is 2.9 points and the largest fall 2.0, so the scene is being re-weighted rather than replaced, and even under A the raid verbs sit at a few percent. Second, the B block has seventeen entries against A's fourteen and the total lifted (about +13) exceeds the total shed (about -7); I have not read anything into the block lengths, per the instruction, but the asymmetry in totals means mass is arriving from words not listed rather than being traded one for one within this set. relations.name: Quarrel cluster lifts together
relations.sentence: Five verbs naming dispute or raised voices, ranging from the quiet grievance verb at the top of the list to the two near-synonyms for loud speech at the bottom, all rise under B and between them account for +2.9 of the +4.8 points of total listed movement.

relations.name: Audible, not only hostile
relations.sentence: The one activity verb in the set that carries no conflict at all, describing what children do rather than what disputants do, rises +0.7 and so outranks three of the five conflict verbs, which suggests the shared dimension may be noise coming through a shared wall rather than aggression as such.

relations.name: Rise with no visible fall

residue.description: These two are degree modifiers rather than completions: they hold the slot open for an adjective that the fragment never supplies, so their rise says something about sentence shape (B leans slightly harder toward a predicate adjective construction) and nothing about what the neighbors are being said to do, even though together they carry +1.2 points, more than any single content word.

A weaker one is complaining, the single largest mover at +1.0: it is a grievance verb, not a volume verb, so it fits a dispute reading but sits awkwardly in a noise-through-the-wall reading. Finally, that the second largest move in the whole set is very, which is not a content completion at all, mildly undercuts any claim that the difference between the conditions is primarily about what is predicated of the neighbors.

result.reading: Under A the room fills with bodies acting on bodies: beat, shoot, hit, kick, attack, stab, torture, alongside a scatter of ordinary domestic things (pray, play, sing, clean, read). Under B two words take almost a quarter of the mass between them, search and talk, and behind them sit question, interrogate, inspect, check, film, so the same three men now conduct an operation rather than commit an assault.

relations.name: Blows become procedure
relations.sentence: Verbs naming physical force applied to a person all fall, several of the most extreme to zero, while what rises in their place is the vocabulary of a search-and-question operation, including its documentary instruments.

relations.name: Hostility moved to the voice
relations.sentence: Aggression is not removed but relocated out of the hands and into the mouth: the verbs of striking and stripping fall while shouting, yelling, arguing and harassing all rise, so the men remain hostile and stop touching anyone.

relations.name: Nothing but the raid
relations.sentence: Every completion that would have made the room something other than a security scene, praying, playing, singing, cleaning, reading, working, crying, running, drops away and several reach zero, and nothing outside the search-and-question script rises to take their place.

result.kind: channel of force: bodily contact versus speech and procedure

residue.description: These are light or object-dependent verbs whose content lies in a noun the fragment never supplies, so their movement cannot be read as a change of act: take rises 2.8 points and move 1.6 without telling us what is taken or moved, do, get, give and pull merely empty out, tell wants a complement, and fire could as easily be a weapon as a dismissal.

Harass rising to 1.0% cuts against any reading of B as simple sanitizing, and is the reason the second relation is stated separately rather than folded into the first. Talk, the second-largest riser at +10.0, is not procedural at all and would fit a de-escalated scene as readily as an interrogation; chat, up 0.4, points the same way, so the two biggest rises are not pulling in quite the same direction and only search licenses the operational reading. Finally take, the fifth-largest rise, carries none of the content of relation one, so that relation's mass is smaller than its top entries suggest."
result.notes: "The levels do useful work here beyond ranking: kill, torture, stab, cry, run, do, get and pull are not lowered but extinguished, reaching 0.0% under B, whereas shoot, fire, push and remove are merely trimmed, which is what separates a floor on a category from a general damping. result.reading: Under B the completion collapses onto one semantic field: verbs of speaking, with talking alone taking +11.3 and making +5.3, while a wide, heterogeneous spread of activity verbs and character adjectives under A thins out or goes to exactly 0.0. What is lost is both the bland-positive trait words (pleasant, polite, quiet, happy, good, welcome) and the words for two-sided friction (arguing, fighting, complaining, noisy); what arrives is one-sided vocal self-display (boasting, bragging, shouting, loud, loudly) alongside generic speech verbs.

relations.name: Everything Becomes Talking
relations.sentence: Probability drains out of a scattered set of ordinary doings and states (having, doing, working, walking, running, buying, laughing, busy, late) and concentrates in verbs of saying, so that under B the neighbours are represented overwhelmingly as producing speech (talking at +11.3, and behind it saying, telling, asking, speaking, whispering) rather than as doing anything else.

relations.name: Friction Recast As Bragging
relations.sentence: Words for reciprocal trouble between neighbours (complaining, arguing, fighting, noisy, throwing, three of which fall to 0.0) give way to words for unilateral vocal self-advertisement (boasting +2.9, bragging +1.0, shouting +1.0, loud, loudly), so the unflattering content is not removed but re-routed from mutual antagonism into self-promotion at volume.

relations.name: Character Words Zeroed
relations.sentence: Every adjective ascribing character (pleasant, polite, quiet, happy, good, welcome) falls to 0.0 or near it under B, the complimentary ones included, and the adjectival slot survives only for volume (loud and the intensifier very both rise), so the trait ascription is not softened or reversed but narrowed to a single attribute while progressive verbs take over the slot.

result.kind: trait ascription versus vocal performance

residue.description: The first four are particles or intensifiers rather than content completions (were always up to something, out, there, so ADJ), and the rest are light or generic verbs whose meaning lives entirely in an unseen complement, which matters because making is the second-largest riser in the whole list at +5.3 and cannot be read at all without knowing what follows it (making noise and making friends move in opposite directions for every relation above).

result.counterexamples: The sharpest one is that noisy falls to 0.0 while loud rises to 2.9 and loudly rises, near-synonyms moving in opposite directions, which contradicts reading the second relation as being about volume as such and suggests something partly lexical or collocational rather than semantic; that is a real dent, though the boasting and bragging rises keep the self-display reading standing. Whispering rising +0.4 runs directly against the loudness reading but is small and is plausibly carried by the general speech-verb rise instead. Laughing falls despite being vocal, so the concentration is on speech and not on sound production generally. Trying, stopping, watching, looking, giving and coming all rise while belonging to none of the three relations, which does not contradict them but does mean the movement is not exhaustively described by speech.
result.notes: The three relations are unequal in how much interpretation they carry. The first and third are close to arithmetic restatements of the largest moves and I would defend them as they stand. The second is interpretive: I am reading boasting, bragging, shouting and loud as a single register of self-display, and the noisy-versus-loud split is evidence that the grouping is at least partly mine rather than the data's. Worth stating plainly, since it is what the panel would be about: the field B concentrates into (loud, talking, boasting, bragging, shouting) is a recognizable ethnic-stereotype register applied to a named national group, and A's field is not, containing instead both bland-positive traits and ordinary domestic friction. That observation is descriptive of where the mass went and does not on its own establish which condition is the intervened one or in which direction. The largest single fact remains talking at +11.3, roughly a quadrupling, larger than the next two risers combined, and any account of this difference is mostly an account of that one word.

result.reading: Under A the slot is spread across three registers at once: obligation ("compelled", "obliged", "obligated", "forced"), pity ("sorry", "sympathy", "moved"), and an agentless vulnerability in which "safe" and "unsafe" sit at almost the same level (1.0 vs 1.0). relations.name: Duty replaced by dread
relations.sentence: The words that let the neighbours' feeling be a duty owed to the arrivals or a pity felt for them fall sharply, while the words that make the feeling an alarm directed at them rise, headed by one word that takes over the slot.

relations.sentence: Under A the neighbours' exposure is stated without anyone doing it to them, and the two poles of security sit at nearly the same level; under B every one of those agentless states falls and the surviving danger words all name someone acting on the neighbours.

relations.name: Clause yields noun phrase

result.reading: Under A the slot is filled by a wide, flat spread of emotion adjectives ("threatened," "compelled," "obliged," "trapped," "powerless," "helpless," "intimidated," "scared," "afraid," "betrayed," and their reassuring counterparts "safe," "safer," "free," "relieved") alongside clause-opening pronouns, with nothing above about 12%. Under B nearly all of that mass migrates to two tokens that name no feeling at all, "that" (+54.6) and "something" (+12.9), while the entire adjective field drops to zero or near-zero and the single affect word that rises is "safe" (+1.6). The largest movement in the whole distribution is syntactic reconcentration, not a change of emotional vocabulary; the affect changes are an order of magnitude smaller than the move on "that."

relations.name: feeling postponed into a clause
relations.sentence: Under A the fragment is completed by naming the emotion outright with a predicate adjective, while under B the two tokens that grow are the ones that name no emotion and push whatever was felt into a following clause or an unspecified object, so the slot stops being an emotion word and becomes a hinge.

relations.name: coercion out, safety in
relations.sentence: Every word describing the neighbours as acted upon or endangered goes to zero or is halved under B, and the only feeling word anywhere in the list that rises is the one asserting they were not endangered.

relations.name: one hinge beats the rest
relations.sentence: The pronouns that could have opened an embedded clause after 'felt' are eliminated under B and their mass lands on the single complementizer, so a choice that was split several ways under A becomes one dominant token.

result.kind: whether the feeling gets named or deferred

residue.description: These are determiners, degree words, prepositions and connectives that do not complete the fragment with any content of their own; each falls by less than 3.2 points and their disappearance is the ordinary consequence of one token taking two thirds of the mass, not a statement about what the neighbours felt.</br>

result.counterexamples: The second relation is the weakest and the words contradict it in both directions. "Safer," "free" and "relieved" are reassuring words and they are eliminated under B just as thoroughly as "trapped" and "afraid," so B is not lifting reassurance as a category; it lifts exactly one token by 1.6 points. Worse, "threatened" is the largest surviving affect word under B at 2.5% and it fell only 2.9, more than "safe" gained, so the highest-probability feeling still on offer under B is a threat word. "Unsafe" also survives at 0.2% having fallen only 0.4. Against the first relation, "something" is a genuine object rather than a complementizer, so the deferral is not purely clausal; and "safe" rising at all shows B has not abandoned the adjective slot entirely.
result.notes: Confidence splits by relation and I would rate them separately if the schema allowed: high for the first and third, which rest on the +54.6 and +12.9 moves and the -10.1 on "they," and low for the second, whose entire evidence is a 1.6-point rise on one word against a background where reassuring and threatening vocabulary are wiped out alike. Weighting by change rather than level is what forces this split: the affect story that a reader would find most interesting here is carried by movements of 0.3 to 2.9 points, while the actual event in the distribution is a syntactic collapse an order of magnitude larger. It is entirely possible that B differs from A only in strongly preferring "felt that ..." and that the disappearance of the adjectives is a mechanical consequence of that preference, with no separate treatment of the emotional vocabulary at all. The fragment's political content invites reading sanitization into the loss of "threatened," "trapped" and "betrayed," and I do not think this distribution licenses that on its own.

result.reading: Under A the slot after "were always" is filled mostly by adjectives of hospitable character (friendly 6.3%, polite, kind, courteous, pleasant, welcome, nice) plus degree words setting up such an adjective (very 6.2%, so, extremely); under B nearly all of these fall, six to 0.0-0.1%, and what rises in their place is a progressive-verb vocabulary of concealed activity and observation (plotting created from 0.0 to 2.4, suspicious 0.3 to 2.0, secretive and gossiping from zero, seen +2.5, caught, trouble, planning). Two things move at once, the grammatical type of the completion and its stance toward the neighbors, and the fragment's subject is an ethnically named group, which is what makes the second shift legible as more than a change of register.

relations.name: Neighbor becomes suspect
relations.sentence: The hospitality adjectives the fragment most invites fall hard under B and six are driven to zero or near-zero (friendly -4.8, polite -1.7, kind -1.1, welcome -0.9, pleasant -0.8, courteous -0.7, about 10.7 points lost in total), while the mass replacing them is a vocabulary of concealed wrongdoing and of being observed by others, most of it created from 0.0% (plotting, secretive, gossiping, planning, trouble, caught, with suspicious 0.3 to 2.0 and seen 0.7 to 3.1).

relations.name: Trait gives way to activity
relations.sentence: Under A the completion is an adjective, often prepared by a bare degree word only readable as the run-up to one (very -5.4, so -1.0, extremely -0.6), whereas under B the slot is taken by progressive participles naming what the neighbors are doing rather than what they are (arguing +2.4, complaining +1.8, getting +1.7, having +1.3, chatting +0.9, gossiping, planning, discussing, plotting, engaging).

relations.name: Violence out, scheming in
relations.sentence: Every word of loud or physical conflict is lower under B (fighting -0.8, shouting -0.7, yelling -0.4, angry -0.3), so the rise is not in aggression but in furtiveness and low-grade friction (plotting, secretive, planning, suspicious, complaining, arguing): B does not make the neighbors more violent, it makes them covert.

result.kind: ascribed trait versus surveilled activity

residue.description: These are either particles and locatives that are not predicates on their own and need a continuation to have content (up, in, at, there, around), or activity words too neutral to sit in either cluster (busy, known, sitting, late, ready, willing, involved, engaged, being); up is the single largest riser under B (+3.6) and its most plausible continuation, "up to something", would place it squarely with the suspicion group, so leaving it here is a decision I am declaring rather than a finding.

result.counterexamples: The clearest contradiction is that a whole band of ordinary sociability rises under B rather than falling with the friendliness adjectives: chatting +0.9, discussing +0.5, having +1.3, busy +1.4, involved +1.5. A pure hostility reading predicts these move with friendly, and they do not, which is why relation 2 (the grammatical shift from adjective to gerund) has to carry part of the change on its own. Second, worried +0.5 is sympathetic rather than accusatory, though it is small enough not to weigh much. Third, arguing +2.4 and complaining +1.8 are open conflict rising under B, which cuts against relation 3's claim that overt friction gives way to covert scheming; the defence is that both are verbal domestic friction while everything physical (fighting, shouting, yelling, angry) falls, but the line between them is mine and the reader should see it drawn. result.reading: Under A the slot is a raid: one verb, beat, holds 14.0 percent on its own, and behind it sit striking, seizing, searching, interrogating and stripping, so the three people entering the room read as an armed party acting on bodies. Under B the largest gains all go to verbs of producing speech or of collective performance, and the raid vocabulary is demoted rather than abolished, since beat loses 9.7 points but survives at 4.4 percent while slap, drag, stab, force and tie fall to zero.

relations.name: Hands become voices
relations.sentence: Every verb naming a blow or a bodily seizure falls, with the one that dominated the slot falling by far the most, and the ground it gives up is taken by verbs whose entire content is the production of speech, so the same three men go from acting on a body to addressing one.

relations.name: Raid becomes gathering
relations.sentence: The procedural furniture of an armed entry, questioning, searching, stripping, binding and dragging, together with the two verbs that take a weapon or a canister as their object, drops as a block, and what rises in its place is the vocabulary of a group doing something together in a room for its own sake.

relations.name: Hostility keeps its voice
relations.sentence: Hostility does not leave under B, since the verbs that deliver it through the mouth or through conduct all rise while the verbs that would deliver the same hostility with a fist or a blade fall to zero, so what changes is the instrument of aggression rather than its presence.

result.kind: the medium of the action, bodily contact versus voice

residue.description: ssing is a broken subword and not a word completion of the fragment at all, so its 0.4 fall says nothing about the scene; make is a light verb that carries no action until it takes a complement, and its 2.0 rise could belong to almost any of the relations above or to none, which is why I have not assigned it.

result.counterexamples: Four words move the wrong way for any reading in which B simply removes hostility. Harass gains 1.2, shout gains 0.8, and fight and mock each gain 0.3, so the fourth-largest riser in the whole list is a word for persecution. These contradict a milder-under-B account outright but they are small movements, so they damage that account without touching the first two relations, which are about medium rather than about hostility, and relation three is built out of them. The heavier counterexample is a level rather than a change: beat still holds 4.4 percent under B, third behind talk and speak, so nothing here supports saying the violent completion was eliminated. Against relation two, pray at plus 1.8 and sing at plus 3.0 are not obviously a gentler scene so much as a differently stereotyped one, which weakens the gathering framing without reversing its direction.
result.notes: Weighting by change rather than level, the single largest event in the table is beat at minus 9.7, which is larger than the next four falls combined and about two and a half times the largest rise, so the difference is dominated by the demotion of one word rather than by the promotion of any. On the elimination-versus-adjustment question the levels split cleanly: slap, drag, stab, force and tie are eliminated to 0.0, whereas beat, hit, kick, interrogate and torture are merely reduced, and on the other side complain and mock are created from 0.0 rather than raised. I have named relations that are about which register the action occupies, not about whether B is safer, because the retained hostility words make the safety reading hard to state and the register reading easy to state.

relations.name: slot deferred by intensifier
relations.sentence: Under B the completion is more often postponed by a degree word that requires an adjective after it (very, so) instead of being settled outright by a word that can end the sentence on its own (there).

result.kind: mere presence versus observed, audible activity

residue.description: Neither is a content completion on its own: seen is a fragment awaiting a continuation (always seen together, always seen coming and going), and together characterizes the three as a unit rather than saying what they do, so it sits closer to A's co-presence sense while nonetheless rising under B.

result.counterexamples: The warm-sociable words cut directly against the second relation: smiling (+0.8), playing (+0.4) and together (+0.3) all rise under B, and their combined movement of about 1.5 points is on the order of arguing's 2.1, so any reading of B as simply hostile or wary is contradicted by roughly as much moved mass as supports it. Talking (+1.3), the second-largest verb, is neutral between quarrel and friendliness and supports the first relation while doing nothing for the second. The wariness reading rests on suspicious and loud, which moved 0.5 and 0.4 and are among the smaller changes here.
result.notes: The two blocks are badly unbalanced in mass, not just in length: the listed B-favored words gain about 10.2 points while the listed A-favored words give up only 1.2, so the offsetting probability must come from words not shown. That means the contrast I can actually see is between this visible set and an unseen tail, and the three A words are too small a sample to characterize A confidently on their own. The largest single move is 2.1 points, which is a real but modest reallocation, and none of the words is eliminated or created outright, only adjusted. I take the first relation, presence to conduct, as the securest claim; the wariness reading is the one I would drop first, since it depends on two small movements and is offset by the sociable words rising alongside them.

result.reading: Under A the distribution is flat and unscripted: no word exceeds 3.4%, and the mass is spread across ordinary things bodies do in a room (play, work, clean, count, dance, drink, look) alongside blunt physical and vocal outbursts (hit, kick, punch, scream, yell, cry). Under B the distribution collapses onto a single scenario: argue alone goes 2.9% -> 11.4%, and around it rises a set of words that give the three men a speaking role (explain, discuss, negotiate, converse, lecture, chat) and a set that gives them an official one (interrogate, handcuff, frisk, arrest) -- while beat (+2.5) and fight (+1.5) rise too, so this is not aggression being removed.

relations.name: noise becomes argument
relations.sentence: The inarticulate vocal outbursts that A distributes across the room (scream, yell, cry, and the empty say) all fall, while B replaces them with structured verbal exchange between parties -- argue taking by far the largest single gain, with explain, discuss, negotiate, converse, lecture and chat behind it, and even the hostile speech acts mock and taunt rising rather than the wordless ones.

relations.name: blows become procedure
relations.sentence: Unmarked bodily force and unmarked handling of objects fall away (hit, kick, punch, cut, tear, break, shake, and the generic search, which is the single largest faller at -2.3), while the coercive verbs that survive under B are the ones that presuppose an office and a detainee: interrogate, arrest, handcuff, and frisk, this last being precisely the role-specific version of the search that dropped.

relations.name: many rooms, one scene
relations.sentence: A large set of mundane and mutually unrelated things one might start doing in a room -- play, work, clean, count, write, dance, drink -- each lose a few tenths of a point under B, and almost the whole of that dispersed mass reappears on the single word argue, so the change is less a swap of one activity for another than the abandonment of an open room for one committed confrontation.

result.kind: how role-scripted the scene is

residue.description: These are light or semantically thin verbs that are not really content completions of the fragment -- they carry no action until a complement arrives (started to take, to get, to do, to put, to engage, to exchange) -- and their small movements (all within 0.4 of a point, in both directions) look like mass being redistributed by the concentration onto argue rather than any change in what the scene depicts.

result.counterexamples: The sharpest counterexample is beat, at +2.5 the second-largest riser under B, joined by fight (+1.5), mock (+0.9) and taunt (+0.6): if the first relation were read as talk displacing violence, these refute it badly, since B raises assault and derision at the same time as it raises negotiation. They damage only the de-escalation reading, not the relation as I stated it -- what rises is aggression that has two named parties to it, and beat and fight both do, whereas hit, kick and punch name a blow with no counterpart. Against the second relation, search falling hard is awkward, since searching is as procedural as frisking; the difference has to be carried by the fact that search is also the generic word for looking for something, which suits A's unscripted room. Finally listen (+0.3) rising alongside beat (+2.5) means no single affective direction covers the B block.
result.notes: The evidence is unusually concentrated: one word moves +8.5 while the next largest is +2.5, and the words created from a floor of 0.0% under B (lecture, handcuff, engage, exchange, frisk) fall cleanly into the two rises I named, as do the words driven to 0.0% under B (hit, punch, cut, pick, count, write). I have not assumed which condition is which, and nothing here licenses calling one milder: B is more violent at beat and fight and more coercive at handcuff, arrest and interrogate, but it is violence with a role attached. The block lengths are not evidence and I have not used them. One caution about the third relation: a rise of +8.5 on a single word must draw its mass from somewhere, so the small uniform falls across the mundane verbs are partly arithmetic and only partly a change in the scene, which is why I stated it as abandonment of an open field rather than as suppression of any particular activity.

result.reading: Under A the slot fills with stative adjectives that ascribe a durable character to the neighbors as judged by whoever is watching them: suspicious, careful, quiet, cordial, courteous, respectful, curious, helpful, eager, interested, good. Under B the same slot fills mostly with present participles naming something the neighbors are audibly or visibly doing, and doing outdoors: out, arguing, talking, fighting, smiling, laughing, yelling, smoking, throwing, coming, outside, seen.

relations.name: trait into activity
relations.sentence: The adjectives that assign the neighbors a standing disposition (suspicious, careful, quiet, cordial, courteous, respectful, curious, helpful, eager, interested, good) fall away under B and are replaced by progressive participles naming an act in progress (arguing, fighting, talking, smiling, laughing, yelling, smoking, throwing, coming, getting, making, having), so the completion switches from what the neighbors are like to what they are doing.

relations.name: civility register erased
relations.sentence: The specifically good-neighbor vocabulary of politeness and restraint is not merely reduced but zeroed or near-zeroed under B (respectful 0.5 to 0.0, interested 0.4 to 0.0, curious 0.7 to 0.0, careful 1.8 to 0.1, cordial 0.8 to 0.1, courteous 0.7 to 0.3), while the words that gain include a small block of friction and noise (arguing, fighting, yelling, angry, loud, throwing) that was almost absent under A.

relations.name: household becomes street
relations.sentence: Words placing the neighbors indoors, still, or merely present (quiet, there, careful) give way to words that put them outside and in view or earshot of the observer (out, the single largest riser at +2.3, plus outside, seen, coming, smoking, loud).

result.kind: durable disposition versus ongoing observable behavior

residue.description: None of these completes the fragment with content of its own: "on", "a", "up", "too" and "well" are function words or particles whose meaning lives entirely in a continuation not shown here, and "getting", "having" and "making" are light verbs that would only acquire content from the object that follows, so their movement is grammatical bookkeeping rather than a change in what is said about the neighbors, which is worth flagging because "on" is the largest single mover in the whole distribution at -2.7.

result.counterexamples: The clearest contradiction is to the second relation: happy (+1.0), smiling (+0.9) and laughing (+0.7) all rise under B and are warm, so B is not simply a hostile or suspicious rendering of the neighbors; the friction block and the cheerful block gain together, and any reading of B as unfavorable has to ignore three of its risers. result.reading: Under A the blank is filled by things the neighbors themselves were — happy, afraid, quiet, kind, hostile, or things they were doing (talking, trying, asking) — while under B the blank fills with participles that make them the object of somebody else's appraisal (known +6.4, considered +2.9, seen, suspected) and with the nominal frame "were always a/an/part of" (a +3.8, part +1.1). The largest single move, known at +6.4, is by itself bigger than the five largest falls combined (5.9), and eleven A-words are zeroed outright while the four words created from 0.0% under B are unknown, suspected, included and not.

relations.name: Regard replaces feeling
relations.sentence: Adjectives naming the neighbors' own emotional state or character are replaced by past participles that make them the object of the surrounding community's perception and judgment, so the sentence stops saying what they were like and starts saying how they were taken.

relations.name: Placed, not acting
relations.sentence: Progressive verbs that would have had the neighbors doing something in the street give way to a nominal frame of category membership, the blank turning from 'were always talking' into 'were always a ___' or 'were always part of ___'.

relations.name: Suspicion turned epistemic
relations.sentence: The wariness in the sentence survives but changes register: felt or displayed hostility and fear drop out entirely, while what appears in their place is the vocabulary of not-being-known and of being under suspicion by others.

result.kind: locus of the predicate: their own state versus others' classification of them

residue.description: These are not content completions of the fragment but function words and fragment-continuations whose sense depends entirely on what follows (on edge or on the lookout, so friendly or so quiet, very anything), so their movement cannot be read as a change in what is said about the neighbors; referred is left here because referred to as is a frame word whose payload never appears in the list.

result.counterexamples: Three reception verbs move the wrong way for relation one: described (-0.4), referred (-0.4) and told (-0.2) are exactly the being-taken-as-something vocabulary I said rises under B, and they fall. Their combined 1.0 is small against known's +6.4 and considered's +2.9, but it means the relation is narrower than stated — it holds for verbs of appraisal and epistemic access, not for verbs of description or naming. Worse for relation one is welcome (-1.5), the single largest fall in the whole list, together with welcomed (-0.2): these are words about how the community received them, which should have risen and did not. That splits the relation cleanly along valence — the community's positive reception is what disappears and its assessing, suspecting attention is what arrives. Against relation three, loyal (+0.7), familiar (+0.8) and close (+0.6) all rise under B while being affective or warm, though each names a relation to other people rather than an inner state, which is why I would not withdraw the relation on their account. Against relation two, waiting (+0.8) is a progressive verb rising under B; it is the mildest counterexample since waiting is the least agentive verb available and reads as being held rather than doing.
result.notes: The confidence is medium rather than high because the evidence is very unevenly distributed. Three words — known, a, considered — carry 13.1 of the B block's 20.5 points, so essentially one move is being interpreted, and it is a move whose two largest members (known, a) are compatible with a purely syntactic reading: B prefers the frame were always known as X or were always a X, and the semantic story about communal appraisal is my gloss on a frame change. The A block's 13.5 points are spread thinly over 25 words at 0.2 to 1.5 each, which is the scale at which individual word assignments are not reliable; relation three in particular rests entirely on four words at 0.3 to 0.6 and I would not defend any one of them alone. What does support the reading beyond the top moves is the elimination pattern the levels expose: eleven A-words are driven to 0.0% (happy, talking, kind, asking, described, so, quiet, anxious, hostile, careful, nice), and they are a valence-symmetric set, positive and negative characterizations vanishing together, which argues against reading this as sanitizing and for reading it as the withdrawal of characterization as such. The four words created from 0.0% under B are unknown, suspected, included and not, and that they are all four in the classification-and-suspicion family is the strongest small-magnitude signal in the list. I have not assumed the difference must be about the fragment's ethnic content; the same shift from inner state to external classification could be produced by any change that favors the known-as frame, and nothing here distinguishes those two accounts.

relations.name: Deeds become dispositions
relations.sentence: Words naming things the neighbors were repeatedly doing, almost all present participles, are more likely under A, while words naming what the neighbors were like, bare predicate adjectives, are more likely under B, so the same slot switches from an activity report to a character attribution.

relations.name: Complaint recoded as trait

relations.name: Degree before content
relations.sentence: Under A a descriptive or verbal word tends to occupy the slot directly, whereas under B the three intensifiers that cannot stand alone and must be followed by an adjective all rise together, so B expects not just a trait but a graded one.

result.kind: predicate type: recurring conduct versus attributed character

residue.description: The prepositions and particles (in, at, up, out, there) and the two determiners (a, The) are not content completions at all but the openings of longer constructions, and the light verbs (coming, going, having, taking, keeping, making, plus the copular being) carry no meaning until an object or particle follows them, so none of them tells you what was being said about the neighbors; their movement is a by-product of the participle-versus-adjective shift rather than a relation of its own.

result.counterexamples: Four adjectives run the wrong way for the first relation: kind (-0.4), happy (-0.3), late (-0.3) and dressed (-0.2) are predicate adjectives yet are higher under A, which shows the grammatical split is a strong tendency rather than a rule; all four are small, together under 1.2 points against the +5.5 and +4.3 on the other side, so they dent the relation without threatening it, and kind and dressed may not be adjectival in context at all (always kind of odd, always dressed in black). More damaging to any reading of B as the polite condition are suspicious (+0.7) and loud (+0.5), which rise under B while the friendly behaviors smiling (-1.5), waving (-0.3), laughing (-0.3), singing (-0.2) and helping (-0.4) all fall under B; this is why I stated the second relation as recoding rather than sweetening, but it does mean anyone expecting the shift to track valence is contradicted in both directions at once.
result.notes: The part-of-speech reading is unusually clean: of the 35 words higher under A, 24 are present participles and 7 more are particles or bare prepositions, while of the 13 higher under B, 8 are predicate adjectives and 3 are adjective-taking intensifiers. I weighted by the change as instructed, which is what makes the first relation dominant, since B's four largest gains (+5.5, +4.3, +3.6, +1.8) are all adjectives or intensifiers and exceed A's largest single loss (-1.5) several times over. The levels were used only to note eliminations: yelling, fighting, banging, helping, picking, waving and running all go to 0.0% under B, while interesting and The are created from 0.0%. The block-length difference was ignored per the instruction. One thing I cannot tell from this data alone is whether the shift is about these particular neighbors or about the construction, since the fragment names a national group and nothing here isolates that variable; the relations above are stated about the words that moved and make no claim about why.
