result.reading: Under B the slot fills with the vocabulary of someone endangered by an arriving group: threatened alone jumps nearly seventeen points, and intimidated, attacked, frightened, afraid, trapped, provoked, insulted and offended all rise, most of them from zero. Under A the same slot carries affiliation and duty instead, with solidarity, sympathy, included and part present and each of them falling to 0.0% under B, alongside a wide spread of ordinary syntactic continuations after felt.

relations.name: Guest becomes intruder
relations.sentence: Words casting the neighbours as fellow-feeling with, or safe alongside, the people who arrived give way to words casting the neighbours as targets of hostility from them, so the same event is completed once as an act of joining and once as an act of menace.

relations.name: Duty becomes coercion
relations.sentence: The register of compulsion survives in both conditions but changes who imposes it: under A the neighbours are bound by something they owe, while under B they are acted upon by an outside force.

relations.name: Slot collapses onto adjective
relations.sentence: Under A the position after felt is spread across several grammatical continuations that need not name an emotion at all, while under B the mass concentrates into a bare predicate adjective and a complement clause, one word taking over sixteen points of it.

result.kind: which party the neighbours are positioned against

residue.description: Empowered belongs to no relation cleanly because it leaves unstated who or what the neighbours are empowered by or to do, so it is not obviously either affiliation or safety; the remaining words are function words and bare continuations rather than content completions of the fragment, and they enter the third relation only as evidence about the shape of the slot, not as things the neighbours are said to feel.

result.counterexamples: Angry, insulted, offended and provoked rise under B but name affront and indignation rather than fear, so they cut against reading the B side as simple endangerment; they still cast the neighbours as wronged party, so the damage is mild rather than fatal to the first relation. Obliged and responsible cut against reading the A side as warmth, since a duty is not a welcome, which is why they were split off into a relation of their own. Safe and safer are the sharper counterexample on the A side: a completion that reaches for safety presupposes that danger was already salient there, so the two conditions may differ in how the danger is resolved rather than in whether it is present. Alienated under B is estrangement, not menace, and sits awkwardly between the two blocks.
result.notes: The levels carry one thing the differences alone do not. Solidarity, sympathy, included, part and something all reach exactly 0.0% under B, and attacked, insulted, offended, trapped, pressured and provoked all come from exactly 0.0% under A. So this is not one distribution nudged along a scale: a vocabulary of affiliation is eliminated and a vocabulary of hostility is created. That is stronger evidence for the first relation than the size of any single move. The concentration is also worth stating plainly, since threatened gains more than every A word loses except the, which means B is not merely reweighting a field of emotions but collapsing it onto one. I am describing a difference and not judging which condition is right; nothing here tells me which direction is the intervention, and the fragment names a specific national group, which is the whole reason the difference is legible at all.

result.reading: Every word that gains under B is a verb of speaking (argue, talk, interrogate, speak, question, ask, yell), and the only two that fall are the two that put hands on a person or thing (stab, tie); the fragment's scene keeps its confrontational shape but changes what the three men are doing with their bodies. The falls are tiny in absolute terms, roughly a halving of already-small values, while the gains total over eleven points, so most of the mass entering the speech verbs came from words not shown here.

relations.name: Body swapped for voice
relations.sentence: The only two completions in which something is done to a body, stab and tie, are roughly halved under B, while every word that rises is a verb of speaking, from the largest gain (argue, +3.6) down to the smallest (yell, +0.5), so what the men begin doing shifts from physical contact to speech.

relations.name: Coercion keeps its asymmetry
relations.sentence: The rising speech verbs are not uniformly pacific: the largest single gain goes to argue (+3.6) and the specific gains go to interrogate (+1.4), question (+1.3) and yell (+0.5), all of which keep one party pressing another, so B is not a conversation replacing a confrontation but a confrontation carried out in words while stabbing recedes.

relations.name: Shaved, not erased
relations.sentence: Neither physical verb is eliminated: stab goes 0.7 to 0.3 and tie 0.3 to 0.1, each losing under half a point and surviving at roughly half its former level, while the seven risers gain more than eleven points between them, so the physical reading is attenuated rather than removed and the mass funding the speech verbs is mostly drawn from words outside this list.

result.kind: channel of the act, bodily contact versus speech

residue.description: All nine are ordinary content completions of "started to ___" and each falls under the body-versus-voice split, so nothing is left over; the nearest thing to residue is tie, which needs an object to complete the clause and so reads as an ellipsis for tying someone up rather than as a self-sufficient completion, but its restraint sense still places it with stab.

result.counterexamples: Against a reading of the second relation as coercion fully preserved, the three largest-or-neutral risers cut the other way: talk (+2.5), speak (+1.3) and ask (+1.1) are unmarked for pressure and together account for nearly half the gained mass, so the confrontational tint of the B side is real but diluted, which weakens that relation moderately without touching the first. Against any reading of the first relation as softening or de-escalation, yell (+0.5) rises rather than falls, and it is the loudest word in the set; that contradicts a mildness reading outright, though only mildly in mass, and it is consistent with the modality claim I actually made. Nothing in the list contradicts the third relation, since both A-side words move in the same direction by comparable small amounts.
result.notes: The split is unusually clean by semantic class, which is why confidence is high, but two cautions. First, the arithmetic does not balance: the two A-side words shed 0.6 points together while the B-side gains about 11.2, so this list shows where mass arrived and only a small part of where it left; whatever else fell is not visible here and could change the character of the relation. Second, no word is created or eliminated in the level sense, since all nine have nonzero mass under both conditions, so this is a reweighting of an existing repertoire and not a foreclosure of the physical option. I have taken the unequal block lengths as carrying nothing on their own, as instructed.

result.reading: Under A the completions script the three entrants as agents of a search-and-interrogation: the big fallers are ask (-2.8), interrogate (-2.3), take (-2.2), question (-1.8), yell (-1.6), backed by a tail of search, examine, inspect, interview, check. Under B the big risers are talk (+3.7), speak (+3.5), discuss (+3.2), argue (+3.1), chat (+2.0), with a smaller set of ordinary occupancy verbs (play, dance, sit, eat, drink) coming up off near-zero, so the same three men are re-scripted from people who do something to the room's occupants into people who are simply in the room with them.

relations.name: Interrogation into conversation
relations.sentence: Speech verbs that presuppose one party with the authority to demand answers (ask, interrogate, question, interview) fall sharply, while speech verbs that presuppose two or more parties on equal footing (talk, speak, discuss, chat, debate, whisper, chatter) rise by the largest margins on the list.

relations.name: Searching the room versus occupying it
relations.sentence: Verbs that treat the room as an object to be gone through (search, examine, inspect, check, look) all fall, and the words that rise in their place are verbs of simply being in a room and using it (sit, eat, drink, dance, play), most of which start near zero and are effectively created rather than adjusted.

relations.name: One-sided force to mutual friction
relations.sentence: Verbs in which the entrants act loudly or physically upon someone else (yell, shout, push, kick, pull) fall, while conflict itself does not disappear but reappears in reciprocal form as argue and fight, both of which rise.

result.kind: the power relation the verb assumes between the entrants and the room

residue.description: take is the third largest fall on the whole list (-2.2) and I cannot assign it confidently, because "started to take" is a light verb whose object does all the work and could be seizure, could be a seat, could be notes; give (-0.3), go (-0.3) and count (+0.4) are likewise verbs that only become content once an object arrives, and their movements are small enough that reading a scene into them would be inventing one.

result.counterexamples: The clearest counterexample is fight, which rises +1.2 under B, and argue, which rises +3.1 and is the fourth largest riser overall; if the difference were simply that B removes hostility from the scene, these two should have fallen with yell and shout. They do not damage the relations as I have stated them, since both are reciprocal verbs and it is one-sidedness rather than conflict that drops, but they do rule out the easier reading and are the reason I did not name the relations in terms of calm or hostility. A weaker objection is that the physical-force group in relation three moves very little (push -0.3, kick -0.3, pull -0.2), so that relation rests mostly on yell (-1.6) and shout (-0.9) and would survive being deleted. Finally whisper rises (+0.3), and whispering is at least as compatible with a covert search as with sociable talk, so it sits in relation one on the strength of its form rather than its scene.
result.notes: The confidence is about the shape of the difference, not about any cause of it: the seven largest movements in each direction fall cleanly on either side of the interrogation/conversation split, which is more coherence than chance would give. Two cautions on reading it. First, I have weighted by the bracketed differences throughout, and used the levels only to note that sit, eat, drink, dance and chatter start at or below 0.4% and are closer to being created under B than adjusted, while ask, interrogate, take and question are large under A and merely reduced, not eliminated. Second, the two blocks differ in length (15 against 17) and I have taken no meaning from that. It is also worth saying that nothing in the data tells me which condition is the intervention and which the baseline; I have described A as the raid scene and B as the social scene, but the relations are symmetric and could be read in the other direction without changing a word of the evidence.

relations.sentence: Under A the slot is most often filled by a word that postpones the emotion into a following clause or complement ("felt that...", "felt it...", "felt they...", "felt the...", "felt there..."), while under B those same continuations lose roughly seventeen points to adjectives that state the feeling outright in the slot itself, chiefly "uneasy" and "threatened".

relations.name: fellow-feeling replaced by endangerment
relations.sentence: Every word under A that casts the neighbours as owing something to the newcomers or feeling with them ( "sympathy", "sorry", "obliged", "compelled", "abandoned"), as unharmed ("free", "safer"), or as feeling nothing at all ("no", "nothing"), drops under B, with "sympathy" and "nothing" eliminated to 0.0%, while every word casting them as the endangered party rises, led by "threatened" at +7.8.

relations.name: many small losses, two large gains
relations.sentence: The losses under B are spread thinly across fifteen different continuations, none losing more than 5.4 points and most under one, whereas the gains are concentrated: "uneasy" and "threatened" alone absorb sixteen of the roughly nineteen points that move, so B is not merely a different distribution but a narrower one.

result.kind: how specified the feeling is, and whom it points at

residue.description: "a" is the third-largest mover in the whole list (+4.5) and I cannot assign it: it is a determiner rather than a completion, and "felt a..." could head either an affect nominal ("a chill", "a sense of unease") or an obligation one ("a duty"), so its rise supports no relation on its own; "for" is likewise a preposition, though if it is the sympathy idiom ("the neighbours felt for them") its fall would belong with the second relation, which is a reading I cannot settle from the numbers; "embarrassed" rises (+0.8) but names a self-conscious social affect rather than an endangerment one, sitting closer to A's register than to B's.

relations.name: Raid becomes gathering
relations.sentence: Verbs of forcible entry performed on a detained person (the largest single mover in the whole set, beat at -3.5, together with attack, kick, hit, frisk, search, tie and remove) give way to verbs of a social occasion among people already at ease (play, dance, sit, eat, drink, laugh), so that the same three entrants are recast from a squad conducting a search to guests joining a room.

relations.name: Interrogation turned conversation
relations.sentence: The verbal verbs stay verbal across both conditions but change who is entitled to speak: under A they are one-directional demands put to a subject (interrogate, question, ask, interview, shout), while under B they are reciprocal exchanges between parties of equal standing (speak, the second largest riser at +2.5, plus discuss, argue and engage).

relations.name: Object must be a person
relations.sentence: Cutting the same data on argument structure rather than on register, nearly every word favored under A demands a human direct object and would be incomplete without one (beat, interrogate, frisk, search, question, tie, kick, hit, interview), whereas the words favored under B are intransitive or take things and activities rather than people (sit, laugh, dance, work, eat, drink, arrange), so what falls away is not only violence but the presence of a second party being acted upon at all.

result.kind: what the entrants are to whoever is already in the room

relations.name: Both poles inflate

result.reading: Under A the slot fills with things the neighbours were made to DO: compelled, obliged, obligated, forced, free, responsible, plus the clause-openers such readings need (they, no, there). Under B nearly all the gained mass is emotional state, split between sympathy for the newcomers (sorry, sad, hurt, concerned) and alarm at them (uneasy, unsafe, scared, disturbed, vulnerable), with "a" gaining 10.9 points as the frame turns adjectival or nominal.

relations.name: obligation into feeling
relations.sentence: The deontic completions that make felt mean coerced-to-act (compelled -3.0, obliged -2.7, obligated -1.1, forced, responsible) fall away, and the mass reappears as named emotional states of the neighbours, running from sympathy (sorry +4.6, sad, hurt, concerned) through alarm (shocked +3.0, uneasy +2.6, unsafe +2.0, scared, disturbed, distressed, worried, fear) to incapacity (powerless, helpless, vulnerable).

relations.name: complement frame swap
relations.sentence: The function words track the same reframing: openers of a finite clause after felt lose mass (they -3.8, no, as, so, there) while the determiners, pro-forms and adjective-selecting intensifiers that introduce a nominal or adjectival feeling gain it (a +10.9, their +1.0, something +0.5, deeply, quite).

relations.name: positive poles erased
relations.sentence: The two completions under A that leave the neighbours better off, free (1.0 to 0.0) and safer (0.3 to 0.0), are zeroed rather than reduced, while their negatives appear or grow under B (unsafe +2.0, vulnerable +0.3, powerless +0.4, helpless +0.3).

result.kind: which reading of "felt": pressure to act versus emotional state

residue.description: Only more is left over: at -0.3 it is a degree word that would suit either frame (felt more obliged, felt more uneasy), so nothing in its movement picks a side, while the other small function words are assigned to the frame-swap relation because each selects one complement type or the other.

result.counterexamples: The clearest counterexample is offended (0.3 to 0.0), an emotional state moving the wrong way for relation one, though at 0.3 points it is an order of magnitude below the movers that define that relation. Free is a mild double case: read as a feeling rather than a permission it also contradicts relation one, which is why it is placed in relation three instead. Angry (+0.4) and frustrated (+0.4) sit oddly beside sorry and concerned but contradict nothing, since relation one claims only that the added words are affective, not that they are sympathetic. Nothing contradicts the frame swap.
result.notes: The three relations are one event seen at three grains: a change in what kind of complement follows felt, which drags content words and function words together, and which incidentally deletes the two outcomes favourable to the neighbours. The largest single move (a, +10.9) is syntactic rather than semantic, so weighting by change makes the frame shift, not any one emotion, the main finding. Worth flagging that the affect gained under B is genuinely ambiguous in reference: sorry, sad and hurt read as feeling for the Palestinians, while unsafe, scared, uneasy and vulnerable read as feeling threatened by them, and the distribution alone cannot say which completion would have followed. I take no position on what conditions A and B are.

result.reading: Under A the slot is dominated by a single verb, beat at 13.7%, heading a block of assault verbs (hit, kick, stab, punch, abuse, torture, assault, rape); under B that concentration collapses to 3.0% and the freed mass scatters thinly across sixteen verbs of speech, leisure and generic action, none gaining more than 2.3 points. The move is almost entirely one word going down and a wide, shallow fan going up, and what falls is specifically the act done to another body.

relations.name: One verb dispersed
relations.sentence: Nearly the whole difference is a single word: beat loses 10.7 points, about three quarters of the 14.4 points of total loss on the A side, and no word under B gains even a quarter of that, the mass instead spreading in fractions of a point across sixteen verbs from speak and play down to circle and get.

relations.name: Blows become talk
relations.sentence: The verbs of physical striking that are likelier under A (beat, hit, kick, punch, stab) give way under B to verbs of speaking and of shared, stationary sociability (speak, argue, discuss, play, dance, sit, drink), so the three men who were entering to strike someone are now entering to talk, play or sit.

relations.name: Antagonism changes channel
relations.sentence: Hostility is relocated rather than removed: every verb of bodily attack falls, while argue rises by 1.2 points to become the third-largest gain under B, so the scene keeps its conflict and loses only its physical contact.

result.kind: whether the act takes a victim

residue.description: These are not content completions of the fragment on their own: take, make, get, move, set, look and engage are light or complement-hungry verbs that decide nothing about what happens in the room until a following phrase arrives (started to take the chairs, started to get angry, started to engage in something), and circle is ambiguous between a physical encircling that would belong with the A block and a neutral milling about, so its +0.3 cannot be assigned; together they account for 3.5 of the 12.5 points gained under B, which means over a quarter of the rise goes into words that specify no action at all.

result.counterexamples: Three things cut against the relations as stated. First, against any reading in which B removes violence by severity: rape (0.4 to 0.2), torture (0.5 to 0.2) and assault (0.4 to 0.1) all survive under B, while stab (0.5), punch (0.4) and abuse (0.3) go to 0.0, so the worst-named acts are the ones left standing and the merely physical ones are the ones zeroed; this is a direct contradiction of a graded suppression, though it lives entirely in moves of 0.5 points and under, so it damages the shape of the story more than its size. Second, against calling the A block eliminated: beat remains at 3.0% under B, which is still the second-highest of any word listed there and close to the top riser speak at 3.7%, so the assault reading is cut down, not removed, and the panel would be wrong to say erased. Third, against Blows become talk as a description of the whole B block: the largest chunk of the rise after speak goes to contentless verbs (take +1.1, look +1.0, set, make, move, get), which are neither speech nor sociability, so the relation covers the top of the B block and not its bulk.
result.notes: Confidence is high for the direction and for relations 1 and 2, which rest on the single largest move in the list and on a coherent block of seven risers; it is lower for relation 3, which rests on argue alone at +1.2, and the uneven-erasure observation in the counterexamples rests on moves of 0.5 and below, near the resolution of the printed figures. One further pattern I did not raise to a relation because it is too small to weight: pray (+0.4), dance (+0.9), drink (+0.6), sit (+0.9) and possibly circle (+0.3) supply an alternative script that is itself culturally legible for the named group rather than a neutral one, so B is not simply emptying the slot of ethnic content; pray was already the fourth-likeliest word under A at 1.3%, and every one of these moves is under a point, so this is a direction worth noting and not a result. Also note engage is created from 0.0, the only word in the list that goes from nothing to something.

result.reading: Almost everything on the list gains under B (thirteen words, +9.4 points in total) while only three words lose, and those three lose 0.8 points between them, so B is mostly redistributing mass onto this whole set rather than trading one reading of the scene for another. Within that broad lift, the biggest gains sit on verbs of handling things in the room (take, remove, pull, clean, inspect, spray) and on verbs of speech and assistance (explain, argue, talk, help), while the three words that fall are the two derisive ones (laugh, taunt) plus the single ranged-weapon verb (fire) -- and hands-on violence (beat +1.4, attack +0.4) rises rather than falls.

relations.name: jeering into handling
relations.sentence: The two verbs that make the men's entrance an act of mockery aimed at someone present lose ground, while the verbs that put their hands on the contents of the room -- taking, removing, pulling, cleaning, inspecting, spraying, setting something down -- take up most of the gained mass.

relations.name: violence changes instrument
relations.sentence: The one verb implying a firearm falls, while the two verbs of bodily assault rise, so the aggression in the completion is not reduced but relocated from a weapon to the hands.

relations.name: mockery becomes exchange
relations.sentence: Speech directed at the others as ridicule gives way to speech that presupposes an interlocutor with a position -- explaining, arguing, talking, helping -- so the men enter as parties to something rather than as a jeering audience.

result.kind: purposive engagement versus expressive display

residue.description: "set" is not really a content completion here: it is a light verb waiting for a particle or complement, and its possible continuations run in opposite directions (set something down, set up, set fire to), so it cannot be assigned to the handling group or against it without deciding what follows it.

result.counterexamples: The sharpest counterexample is "beat" at +1.4, the second-largest gain on the list: any reading of B as a more domestic, procedural or pacified scene has to survive the fact that the verb for assaulting a person rises almost as much as the largest mover, and "attack" rises too, so the first relation's "handling replaces display" holds only if hands-on violence is quietly excluded from display. That "help" (+0.6) and "beat" (+1.4) rise together also means the B side is not internally uniform, which weakens any claim that the gained mass has a single character. The second relation is the most fragile: it rests on "fire" falling by 0.2 points, small enough that it could reverse on a re-run, and "fire" is itself ambiguous between discharging a weapon and setting something alight, which would put it with "set" rather than against "beat". Finally, "laugh" falling cuts against reading B as the more sociable or benign condition.
result.notes: Two structural caveats. First, the gains and losses do not balance (+9.4 against -0.8), so the mass B adds here is drawn from words not shown; the three A-words are not the source of the thirteen B-words' gains, and the relations should be read as "what B piles onto" rather than as trades. Second, the A block has only three members, so three relations cannot avoid reusing them: "laugh" and "taunt" appear on the A side of both relation 1 and relation 3, distinguished by which sense of them is being contrasted (derisive display against handling; mockery against argument), not by partitioning the words. All movements are small in absolute terms -- the largest is 1.8 points and nothing is eliminated or created -- so this is an adjustment of an already diffuse distribution, not a rewriting of it, and I would not defend any of the three relations against a re-run without seeing the variance.

result.reading: The fragment invites a word for how neighbours feel about Palestinians arriving on their street, and the single dominant motion is "threatened" gaining six points, with "unsafe", "uncomfortable" and "betrayed" moving the same way in miniature. What falls is a scattered set of interior or self-implicating states: "obliged", "insecure", "free", "fear", "sorry", alongside two negation-shaped or demonstrative openers, "no" and "this".

relations.name: Threat pulled outward
relations.sentence: Words naming a diffuse or interior unease that the neighbours simply have ("insecure", "fear") give way under B to words naming a condition inflicted on them from outside ("threatened", "unsafe", "uncomfortable", "betrayed"), so a broadly similar affect is re-described as something done to them rather than something they are.

relations.name: Duty and remorse dropped
relations.sentence: The completions that would give the neighbours a moral or civic stance toward the arrival ("obliged", "sorry", "free") fall nearly to zero under B, with "obliged" the largest single fall on the list, while the mass they lose turns up in the endangerment vocabulary led by "threatened".

relations.name: Toward a noun phrase
relations.sentence: Among the words that are not themselves the feeling, the openers of a negated or demonstrative continuation ("no", "this") fall while the openers of an indefinite, possessed or comparative phrase ("a", "their", "like") rise, with "a" the second-largest single move anywhere in the difference.

result.kind: attribution and sharpness of the felt threat

residue.description: These two rise under B alongside the threat words but mean the opposite of them, so they join no relation I can state and are handled below as counterevidence; the phrase-openers "a", "their", "like", "no" and "this" are not content completions at all, and I have grouped them only as a syntactic shift rather than as an affect.

result.counterexamples: "safe" (+0.4) and "safer" (+0.3) rise under B, which contradicts any reading in which B simply intensifies danger; and "insecure" (-0.8) and "fear" (-0.3) fall under B even though they are threat words, which contradicts a simple claim that B raises the threat vocabulary as a class. result.notes: Only "threatened" (+6.0) and "a" (+2.7) move enough that I would defend them from this single comparison; everything else sits between 0.2 and 1.3 points and could be noise, so the two smaller relations are readings of a pattern rather than of any individual number. I have also not treated the fall of "insecure" and "fear" as evidence that B is less fearful; the more economical description is redistribution within a single affect field toward its most canonical externally-caused term.

result.reading: Twelve of the sixteen listed words rise under B, and they are almost one vocabulary: past-participles and adjectives for being harmed (threatened +4.9, abandoned +1.9, violated +1.2, betrayed +1.0, humiliated +0.9, then a tail of unsafe/insecure/vulnerable/uncomfortable/endangered/harassed/invaded at +0.4 to +0.7). What falls is not a rival feeling but four continuations in which "felt" is not an emotion predicate at all: themselves, sure, in, we, each losing 0.2 to 0.3. The two blocks are also very unequal in mass, about +13.4 points gained against about -0.9 lost, so most of what B added came from words not shown here rather than from the four that fell.

relations.name: grammar yields to grievance
relations.sentence: Under A the slot still draws measurable weight from continuations in which "felt" is not naming an emotion at all (a reflexive pronoun, an epistemic adjective after "felt", a bare preposition, a clause-opening subject pronoun), whereas essentially all of B's added mass goes to participles and adjectives that name being harmed, so the difference is less about which feeling is chosen than about whether a feeling occupies the slot.

relations.name: inflicted over ambient
relations.sentence: Within B's own block the largest gains go to participles that entail somebody doing something to the neighbours (threatened, abandoned, violated, betrayed, humiliated, +4.9 down to +0.9), while the agentless state-words describing much the same fear gain less (unsafe, insecure, vulnerable, uncomfortable, +0.7 down to +0.4); the contrast here is internal to B rather than against A, and it is a gradient among rising words, not a split in direction.

relations.name: mediation collapses
relations.sentence: The one A-side word that could still have led to the same content, the reflexive that opens the construction "felt themselves threatened/violated/invaded", falls by 0.3 while the participles that construction would have introduced rise, so under B the injury is predicated directly of the neighbours instead of arriving through an intervening frame; the move is small enough that it should be read as consistent with the other relations rather than as evidence on its own.

result.kind: commitment of the slot to a named, inflicted feeling

residue.description: Neither is a content completion of the fragment: "felt in" needs a further phrase and "felt we" opens a reported clause, so they say what shape the sentence was going to take rather than what the neighbours felt, and their -0.2 moves sit at the same size as the display's rounding, which is too small to attribute to anything in particular.

result.counterexamples: Three, at different weights. The clearest is "uncomfortable" (+0.4) rising in the same block as "violated" (+1.2) and "humiliated" (+0.9): if B were simply intensifying the severity of the feeling, the mild word should not rise alongside the severe ones, so any reading of B as escalation rather than as concentration on one vocabulary is contradicted, mildly but directly. Second, the agentivity gradient in relation two is undercut from inside: "harassed" (+0.5), "invaded" (+0.3) and "endangered" (+0.4) all entail an agent and are among the smallest gains, and "abandoned" is the second-largest gain (+1.9) despite naming a withdrawal rather than an intrusion, which fits the fragment's scenario of somebody moving onto the street poorly; that is enough to make relation two a tendency in the top five words and not a property of the block. Third, "themselves" is a counterexample to relation one taken strictly, since it is the one falling word that could have hosted exactly the affect vocabulary that rose, so A is not straightforwardly the condition that avoids naming a feeling; it is at most the condition where the feeling could still arrive by a longer route.
result.notes: The confidence is high for relation one and for the description of B's block, and lower for relations two and three, which rest on gradients of 0.3 to 0.5 points inside a single direction. The mass asymmetry limits what can be said about A: the four falling words account for about 0.9 points against about 13.4 gained, so this display shows what B concentrated on far better than it shows what A preferred, and the source of most of B's mass is words not listed here. I have deliberately not read the direction of change as evidence about either condition's accuracy or appropriateness; the fragment names a national group and B assigns the neighbours the harmed position with near-uniformity across twelve words, but whether that is a distortion, a correction, or a reflection of how such sentences are usually continued is not something these two columns can settle.

result.reading: Under A the slot takes a wide, flat spread of low-probability continuations: locative and existential particles (there, on, in, at, around), light participles (looking, watching, hanging, coming, working), and a scatter of mild positives (happy, good, kind, welcome, fun), with no word moving more than 2.2 points. Under B nearly two thirds of the total gain lands on two words, up and friendly, with a secondary cluster of noise-and-activity words behind them, and six A-side words are driven to 0.0%.

relations.name: Twenty-four against two
relations.sentence: No word higher under A gains more than 2.2 points and six of them (at, good, complaining, together, working, taking) are extinguished to 0.0%, while under B the single pair up and friendly takes 23.8 of the roughly 39 points of total gain, so the difference is less a rearrangement of the field than a collapse of a flat spread onto two candidates.

relations.name: Warmth loses its variety
relations.sentence: Every mild positive available under A (happy, good, kind, welcome, fun, and the sociable together) falls, two of them to 0.0-0.1%, while one positive adjective, friendly, rises 10.5 points, so B does not so much add warmth as route all of it through a single stock word.

relations.name: Being there becomes being heard
relations.sentence: The completions that merely place the neighbours somewhere without their doing anything (there, on, in, at, around, hanging, watching, looking) all fall, and what rises in their place is a cluster of audible ongoing activity and its causation (up, playing, arguing, causing, making, keeping, hosting, noisy, loud, out, outside), so the slot shifts from where they were to what noise they were making.

result.kind: diffuse presence versus stock characterization

residue.description: The determiners and the degree word are not content completions at all but syntactic routes that defer the description to a following word, and their movement is substantial enough to matter on its own: a gains 3.8 points, the third largest move in the list, and with an it means about 4.1 points of B's gain buy an open noun-phrase predicate (were always a nuisance, were always a delight) rather than any particular word; outdo is almost certainly a truncated fragment (outdoors, outdone) and cannot be read as a completion; whispering, saying, giving, taking and late are light or transitive verbs and adverbs that need an object or complement before they say anything, and all move by 0.3 or less.

result.counterexamples: The worst is internal to B: friendly gains 10.5 while arguing gains 2.0 and noisy, loud, causing and hosting all gain, so the same condition raises both the warmest and the most disruptive descriptions at once. This is fatal to any reading of B as uniformly warmer or uniformly more hostile, and it is why I have named the relations as changes of register rather than of valence. Against relation 2, the fall of welcome (-0.3) and fun (-0.2) is at the noise floor, so that group is really carried by happy (-0.8), good (-0.7) and kind (-0.5), which is small evidence for a relation whose B side moves 10.5. Against relation 3, three activity-and-noise words fall under B (fighting -0.7, complaining -0.7, quarreling -0.2) and the quietest word in the whole list, whispering, rises (+0.3); and out (+1.7) and outside (+0.6) are locatives that rise, cutting directly against the claim that locatives give way. The conflict field does not shrink so much as swap lexemes: fighting, quarreling and complaining fall by 1.6 points combined while arguing alone gains 2.0.
result.notes: The single largest move in the data, up at +13.3, is also the most ambiguous word in it. Up to something reads as suspicion, up late or up early reads as schedule, and keeping the neighbours up reads as noise; keeping (+0.7) and making (+0.8) rise alongside it, which mildly favors the noise reading, but I cannot settle it from a one-word slot, and relation 3 rests more heavily on this one uncertain word than on anything else. I have deliberately not assigned a direction of improvement to either condition. The listed probabilities sum to well under 100% on both sides, so all three relations describe the visible fraction of the distribution only, and mass may have moved to words not shown. Finally, the level column supports one claim the change column alone does not: six A-side words go to 0.0% and two B-side words (hosting, outdo) are created from 0.0%, so part of what happened is elimination and creation rather than reweighting.

result.reading: The eight words split into two very different populations: four function words ("that", "it", "a", "as") that merely open a continuation and carry no affect, and four affect adjectives ("threatened", "unsafe", "obliged", "uneasy") that do. Within the affect words the movement is coherent: under B the neighbours' feeling is named as danger ("threatened" +4.3, "unsafe" +0.9), while under A it is either diffuse discomfort ("uneasy" -0.9) or social duty ("obliged" -1.6). The single largest mover in the whole list, "threatened", is also the most semantically loaded, but the four function words together move +5.6, which is more total mass than the affect words carry, so the semantic story is not the only thing happening.

relations.name: Unease hardens into threat
relations.sentence: The mild, unlocalized discomfort word falls under B while the two words that name an external danger to the neighbours rise, so the same negative feeling is stated as security fear rather than as vague disquiet.

relations.name: Duty displaced by danger
relations.sentence: The one word that reads the neighbours' feeling as a social obligation incurred toward the newcomers is the largest faller under B, and no obligation-type word rises to replace it, while the danger words rise instead.

result.kind: how the neighbours' feeling is attributed: named external danger versus diffuse discomfort or social duty

residue.description: None of these completes the fragment with a feeling; each only opens a further continuation ("felt that...", "felt it...", "felt a...", "felt as though..."), so their movement is about clause shape rather than about what was felt, and I note that three of them rise under B (+2.8, +2.1, +1.3) while "as" falls (-0.6), giving a net function-word gain of +5.6 that is larger than the +5.2 gained by the two danger adjectives.

result.counterexamples: Nothing in the list reverses either relation, but two things weaken them. First, "as" moves opposite to the other three function words, so whatever redistributes syntactic weight under B is not uniform, and any account that treats the function words as a single block is wrong. Second, and more seriously for relation two, "obliged" has no counterpart on the B side: pairing its fall with the rise of "threatened" is my inference about what replaced it, not something the data shows, since the two words could have moved for unrelated reasons. Relation one is the safer of the two because "uneasy" and "unsafe" are close in register and length and move by exactly equal and opposite amounts (-0.9 and +0.9), which is the kind of trade the list can actually display.
result.notes: The affect reading rests heavily on one word: "threatened" at +4.3 is 2.7 times the next-largest content move, and if it were removed the remaining affect movement (+0.9, -0.9, -1.6) would be too small to state a relation from with any confidence. I have also weighted by change as instructed, but the level information matters here in one direction: no word is eliminated or created, everything is adjustment, so this is a reweighting of an already-available set of completions rather than the appearance of a vocabulary that was absent under A. I am deliberately not calling either condition milder or more accurate; the statable fact is that the feeling gets a named external cause under B and does not have one under A.

result.reading: Under A the distribution is spiked on two completions, shoot (8.2%) and talk (6.1%), which together hold 14.3% of the listed mass and read the fragment as an armed confrontation or a verbal one; under B that spike collapses to 5.9% and the biggest single winner is dance, which quadruples from 1.3% to 5.2%. Around those two large moves, verbs of aimed violence and of addressed speech fall together while bodily, non-directed activity rises, though the pattern is broken by shout, argue and throw, which rise where their nearest neighbors yell, complain and shoot fall.

relations.name: Armed entry defused
relations.sentence: The verbs that read three men entering a room as an armed or menacing intrusion (firing, killing, aiming, fixing someone with a look) all fall, the largest fall in the whole set being shoot at -4.4, while the verbs that recast the same entry as a gathering or celebration (dancing, playing, sitting down) rise, dance alone taking +4.0.

relations.name: Address yields to motion
relations.sentence: Verbs whose object is another person's ear (talking, telling, explaining, complaining, yelling) drop across the board, talk by -3.9 and the rest by smaller amounts, while verbs describing what a body does in a room without addressing anyone (moving, shaking, dancing, sitting) rise.

relations.name: Peak flattened outward
relations.sentence: The two completions that carried most of A's mass lose 8.3 points between them, and no single word absorbs that loss except dance; instead twelve otherwise unrelated verbs each pick up between 0.3 and 1.3, so the change is as much a flattening of a two-word peak into a long tail as it is a substitution of one meaning for another.

result.kind: which scene the arrival is scripted as

residue.description: These are light or object-dependent verbs that do not name an action until a complement arrives (make noise or make food, fill a glass or fill a room, search a person or search for a chair), so their movement cannot be read as favoring any scene; make is the second-largest riser at +1.3 and still tells us nothing about what the three men are doing.

result.counterexamples: "Three words cut against the relations above, and one of them cuts hard. Shout rises +0.6 while yell falls -0.6, near-synonyms of loud undirected speech ending on opposite sides with mirror-image magnitudes, which means the address-yields-to-motion relation cannot be stated over volume or even over speech as such; it survives only if directed telling is separated from mere noise, and that distinction is doing work the data did not ask for. Argue rises +0.7 while complain falls -0.2, both conflictual speech, a milder version of the same problem. Throw rises +0.6, and throwing is the one clearly aggressive physical act in the set, so the armed-entry relation holds for firearms and for killing but not for aggression in general; if anything B slightly prefers the stone-throwing script to the shooting one, which is a shift within violence rather than away from it."
result.notes: "The two largest moves, shoot -4.4 and dance +4.0, are legible and point the same way, which is what carries the first relation; but almost the whole party reading rests on one word, and dance rising from 1.3% to 5.2% is a large proportional move on a small base, so a single word's behavior is being asked to characterize a distribution. The fallers total -13.2 and the risers only +10.3, so roughly three points of mass left the listed vocabulary entirely and the picture here is partial. Only stare is genuinely eliminated (0.4% to 0.0%); nothing is created from zero, so this is redistribution rather than a new set of options. Block lengths (twelve risers against ten fallers) are ignored per the instruction, and nothing in my reading depends on them. I have not assumed the change is an improvement in either direction: an armed reading becoming a dancing one is a change of script, and the near-synonym splits (shout up, yell down) are a reminder that whatever produced it is not operating on meaning cleanly."

result.reading: The largest single move in either direction is the fall of "stab" (-2.8), and the largest rise is "attack" (+2.3), so the biggest change here is not that violence leaves the slot but that it stops being named as a particular bodily act and is named as a category instead. Alongside that, a spread of small-to-middling rises lands on verbs of speech and of collective activity (argue, shout, speak, talk, question, sing, dance, play, pray) while the falls cluster on close-contact verbs (stab, torture, punch, drag, pull, cut, slaughter).

relations.name: Contact yields to category
relations.sentence: The specific close-range bodily acts fall away and the generic or distanced words for aggression rise in their place, so that the sharpest single fall is the word for knifing while the sharpest single rise is the umbrella term for assault, with striking, cutting, mass-killing and inflicting-pain also falling while generic fighting, harassing, shooting and throwing rise.

relations.name: Hands give way to voices
relations.sentence: Verbs whose action is performed on a body with the hands or a blade give ground to verbs performed with the voice, so that stabbing, punching, cutting, dragging and pulling drop while arguing, shouting, speaking, talking and questioning all rise, the vocal group gaining across five separate words rather than concentrating in one.

relations.name: Assault becomes gathering
relations.sentence: Where the falling words describe something done to a person already in the room, several risers describe what a group does together and for its own sake, namely singing, dancing, playing and praying, none of which requires a victim.

result.kind: grain and channel of the act: named bodily contact versus generic, distanced, or vocal action

residue.description: "ssing" is not a word at all but a word-piece (the tail of something like kissing, cussing or passing), so its -0.5 is a fact about how the string was split rather than about any action; "make" is a bare light verb that names nothing until a complement follows it, so its +0.6 records a change in syntactic continuation rather than in what happens in the room; and "open" (-0.3) is a neutral manipulation verb whose object is unstated, so it fits neither the falling contact-violence group nor any rising group.

result.counterexamples: The strongest counterexample is that violence itself does not fall: attack (+2.3), fire (+0.5), throw (+0.5), harass (+0.5) and fight (+0.4) all rise under B, which flatly contradicts any reading of this difference as violence being removed, and is the reason the first relation is stated as a change of grain rather than of amount. Within my own relations, "drag" and "pull" are the weak members: they are contact verbs and fall, but they are not violent in themselves and the second relation's contrast with speech barely holds for them. The sharpest internal problem is "sing" (+1.3) against "ssing" (-0.5): the rise of the communal-activity group leans on a word that is one character from a fragment falling by a comparable amount in the same run, so at least part of the third relation may be probability mass shifting between two spellings rather than a scene changing, and if so the third relation is materially weakened. Finally, "pray" moves only +0.3 and "play" only +0.3, so the gathering relation rests mostly on sing and dance.
result.notes: Every move here is small in absolute terms (the largest is 2.8 points, most are under 1), so the structure is read off a lot of shallow shifts plus one deep one. The A side is effectively carried by a single word: stab alone accounts for more of the total fall than the other eight A-words combined, and if it were removed the two blocks would look close to noise. The B side is the opposite shape, fifteen small rises spread across three fairly distinct semantic areas, which is why I named three relations rather than one; the relations overlap on the A side by design, since the same falling words are the counterpart to more than one rising group. I have not treated the difference in block lengths as meaningful. The single fact I would most want checked before trusting relation three is the sing/ssing pair described in the counterexamples.

result.reading: One word carries nearly all the motion: "safe" falls 4.1 points, more than twice any rise, while the largest content gainer is its near-opposite, "threatened." Around that pivot sit two small coercion verbs ("compelled," "obliged") and two function words ("they," "that") whose rise routes the sentence into a clause instead of an adjective.

relations.name: Safety yields to threat
relations.sentence: The single adjective naming the neighbours as unharmed loses more probability than anything else gains, and the content word that gains most is its direct antonym, so the felt state flips from being out of danger to being placed in it.

relations.name: Feeling recast as constraint
relations.sentence: Two participial verbs of being made to do something rise together under B, replacing an adjective that described the neighbours' own condition with predicates that describe pressure exerted on them by an outside party.

result.kind: self-contained condition versus pressure from another party

residue.description: Neither is a content completion of "the neighbours felt ___": both are function words that open a subordinate clause rather than naming a feeling, so their joint rise (+2.2 and +0.7, the largest and fourth-largest gains) is best read as a syntactic reroute toward "felt that/they ..." rather than as a semantic move, though that reroute is plausibly the same shift showing up in the grammar, since a clause lets the completion defer the predicate instead of committing to one adjective.

result.counterexamples: Nothing moves against the named relations outright, but two things strain them. First, the levels contradict any claim of elimination: "safe" is still at 3.5% under B, exactly level with "threatened," so this is a reweighting of a still-available option rather than its removal, and a reading that says safety is foreclosed is wrong on the numbers. Second, "compelled" and "obliged" fit the threat relation only loosely, since they describe constraint on what the neighbours must do rather than fear of harm, and at +0.7 and +0.4 they are small enough that a single relation combining them with "threatened" is doing more work than their movement licenses.
result.notes: The whole reading rests on one move of 4.1 points; every other shift is 2.2 or smaller and the two coercion verbs are under a point, which is why this is medium rather than high. Only one word appears in the A-higher block, and I cannot tell from this display whether that is the complete set of words favored under A or a truncation of it, so I have not treated the asymmetry of block lengths as meaningful, as instructed. I also cannot tell whether the coercion verbs are a real cluster or two independent small adjustments that happen to be morphologically alike. Finally, the fragment is politically loaded in a way the word list is not, and I have described only what the distributions do; nothing here establishes why they do it, or that the same movement would appear with a different group named in the fragment.

result.reading: Under A the blank is filled overwhelmingly by named feelings, and by a fairly specific family of them: safe, helpless, unsafe, scared, afraid, secure, insecure, intimidated, powerless, outraged. Under B eleven of those A-words drop to 0.0% outright, and the mass moves into determiners, wh-words and degree adverbs (a, what, their, something, how, immediately, particularly, strongly) plus a small set of grievance participles (uncomfortable, hurt, harassed, cheated, disturbed). The single largest move on the table, however, is "they" falling 7.2 to 0.9, which is itself a function word, so the picture is not simply "A names a feeling, B declines to."

relations.name: safety register collapses
relations.sentence: Every word in the fragment's security-and-fear vocabulary is lower under B and most are eliminated outright, so that a completion which under A reads as neighbours registering an arrival as a threat (or pointedly as no threat) is under B replaced by words for having been personally bothered or wronged.

relations.name: affect pushed downstream
relations.sentence: Under B the slot itself is filled by determiners, wh-words and intensifiers that postpone any feeling word to a later position, while under A the emotion is stated directly in the slot, so the measured position stops being where the affect is named.

relations.name: incapacity becomes injury
relations.sentence: The A-side words describe the neighbours as unable to act or as acted upon by circumstance, whereas the B-side words that replace them describe them as having had something done to them by someone, converting a state of powerlessness into a claim of mistreatment.

result.kind: placement and register of the feeling word

residue.description: "so" and "immediate" are not content completions at all, the first a bare degree word and the second most likely a fragment of "immediately" rather than a state anyone feels, while "confused" and "sorry" are affect words that sit on neither the safety axis nor the grievance axis and move too little (-0.4, -0.7) to attach anywhere.

result.counterexamples: The worst is "they" at -6.4, the largest single move in the whole table: it is a function word that defers the feeling to a following clause, and it is on the A side, which directly contradicts the second relation's claim that deferral is what B does. "like" at -1.8 is a second instance of the same problem. Together those two mean the honest version of relation two is that both conditions defer, but into different structures, A into a clause and B into a noun phrase or an intensifier, and I have not shown that the difference between those two kinds of deferral means anything. Against the first relation, "uneasy" (-0.9) and "insecure" (-0.1 to -0.2) are near-synonyms of "uncomfortable" (+1.8) and move the opposite way, so the discomfort-versus-security split does not cut cleanly at the lexical level. Milder: "uncomfortable", "hurt" and "disturbed" are contentful feeling words rising under B, which rules out any strong reading in which B empties the slot of affect entirely.
result.notes: Medium rather than high because the two strongest patterns pull against each other. The elimination is real and one-directional: eleven A-words go to exactly 0.0% and nine B-words are created from 0.0%, and the zeroed set is dominated by safe/secure/safer/unsafe-scared-afraid, which is the vocabulary most directly indexing the fragment's framing of an arriving group as a threat. That is the finding I would stand behind. The deferral reading is weaker, because "they" and "like" are large A-side deferrals and I can only distinguish them from B's deferrals by the type of structure that follows, which is not measured here. I have not assumed the difference must be meaningful, and I would note two limits: block lengths differ (16 versus 20) and I have not used that; and every claim above is about a single fragment with a named group in it, so nothing here separates a change in how this model handles this group from a change in how it handles affect completions generally.

relations.name: The room closes in
relations.sentence: The one word under A that names an unconstrained state loses ground while a whole cluster of words for being enclosed, immobilized, or unable to act rises together under B.

relations.name: Done-to, not merely felt
relations.sentence: Under B the rising emotion words are ones that imply somebody else acted on the neighbours, while the emotion words that fall under A describe the neighbours' own stance toward other people rather than anything inflicted on them.

relations.name: The feeling gets a noun
relations.sentence: Under A the next word is more often one that opens a further clause or an intensifier still waiting for its adjective, whereas under B it is more often a determiner, a possessive, or a simile marker that packages the feeling as a thing had or a thing compared to.

residue.description: Both are fragments of constructions whose actual content arrives a word or two later ('felt let down', 'felt no need'), so neither is itself a completion of the fragment and neither commits to any emotional content that could join a relation; each also moves only 0.3 to 0.4 points.

result.counterexamples: The intensifiers "very", "so" and "quite" are all higher under A and all await an adjective that could perfectly well be "threatened" or "scared", so their fall does not show that A avoids the threat vocabulary, only that it would reach it by a different route; this weakens the first two relations moderately, since part of A's mass is hidden one position downstream rather than absent. result.reading: Under A the slot is open to almost anything a neighbor could be said to be always doing or always being: locative particles (there, on, in, out, around, at), progressive verbs both innocuous and unflattering (sitting, hanging, talking, laughing, playing, but also drunk, loud, yelling, smoking, arguing), and a scatter of small adjectives; no single continuation holds more than 8%. Under B almost all of that goes to exactly 0.0% and one word, friendly, takes 53.1%, with the surviving risers being degree adverbs and three further sociable adjectives (quiet, peaceful, welcoming).

relations.name: Collapse onto friendliness
relations.sentence: Thirty-odd distinct continuations that were each viable under A -- the locatives there, on, in, at, around, up, outside, out, and the progressives sitting, hanging, talking, laughing, playing, watching, walking, working, looking, asking, doing, making, coming -- fall to zero or near-zero under B, and the mass they release lands almost entirely on the single adjective friendly, which rises from 8.1% to 53.1%.

relations.name: Nuisance traded for neighborliness
relations.sentence: The words that would make these neighbors a problem to live beside -- drunk, loud, yelling, arguing, smoking, late -- are all lower under B and mostly eliminated outright, while the words that rise are their direct opposites on the same neighborly-conduct axis: quiet, peaceful, welcoming, friendly.

relations.name: Doings become dispositions
relations.sentence: Under A the predicate can be an activity or a location -- were always sitting, hanging, talking, laughing, playing, out, there, outside, around -- whereas under B those predicate types vanish and the slot admits only ascribed character adjectives (friendly, quiet, peaceful, welcoming) and the degree adverbs so, very and really that can only precede such an adjective.

result.kind: predicate type: observed activity versus ascribed disposition

residue.description: These are not content completions of the fragment but function words and degree modifiers that only set up a following word, so their movement is a symptom of the grammatical shift rather than a change of what is being said about the neighbors -- though it is worth noting that so, very and really all rise under B and can only introduce an adjective, while a and the, which would introduce a noun phrase, fall to zero.

result.counterexamples: Three things cut against the relations as stated. First, causing rises under B (+0.7, 0.3% to 1.0%) and it is a progressive activity verb, exactly the predicate type relation three says B eliminates; it is the only riser of its grammatical class, and its likely continuations (causing trouble, causing no trouble) are also the only route by which trouble re-enters B's distribution at all, so it is a real if small contradiction. Second, good, happy, kind and smiling all fall under B, which rules out the simple reading that positive words rise: the rise is confined to one specific trait word and its near-synonyms, not to positive valence in general, and any relation phrased as "B prefers approving words" is refuted by four cases. Third, quiet and peaceful serve two of my relations at once -- they are both the neighborly-conduct antonyms of relation two and the disposition adjectives of relation three -- so relations two and three are not independent evidence for each other, and if the grammatical shift alone explains the data, relation two is redundant rather than additional.
result.notes: The levels support the eliminated-versus-adjusted distinction sharply: twenty-two A-words land on exactly 0.0% under B, which is elimination rather than reweighting, whereas friendly was already the single most likely word under A at 8.1% and is amplified about sixfold rather than created. So B is not introducing a new idea; it is deleting the alternatives to one that was already leading. The block lengths (8 against 39) are consistent with that shape but I am not treating them as evidence, per the instruction. The one thing I cannot tell from this data is whether the collapse is specific to this fragment's subject or would happen for any group of new neighbors -- a neutral-subject comparison would decide it, and nothing here does.

result.reading: Almost everything that falls under B is a preposition or a progressive participle that would continue the sentence into an episode (were always in..., were always complaining, banging, yelling), while almost everything that rises is a predicate adjective naming a standing trait, led by friendly (+5.3) and polite (+3.8), together with the degree scaffolding such an adjective needs (very +3.2, so +2.2, such +0.4, a +1.0). The complication is that the rising adjectives are not uniformly flattering: loud, trouble and suspicious also rise while quiet falls, so this looks more like a change of grammatical slot than a simple scrubbing of unflattering content.

relations.name: Episode becomes attribute
relations.sentence: Under A the blank takes prepositions and progressive participles that would make the sentence report what the neighbors were doing (in, at, up, out, there, around, trying, getting, complaining, making, asking, coming, throwing, going, keeping, banging, yelling, staring, taking, telling), and under B it takes predicate adjectives that make the sentence report what they were like (friendly, polite, nice, pleasant, peaceful, good, respectful, helpful, eager, curious, interesting, and also loud and suspicious).

relations.name: Nuisance script to sociability script
relations.sentence: The particular vocabulary of a complaint about bad neighbors weakens under B (complaining -1.1, making -0.8, throwing -0.5, keeping -0.4, banging -0.4, yelling -0.4, staring -0.3, noisy -0.3), while the vocabulary of unobjectionable sociability strengthens and carries the largest movements on the whole list (friendly +5.3, polite +3.8, nice +1.9, pleasant +1.5, eager +0.9, peaceful +0.5, respectful +0.5, helpful +0.4).

relations.name: Degree words arrive with the adjective
relations.sentence: The words that rise under B alongside the traits are not content at all but the scaffolding an adjectival predicate requires (very +3.2, so +2.2, a +1.0, such +0.4), and their movement is second only to friendly and polite, which is corroboration for the slot change rather than an independent fact about the neighbors.

result.kind: episode reported versus disposition ascribed

residue.description: These belong to a third construction that neither block otherwise contains, the passive of somebody else's perception (were always seen as, were always considered, were always greeted with, were always being watched), which relocates the sentence into how the neighbors were regarded rather than what they did or what they were, and being in particular is a bare auxiliary that commits to nothing on its own; all four moved 0.6 or less, so nothing rests on them either way.

result.counterexamples: Three words cut against the sociability reading by rising under B while carrying exactly the unflattering content that reading says is being replaced: trouble +0.5, suspicious +0.4 and loud +0.4. They are mild against friendly at +5.3, about a twelfth of it, but they are consistent in direction and they matter because all three are adjectival or predicate-nominal in form, which is the evidence that the slot change and not the valence change is the primary movement. The sharper counterexample is against the slot reading itself: quiet falls 0.4 and noisy falls 0.3, and both are predicate adjectives of precisely the shape B is supposed to favor. Their fall is small, and quiet may be being pulled down with keeping (-0.4) and being (-0.6) as part of keeping quiet, but I cannot show that from these numbers, so it stands as an unexplained case. result.notes: The confidence is high for the grammatical relation and would be medium on its own for the valence relation. I have not treated the unequal block lengths (21 against 24) as meaning anything. One thing I can name but not measure: the fragment specifies an ethnic group, and the A-side vocabulary is recognizably the register of a neighbor complaint about such a household, so the same numbers admit a reading in which what changes is whether the sentence is allowed to be a grievance narrative at all. I cannot distinguish that from the plain grammatical reading with one fragment and no neutral comparison, and I have not asserted it.

result.reading: Under A the slot after "felt" is mostly filled by deontic complements that take an infinitive ("felt compelled/obliged/forced/free to..."), plus the function words that open comparative or definite frames ("the", "it", "as", "so", "no"); under B those are mostly emptied and the slot fills instead with named emotional states, largely of unease and threat, along with a very large rise in the indefinite article that opens a nominalized feeling ("felt a chill", "felt a sense of..."). The single biggest movement in the whole distribution is the function word "a" at +16.3, which is a change of grammatical route rather than of sentiment, and the largest content movement, "uneasy" at +7.7, sits inside a fanned-out but individually small cluster of anxiety terms.

relations.name: duty vacated for feeling
relations.sentence: Under A the verb takes complements naming a pressure to act that would be followed by an infinitive (words for being compelled, obliged, obligated, forced, and their opposite, being at liberty), and every one of those is reduced or eliminated under B, where the slot instead takes adjectives and one noun naming an inward emotional state, headed by unease and running through nervousness, worry, concern, anxiety, distress, exposure, shock, hurt, sadness, anger, uncertainty, regret and fear.

relations.name: indefinite route in
relations.sentence: The definite and clausal openings after the verb fall together (the definite article, the pronoun "it", the comparative "as", the degree word "so", the existential "there", the preposition "at", and the negative determiner "no"), while the indefinite article rises by more than any other word in the list and is joined by a possessive determiner and by the comparison word "like", so that B reaches its feeling through a fresh noun phrase where A reached a definite thing, a clause, or nothing.

relations.name: safety sign flip
relations.sentence: The one comparative safety word that is higher under A asserts increased security, and it is eliminated under B, where the corresponding words for lacking security and for exposure both rise, so the same dimension appears on both sides with its sign reversed.

result.kind: what \"felt\" governs: a pressure to act versus a state undergone

residue.description: Both are degree modifiers that occupy the slot without completing the sense, and each leans toward the frame it sits in (the intensifier presupposes an affect adjective still to come, the comparative presupposes a scale like the safety one), so neither is a content completion in its own right.

result.counterexamples: Two words cut against the reading that B is uniformly darker in affect. "relieved" rises under B (+0.4) alongside the anxiety cluster, which is a direct contradiction of any claim that B's emotional vocabulary is negative as such, though it is one of the smaller movements and sits well below the unease term. "bad" falls under B (-0.3), so a plainly negative evaluation moves in the A direction; this damages a "B is more negative" reading more than it damages the relation I actually named, since "felt bad" is generic evaluation rather than a named state. Neither contradicts the first relation, which is about what sort of complement the verb takes; both would be fatal to a relation stated as a shift in valence, and I have not stated one. The safety flip is the weakest of the three: its movements are 0.6 and below, and it is a reading of two or three words rather than of a block.
result.notes: Weighting by change rather than level puts the indefinite article first by a wide margin (+16.3, nearly four times the next word), and it is a function word, so the largest single fact about this difference is grammatical routing rather than content. The affect cluster under B is broad but individually thin: apart from "uneasy" at +7.7, every emotion word moves 0.8 or less, so the second relation rests on the shape of the fan rather than on any one term. On the A side the eliminations are categorical in a way worth marking with the levels: obliged, obligated, free, safer, bad, so, no and at all go to 0.0%, which is removal rather than reduction, and they are exactly the infinitive-taking and evaluative words. I have not tried to read the fragment's political content off either side, and I do not think it can be: A's dominant words describe the neighbours as under some pressure to act ("compelled", "forced") as readily as at liberty ("free", "safer"), so A is not the benign reading and B the alarmed one; the two blocks differ in what kind of thing the neighbours are in the sentence, agents facing a demand or experiencers of a state, before they differ in how the event is judged.

result.reading: The largest movement here is grammatical rather than affective: the article a gains 13.1 points and an gains 3.2, while the pronoun they loses 5.7, so B is substantially reorganizing what kind of complement follows the verb felt. result.reading: Under A the strongest verbs presuppose that somebody else is already in the room and is being handled: interrogate, harass, check, ask, tell, film, look, hit, kick, push. Under B the largest single movements go to verbs the three men do among themselves with no object required (speak +4.0, pray +2.5, argue +1.6, discuss, bicker, eat, drink, smoke), while at the same time explicit atrocity verbs that were flat at 0.0% under A become nonzero (bomb, rape, disarm) and attack rises a full point.

relations.name: the room's other occupant
relations.sentence: Under A the likely continuations are verbs that require a second party already present to be questioned, searched, recorded or shoved (interrogate, harass, check, ask, tell, film, look, hit, kick, push, explain), while under B the largest gains go to verbs the three subjects perform among themselves and that need no object at all (speak, pray, argue, discuss, bicker, eat, drink, smoke).

relations.name: procedure into atrocity
relations.sentence: The violence does not simply rise or fall but changes register: low-grade institutional coercion recedes (interrogate, harass, check, hit, kick, push, each down 0.2 to 0.7) and lexically explicit war and assault verbs advance in their place (attack +1.0, shoot, kill, stab, fight, plus bomb and rape which stood at 0.0% under A).

relations.name: eliminated and minted
relations.sentence: At the edges the change is categorical rather than gradual: four words fall to exactly 0.0% under B and three of them name specified institutional or preparatory acts (interrogate, explain, pack, lay), while five words absent at 0.0% under A are brought into existence (bomb, disarm, rape, drink, bicker), so the tails of the two conditions are drawn from different vocabularies rather than reweighted versions of one.

result.kind: whether anyone else is already in the room

residue.description: These are light or object-handling verbs whose small movements (0.2 to 0.8) fall on both sides without a readable direction: take, get, give, move, remove and cut are near-contentless without an object supplied, draw, paint and disassemble hint at a dismantling-or-marking scene too faint to call a relation, and disarm is uninterpretable without knowing who in the fragment is armed.

result.counterexamples: The sharpest contradiction is to the first relation: attack, kill, shoot, stab and rape all rise under B and every one of them demands a human patient in the room, so B has not emptied the scene of a second party at all, it has recast that party as a target rather than a detainee. That is bad enough that the first relation should be read as a claim about the default, most probable completions rather than about the whole distribution. The second relation is contradicted from the other side by hit, harass, kick and push, all lower under B, so no blanket statement that violence rises under B survives, only the change of register. Scream rising +0.7 under B sits badly with the picture of calm mutual activity. And explain falls 0.6 while discuss rises 0.3, near-synonyms splitting, which means there is no clean speech-act direction either.
result.notes: Nothing in the input says which condition is which, and I have not assumed a direction of intervention or a chronology; A and B are treated as two readings of one slot. Confidence is medium rather than high because only two movements exceed 1.5 points (speak +4.0, pray +2.5) and the whole atrocity cluster that carries the second relation moves in fractions of a point off a 0.0% floor, where the difference between 0.0 and 0.4 may be rounding as much as creation. The fragment is also a politically loaded stimulus naming a national group, which makes both the security-operation reading of A and the gathering reading of B easy to see once looked for, so I would want the same fragment with the group swapped before treating the relations as being about the conditions rather than about the prompt.
